Beef Prices Are at Record Highs—But There’s a Smart Way You Can Save Cash and Score Quality Meat

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2715 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Editor’s Note: When I originally reported this article in 2014, a pound of ground beef cost roughly $3.50.
  • And, if you can spring for grass-fed beef, there’s been more recent published research to show that it might be healthier for you than the grain-fed variety.
  • Sources indicate that while eating healthier is great, doing so has to taste amazing too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s Note: When I originally reported this article in 2014, a pound of ground beef cost roughly $3.50. Now that same amount of protein costs you $6.75. But nothing about buying beef wholesale has changed: You will still save more money over time if you purchase an eighth, a quarter, a half, or even a whole cow given you have the upfront cash and deep freezer space to store it all. (A quarter of a cow from the same farm I purchased mine now costs $1,100, in case you were wondering.).

And, if you can spring for grass-fed beef, there’s been more recent published research to show that it might be healthier for you than the grain-fed variety. In 2022, South Korean researchers found that grass-fed beef contained a healthier fatty acid profile than grain-fed beef. Same goes for a 2026 study published in the Journal of Animal Science.

Sources indicate that while eating healthier is great, doing so has to taste amazing too. Luckily that hasn’t changed about grass-fed beef either.

THE COW I ate was born in rural Pennsylvania. Cathy Pomanti, the owner of Sugar Hill Farm, midwifed my calf into the world. Pomanti raises grass-fed organic Scottish Highland Cows, a shaggy breed yielding meat that’s among the tastiest on the planet. On one farm visit, my fiancee saw a highlander, went quiet, and then said, “I don’t want to eat them. I want to hug them.” But I was hungry for a cow to call my own.

As a pleasure-seeking meat eater, disappointed by grain-fed supermarket beef. Rib eyes require a slick of steak sauce to taste meaty. Ground beef has a tacky, greasy consistency. Tenderloin, even with tender care, always leaves me underwhelmed. So I decided to stop complaining about mass-market beef and find a rancher. I wanted to know my cattle producer. I wanted to know my cow.

Sources indicate that my cow never had a name; Pomanti can’t bring herself to name cows headed for slaughter. But he did have a good life. My cow spent his first 10 months growing strong on his mother’s milk, sticking close by her side. Then Pomanti separated my cow and his mother into different pens. My cow bawled. His mother mooed. It was for the best. Once Mom stopped producing milk, the two were reunited, but my cow now preferred delicious, nutritious grass.

Over the next year and a half, my cow grew an impressive coat of thick, coarse hair. Because he wouldn’t be subjected to the diseases and indignities of the industrial feedlot, he didn’t need antibiotics or growth hormones. Those substances wouldn’t end up in me or my fiancée, either.

Last October, my cow was loaded onto a truck and taken to Rising Spring Meat Company, an organic butcher outside State College, Pennsylvania. There he was held in a pen, calm and comfortable, until he was humanely shot in the head. The carcass was then halved and hung in a cooler to dry-age, a process that helps tenderize the meat, for about 14 days. Next my cow was cut into pieces, vacuum-sealed, and delivered to Pomanti.

In a recent development, she summoned me for the handoff. Out of her massive freezer units she pulled bags bursting with marrow bones, globular ground beef portions, and a tenderloin the size of Popeye’s forearm. I drove the box of beef back home that day, dreaming of meals to come, under a sky with clouds that looked like heifers.

Sources indicate that AS A TYPICAL American, you ate a hefty 51 pounds of beef last year, the USDA indicates. That’s roughly the equivalent of 65 T-bones or 204 quarter-pound burger patties.

Industry observers note that the National Cattlemen’s Beef Association notes that less than 1 percent of beef sold at retail is labeled as grass-fed. During the “finishing,” the animal begins to lay down more fat in relation to muscle and bone growth, notes Cindy Daley, Ph.D., who studies beef at California State University.

Recent findings suggest that until the 1950s, ranchers finished cattle exclusively on grass. But industrial producers realized that grain feeding improved fat marbling while cutting the days until slaughter. After decades of eating the stuff, we now prefer fattier beef. But at the same time, our rates of diseases linked to inflammation rose.

Recent findings suggest that could grain-fed cows and inflammation be connected? A 2011 Irish study found that people who replaced their regular red meat with three weekly servings of grass-fed red meat for a month improved their inflammation-fighting omega-3 fatty acid profiles by 37 percent over those of people who ate the same amount of grain-finished red meat.

Though the diet studies are too small to be conclusive, a 2010 research review led by Daley found that grass-fed beef outclassed grain-fed nutritionally, with triple the immune-boosting vitamin E, up to five times the heart-healthy omega-3 fatty acids, and seven times the antioxidant carotenoids.

In a recent development, if grass-fed beef was going to treat me better, I needed to return the favor. So I began contacting chefs. The recipes that follow taught me key kitchen skills, but they also taught me something deeper: If you know your beef, you love it even more.

THERE’S A CERTAIN comfort in dissociating yourself from the animal you’re eating for dinner. If you don’t think about where on the cow’s body the meat comes from, you don’t have to contemplate the death and dismemberment involved in its trip to your plate. The oxtail, however, made a very specific statement about its origins. It came to me in three pieces, which, because of my morbid curios- ity, I arranged to reconstruct the entire appendage. I imagined my cow using it to swat flies. It wasn’t simply a meal. It was a sacrifice.

According to recent reports, alice Waters, executive chef of Chez Panisse in Berkeley, California, and founder of the Edible Schoolyard Project, recommends cooking oxtail in a classic braise. “With grain-fed beef, you’re tasting a richness and tenderness, but it’s not the real flavor,” Waters claims. “It’s like cooking vegetables with a lot of butter: You can’t taste the vegetables.” Her technique, inspired by a recipe from Zuni Café in San Francisco, matches the beautiful beefiness of the rustic cut while also turning it fork-tender.

Bonus: You can apply the same braising technique to other tough bone-in cuts your purveyor may pass along, such as shanks or short ribs.

2 lb grass-fed oxtails1 Tbsp Kosher salt4 cups beef stock2 Tbsp olive oil1 ¾ cups red wine2 bay leaves1 small head garlic, halved crosswise1 sprig thyme3 black peppercorns1 large carrot, peeled and roughly chopped3 celery stalks, roughly chopped1 medium yellow onion, quartered1 cup drained canned tomatoes, roughly chopped.

Sources indicate that 1. For the best flavor, salt the oxtails two days before cooking.

It has been revealed that 2. Trim the oxtails of excess fat. In a medium saucepan, cook the stock over medium heat until reduced by half, about 30 minutes.

3. In a skillet, heat the oil on medium. Pat the oxtails dry and brown them, 3 to 4 minutes. Set aside. Wipe the skillet, add the wine, stir, and cook it down by half, about 5 minutes. Add the stock.

It has been revealed that 4. Preheat the oven to 300°F. In a roasting pan, add the remaining ingredients; add stock to cover by a third. Simmer on medium low. Cover.

5. Place the pan in the oven and cook 3 to 4 hours. Then crack the lid and cook until the meat is very tender, another 20 to 30 minutes. Serve oxtails with sauce. Makes 8 servings.

I NEEDED TO do something special with the most prestigious cut of my cow: the 14-pound standing rib roast. The meal should be special but also very simple, says Donald Link, owner and executive chef of Cochon and Butcher in New Orleans. Anything too fussy would only detract from its intense, glorious beefiness.

For maximum flavor, you want to cook this behemoth roast only to medium rare, Link told me. Because the cut is so large, the preparation and resting stages are critical. If the meat is too cold before it enters the oven, it’ll be raw in the center when it exits. If you carve into it immediately after cooking, you’ll lose a reservoir of delicious juices. Patience is paramount.

And the rewards are well worth the wait: “Good grass-fed beef tastes cleaner. You don’t have that heavy feeling in your gut after you eat it,” Link indicates. I heard similar accolades from the friends and family members I invited over to dinner. In fact, most people said the steaks, liver, or carne asada I’d served them tasted “like beefier beef” and “less greasy.” One guest who tasted the rib roast said she woke up the morning after our dinner fantasizing about the beef from the night before.

1 grass-fed beef rib roast (14 lb)Olive oil.

According to recent reports, 1. To promote even doneness, remove the roast from the refrigerator 2 hours before cooking.

Recent findings suggest that 2. Place the roast on a wire rack set on a baking sheet. The last 30 minutes prior to cooking, place a fan in front of the meat to dry excess moisture and foster caramelization.

It has been revealed that 3. Preheat the oven to 450°F. Lightly rub the roast on all sides with olive oil and then liberally coat it with salt and freshly ground pepper. Set it back on the wire rack atop the baking sheet and place it in the oven.

4. Cook until well browned on the outside, about 20 minutes. Lower the heat to 275°F and continue to cook until a digital thermometer inserted into the center of the roast reads 140°F, about 2 hours. Remove the roast and let it rest until it’s almost at room temperature, about 45 minutes.

5. Serve with roasted potatoes and a simple salad. Makes 20 to 25 servings.

OF THE 51 pounds of cow you ate last year, about half was ground. Here’s a scary fact: U.S. ground beef is not easily traced and may not even be from the United States, a 2013 review in Meat Science reveals. All the more reason to buddy up to a rancher.

In a recent development, you can make a grass-fed beef burger (I did), but you’d be depriving your tastebuds if you didn’t venture beyond familiar ground. “Grass-fed beef is very lean by nature. Grinding beef for burgers involves adding fat, and if you’re using grass-fed, you lose something,” claims Sang Yoon, executive chef of Father’s Office and Lukshon in L.A. That something, he says, is the herbaceous flavor imparted by the cow’s diet. Make larb instead, Yoon says. This Southeast Asian dish packs a barrage of fresh herbs to flatter grass-fed beef.

1 Tbsp uncooked jasmine rice6 Tbsp peanut oil12 oz grass-fed ground beef1 shallot, minced2 garlic cloves, sliced2 fresh Thai chiles, thinly sliced1 Tbsp palm sugar2 Tbsp fish sauce¼ cup lime juice1 head cabbage, leaves separated½ cilantro leaves½ mint leaves½ Thai basil leaves4 scallions, sliced.

According to recent reports, 1. In a small pan on medium heat, toast the rice, stirring often. Cool and grind the rice to a fine powder in a clean coffee or spice grinder.

According to recent reports, 2. In a wok or big cast-iron skillet, heat the oil on medium high until it shimmers. Add the beef; cook, stirring occasionally, until it begins to brown, 2 to 3 minutes. Add the shallot, garlic, chiles, palm sugar, and fish sauce.

3. Remove from the heat and add the lime juice and rice powder. Stir well and season with salt.

4. Let the mixture cool slightly before serving. Spoon the mixture into individual cabbage cups and garnish with herbs and scallions. Makes 6 to 8 servings.

MARC FORGIONE, OWNER and executive chef of Restaurant Marc Forgione in Upcoming York City, told me I should start by not cooking the beef at all. “The best way to experience grass-fed beef, because it’s so lean, is to eat it raw,” notes Forgione.

Industry observers note that when I asked him if it was dangerous to eat DIY steak tartare, Forgione told me that as long as the beef is high in quality and its temperature never rises above 40°F for longer than 40 minutes, your risk of illness will be very low, he says. And Pomanti, for her part, says bacterial contamination among her cattle is vir- tually nonexistent. (It pays to know your source.).

So I sharpened my knives for a rare opportunity. The result was a luscious tartare that topped variations I’ve tasted at the country’s top steakhouses.

1 Tbsp minced onion1 Tbsp minced cornichons1 tsp minced parsley2 anchovies, minced½ Tbsp Dijon mustard2 or 3 dashes Tabasco sauce2 tsp Worcestershire sauce½ cup, plus 2 Tbsp olive oil1 lb grass-fed beef tenderloinWarm toast.

It has been revealed that 1. In a small bowl, mix the onion, parsley, cornichons, and anchovies. Reserve.

Recent findings suggest that 2. In a blender or food processor, add the mustard, Tabasco, Worcestershire, and 2 Tbsp olive oil. Puree, gradually adding the remaining olive oil until emulsified. Reserve.

Recent findings suggest that 3. Place the tenderloin in the freezer for about 5 minutes for easier cutting. Then, working swiftly, slice it into ¼-inch-thick pieces.

4. In a medium serving bowl, combine the meat with the reserved ingredients. Season with salt and pepper to taste. Mix well.

Recent findings suggest that 5. Chill in the fridge for 10 minutes before serving atop warm toast. Makes 8 servings as an appetizer.

According to recent reports, WHEN MY TOUR of the special cuts was complete, I dug for the last of the T-bones that were stashed aside the cow’s heart (yes, the heart) in the freezer. Steaks were the first cuts I cooked, and I still craved them. Naomi Pomeroy, the executive chef of Beast in Portland, Oregon, had taught me to sear them to a juicy medium rare. She’s a pro; she cooks grass-fed beef exclusively.

I preheated my oven to 350°F and placed a cast-iron skillet over medium heat. I cranked some freshly ground black pepper and scattered kosher salt over each side of the steak. Then I added a good knob of butter to the skillet, allowed it to melt, and followed it with the steak and a few sprigs of parsley and thyme. I listened for the sizzling to subside, awaiting the aroma of a baseball field on a hot summer day. Those signs told me it was time to flip the meat and then slide it into the oven, skillet and all. There it basked for five minutes until the interior temperature reached 122°F. Out of the oven it came. I then basted it reverently with the rest of the melted butter, tented some aluminum foil over the skillet, and let it rest for what seemed like an eternity. Okay, five minutes. And then I savored every last juicy, earthy, hearty, powerful, tender bite. The celebration of my cow was complete.

Yes, grass-fed beef costs more money than the grain-finished variety, but you’re making that investment to enjoy superior meat that is less fatty, more nutrient-dense, better for your body, and certainly better on the palate.

And if you purchase your grass-fed beef in bulk, so much the better. It can be less expensive than grass-fed cuts you’d find in the store, for one thing. There’s also something deeply comfort- ing about possessing a large amount of premium meat. (Zombie apocalypse be damned!) But because you know the life of your cow, and the rancher who raised that animal, you also want to honor that cow in death. It’s not just dinner. It’s your duty.

You can have a heart—and cook one, too.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›.

Apple’s $299 smart display has been sitting on my kitchen counter for about a week. It looks like a hybrid between an old-school iMac and a giant Apple Watch, but it’s a dedicated home for the recently revamped Siri. It’s an easy addition for anyone already committed to Apple gear. If your smart home runs on cameras, locks, or sensors that don’t work with Apple Home, though, you’ll want an upgrade plan before you buy one.

Recent findings suggest that the HomeView comes in two versions, and both cost $299 in the US. I tested the tabletop model, which mounts a 7-inch square touchscreen on a domed aluminum speaker base and includes a 30W power adapter and USB-C cable in the box. You can have it in any color you want, as long as it’s silver, starlight, rose pink, or space gray. The Apple HomeView (Wall Mounted) drops the base and its extra speaker hardware, as well as the starlight/rose pink color options, and the panel costs more to put on a wall than its sticker price suggests. It requires a Schneider Home mount sold separately, and those start at $59.95. The cheapest USB-C mount also needs a power adapter of at least 20W, which you’ll have to supply yourself.

The HomeView looks the way you’d expect an Apple product to look. Once you take off the protective coverings, the 2.1-pound, 6.82-inch tall device is pretty right out of the box. And it looks great between a breadbox and a butcher’s block, especially compared to an older smart screen that I’ve had there for years, which looks ancient next to it. A stainless steel hinge connects the screen to the base, so you can tilt the display toward wherever you’re standing. The screen stays firmly in place after you position it, even if you tap aggressively like I tend to. It doesn’t wobble or shake as you navigate on-screen menus.

Sources indicate that setting up the HomeView feels like setting up an iPhone or any other recent Apple device. It requires an iPhone running iOS 27.2 or later (or an iPad on iPadOS 27.2), so if your phone isn’t there yet, like mine wasn’t, you’ve got to stop and run the enhancement first. The HomeView played a soft, heavenly drone the whole time it waited, which is a much nicer way to sit through a software update than staring at a progress bar. Also, when you first boot things up, you might think you can immediately start asking for the kind of stuff you ask Siri on your iPhone, but you may have to go through a round or two of launching apps on the HomeView to give them permission to access your account even if your iPhone is with you.

According to recent reports, the HomeView’s Liquid Retina LED backlit screen has looked great in every lighting condition I’ve put it in. Apple rates the 1088-by-1088-pixel (220 ppi) display’s brightness between 0.3 and 500 nits, and that bottom end is what makes it work on a nightstand. In a dark kitchen, it reads as a soft glow instead of a floodlight.

Recent findings suggest that the multitouch True Tone touchscreen responds promptly, and it kept registering taps even when my fingers were slightly wet (even though the device doesn’t have a specific water-resistance rating). That’s a real advantage for a screen that spends its life in a kitchen.

Recent findings suggest that the upcoming, more conversational Siri AI on the HomeView is a big jump from the old Siri. The HomeView’s four-mic design ensures Siri can hear you from throughout the room and, when a paired Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone is nearby, it can pull from personal data. If you ask about an upcoming concert, it can also check the calendar on your Apple account and tell whether you’re actually free to go.

That personal access runs through the HomeView’s 12MP Center Stage camera. It can recognize up to six Home app-registered household members by face, and it only indicates someone’s personal information when it recognizes that person and their paired iPhone or iPad is on the same Wi-Fi network—with support for Wi-Fi 6E (802.11ax) with MIMO—and was recently unlocked. The HomeView’s A18 chip uses what Apple calls Secure Exclaves to process the camera and microphone feeds in a separate compartment, and Apple claims neither the operating system nor Apple itself can access it. Those safeguards are reassuring on paper, though they aren’t something I could independently verify while testing a smart display in my kitchen.

That reliance on a nearby iPhone or iPad is also the source of the HomeView’s most frustrating quirk. With my phone on me, Siri sometimes can’t decide which device should answer. The first few times I tried to set a simple timer, it turned into a dance between the HomeView and my phone before one of them finally took the request. It takes a little getting used to.

In a recent development, your iPhone also supplies a significant share of the HomeView’s apps. There’s no App Store on the device. It ships with 15 built-in apps, including Safari, FaceTime, Music, and Home, and it pulls a handful of other Apple apps, like TV and News, from your phone. So, if you don’t mind some severe letterboxing, you can watch TV and movies on there. Supported third-party audio and video apps show up from a paired iPhone, too, through a system that works a lot like CarPlay. If a service you rely on doesn’t support it, there’s no way to install it on the HomeView directly.

The HomeView’s main job is running your smart home, and that’s where my experience was most mixed. It controls accessories you’ve added to Apple Home, which includes supported HomeKit and Matter devices. My Ring cameras don’t integrate with Apple Home natively, so they never appeared in the HomeView’s Home Camera face, which can otherwise show up to nine live feeds at once. It worked easily with my smart lighting and other natively compatible devices.

Recent findings suggest that check whether your current cameras, locks, sensors, and thermostat show up in Apple Home before you initiative to run the whole house from this screen. If they don’t, budget for HomeKit or Matter replacements that do (and Apple has a whole suite of latest options developed alongside LG and Schneider Electric).

The actual smart hub interface that displays on screen is handy for keeping tabs on what’s going on in your home. It’s important to note that this thing looks like a thermostat when it’s on the wall, but it isn’t one. Maybe a future model with a built-in thermostat could free up some wall space.

The HomeView turned out to be a great cooking assistant. Once you open a recipe page on the web, either on your iPhone or in Safari on the HomeView, a Start Cooking button reformats it so you can follow the steps in real time while you work. Recipe pages vary wildly in how they’re formatted and coded, and I expected that mess to trip it up. It has worked without a problem every time I’ve used it so far.

According to recent reports, I made a fairly simple recipe for peanut butter noodles, and the instructions and timers were helpful and easy to use. More complicated recipes are more of a challenge, especially since you can’t really perform more than one step at a time, so don’t expect it to turn you into Gordon Ramsay overnight.

Industry observers note that as for the audio, the tabletop HomeView sounds full for its size. Its base holds a down-firing woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators, almost like a subwoofer in miniature (but without the extension), and the display adds two custom full-range down-firing drivers of its own. I’d been using an older Google smart display before this, and the jump in sound quality is obvious.

In separate tests, PopSci editor Tony Ware spent a couple of nights with his own HomeView and some of his favorite songs and came away with positive impressions. Compared to a HomePod mini, the beat hits more convincingly. While there’s not much room for excursion in the base, output manages to be surprisingly potent without sacrificing clarity. It won’t beat some recent whole-home audio-focused connected speakers (or Apple’s own full-sized 2nd-gen. HomePod, for that matter), but it’s plenty room-filling for such a compact, multipurpose enclosure. Whether you’re chopping carrots or choppin’ it up with friends, the HomeView is more than enough speaker for a smaller space.

What was more impressive was the airy, open presence of Dolby Atmos tracks from Apple Music, given the use of reflections and computational audio rather than an actual array of directional drivers. With accelerometers and Apple silicon adjusting the acoustic system’s EQ and output based on the screen’s tilt, the result is more incisive than immersive … how it will always be when you can’t surround yourself with speakers. Still, it projects clearly without sounding overly bright or edgy, which is good for podcasts to playlists.

There are occasional kinks, however. If you’re into spatial audio, the best way to ensure you’re getting the correct version of a track is to ask the HomeView to pull Apple Music directly from the cloud; sometimes the Dolby Atmos badge won’t pop up when you send a track from your phone over AirPlay, so you can’t be certain it’s not just stereo. Alternatively, you can hand off whatever is playing on your phone by bringing it close enough to the HomeView to get an AirDrop ripple animation and the album art to show up. Also, you might find yourself instinctively running your finger along the edge of the display looking for volume buttons, but there are no physical controls, which isn’t surprising from an aesthetic standpoint but still feels like a shortcoming.

The Apple HomeView makes the most sense on a nightstand, on the wall next to your thermostat, or in the kitchen. Its Photos face turns it into a digital picture frame, which keeps it from looking like a giant Apple Watch stuck to your wall or sitting on your table (though the clock faces are cute and colorful).

If your home already runs on an iPhone and Apple Home accessories, HomeView slots right in and puts it all on one screen you’ll actually want to look at. If you’ve built your smart home around gear that doesn’t work with Apple Home, however, strategy to replace it before you make the jump.

#121285. Breaking: Taking Fish Oil to Boost Brain Health? A 2-Year Study Questions the Benefits

Breaking: Taking Fish Oil to Boost Brain Health? A 2-Year Study Questions the Benefits

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1056 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A clinical trial found that taking high dose omega-3 supplements for 2 years did not help memory or thinking skills in older adults at increased risk of Alzheimer’s.Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC led the study, which was published in eBioMedicine.
  • Getting omega-3s from food or supplements is crucial since the body cannot make them.
  • Keck Medicine researchers enrolled 365 adults who did not have dementia, and whose ages ranged from 55 to 80, with an average age of 66.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A clinical trial found that taking high dose omega-3 supplements for 2 years did not help memory or thinking skills in older adults at increased risk of Alzheimer’s.Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC led the study, which was published in eBioMedicine. Participants took either a daily high dose supplement of omega-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) or a placebo.Fish oil is one of the most familiar ways people get omega-3s. However, the supplement in this clinical trial wasn’t made from fish, Hussein Yassine, MD, director of the USC Center for Personalized Brain Health with Keck Medicine of USC and the study’s lead researcher, told Healthline. This article uses the broader term omega-3 supplements.The researchers found that taking supplements raised omega-3 levels in participants’ brains, yet it didn’t change their memory, thinking skills, or brain structure.Dung Trinh, MD, an internist at MemorialCare Medical Group and chief medical officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, California, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings challenge the common belief that omega-3 supplements, such as fish oil, can help prevent Alzheimer’s disease or improve memory.Millions of older adults take omega-3 supplements. In a 2017–2018 federal survey, 21.8% of U.S. adults age 60 and older reported taking an omega-3 fatty acid supplement in the past 30 days, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Getting omega-3s from food or supplements is crucial since the body cannot make them.

Keck Medicine researchers enrolled 365 adults who did not have dementia, and whose ages ranged from 55 to 80, with an average age of 66.

Subjects obtained little DHA from their diets and had at least one risk factor for dementia. Of the 365 people who enrolled, 225 completed the trial, according to the study. Nearly half (47%) carried APOE4.Participants took either 2,000 milligrams (mg) of DHA or a placebo every day. Neither participants nor researchers knew who received the supplement.

The supplement in the trial contained more than 90% DHA and about 1% EPA, Yassine said.

Researchers found that high dose omega-3 supplements raised DHA levels in the fluid around the brain and spinal cord by 17%.

Sources indicate that both groups in the trial scored about the same on memory and thinking tests. Brain structure appeared the same in both groups.

Industry observers note that the supplement also raised omega-3 levels in the blood. Over two years, participants’ omega-3 index, a measure of EPA and DHA in red blood cells, rose from 4.9% to 11%.“That’s a massive increase, but that doesn’t translate into clinical outcomes,” Yassine said.DHA reached the brain equally well in people with and without the gene variant APOE4, which is linked to a higher risk of Alzheimer’s disease, according to the study.Earlier trials couldn’t tell whether DHA failed to reach the brain or reached it without helping, the study’s authors say. This trial answers that open question, since the DHA got there.“This tells us that just because a supplement reaches the brain doesn’t necessarily mean it will improve brain function or prevent cognitive decline,” Trinh said.

It has been revealed that the lack of measurable change in memory and thinking may come down to how the body uses omega-3s, according to Yassine.He mentioned it’s “really important to distinguish between omega-3 metabolism and omega-3 supplements.”A supplement can raise omega-3 levels, yet the body may still break them down before they reach the right places. Obesity, smoking, and a lack of exercise can all reduce how much omega-3 gets into the brain, he said.

Industry observers note that some fish and fish oil supplements may offer more than omega-3s. These sources may also include other nutrients such as lutein, vitamin E, and selenium, Yassine remarked.A supplement can raise the level, but if you don’t change the holistic program, just going and increasing the level by itself may not be sufficient,” he said.Researchers tend to fall into two camps on how to read the results, according to Yassine.

Some see the findings as evidence that supplements don’t work in isolation. Others argue the trial would need a longer follow-up or sicker participants to answer the question.Trinh pointed to the study’s length. “It’s also important to recognize that Alzheimer’s disease develops over decades, so a two-year study may not be long enough to determine whether DHA supplementation has any long-term preventive benefits,” he noted.

Fish oil supplements contain two omega-3 fatty acids, eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and DHA, according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH).

Foods such as fish and flaxseed also contain omega-3s, according to the National Institutes of Health’s Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS).Research suggests omega-3s may help reduce inflammation, support heart health, and promote childhood growth and development.

Some observational studies link diets high in omega-3s with a lower risk of cognitive decline and dementia.

It has been revealed that researchers say omega-3s may help preserve cognition by supporting brain cells in continuing to function and maintain their membranes, according to the ODS.“Omega-3s are important for the brain, and we and many others have shown that having higher levels of omega-3s is associated with less Alzheimer’s pathology, better cognition, and many other protective outcomes,” Yassine stated, in contrast to the trial findings.Trinh agreed. “DHA plays an essential role in maintaining healthy brain cells, and there is evidence that eating fish as part of a healthy dietary pattern may support long-term brain health,” he said.Research on omega-3s and brain health is ongoing, and there is insufficient evidence to draw firm conclusions about their effectiveness.

Some people may still benefit from a supplement, according to Yassine, including:.

Some neurologists test omega-3 levels, though the test isn’t standard, Yassine said.People with nutritional deficiencies or certain genetic or metabolic traits may respond differently to omega-3 supplements, and researchers still need to learn who might benefit, Trinh said.

People who already take fish oil or other omega-3 supplements for other reasons, such as high triglycerides, should make those decisions with their healthcare professionals, he noted.

Trinh noted he tells his patients that “what is good for the heart is generally good for the brain.” He recommended the following healthy habits:.

“Overall, this study reminds us that there is no magic pill for preventing Alzheimer’s disease and that maintaining brain health requires a much broader approach,” Trinh said.

#121284. Breaking: Motorcycles are notoriously dangerous. Could electric motorcycles actually change that?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1713 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Motorcycles are notoriously dangerous. Could electric motorcycles actually change that?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1713 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s no particularly comfortable way to talk about motorcycle safety.
  • But that simple statement also hides something important.
  • Not because electricity is somehow safer than gasoline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s no particularly comfortable way to talk about motorcycle safety. Motorcycles are dangerous. All the statistics point to the fact that per mile, motorcycles are significantly more dangerous. And as someone who promotes them as a better alternative to large cars and trucks for many trips, it’s an uncomfortable reality that must be grappled with.

But that simple statement also hides something important. Not all motorcycles, riders, or riding behaviors carry the same risk. And as a fresh generation of smaller electric motorcycles begins to emerge, I think there’s an interesting question worth asking: Could electric motorcycles inadvertently make motorcycling safer?

Not because electricity is somehow safer than gasoline. It isn’t. Rather, because electrification may fundamentally change the type of motorcycle that hits the road.

In 2024, 6,228 motorcyclists were killed in the US, accounting for 16% of all traffic fatalities, according to the NHTSA.

Obviously, motorcycles have a fundamental disadvantage here. You don’t have a steel cage around you. There aren’t crumple zones separating your body from an oncoming SUV. There’s no seatbelt holding you in place or curtain airbag waiting to catch your head.

But there’s another component to motorcycle fatalities that is harder to ignore: rider behavior.

Industry observers note that around 35% of motorcyclist deaths in 2024 occurred in single-vehicle crashes, according to the IIHS. In other words, more than one-third of those deaths didn’t involve a rider being hit by another vehicle. At that point, whether or not a crash occurred was essentially in the hands of the rider.

Alcohol is another major factor. Among riders killed in single-vehicle crashes, the NHTSA reports that 40% were alcohol-impaired.

Then there are the bikes themselves.

Supersport motorcycles stand out for all the wrong reasons. Of the riders killed on supersports in 2024, 59% were under 30. Compare that to cruiser and standard motorcycles, where just 19% of killed riders were under 30, or touring motorcycles at only 7%.

That’s not proof that powerful motorcycles are causing those deaths, of course. There are all sorts of confounding factors, including the type of person attracted to different motorcycles and how those motorcycles tend to be ridden.

But it’s hard to ignore the broader picture.

To put it more plainly, a huge portion of motorcycle deaths are caused by riders simply going too fast, doing something wrong (like drinking or taking turns too aggressively), or because they couldn’t handle the power of an insanely high-performance crotch rocket. So while figures such as “motorcycles are 27x more deadly than cars” might be true in a broad sense, that doesn’t mean you have a 27x higher chance of death – especially not if you aren’t a 25-year-old hooligan on a second-hand liter bike.

One of the strange things about motorcycling is just how cheaply you can buy extraordinary performance.

Someone with relatively little riding experience can buy a used supersport capable of acceleration that would have required an exotic supercar not long ago. The motorcycle may weigh around 400 lb, produce well over 100 horsepower, and be capable of speeds approaching three times a typical US highway speed limit.

And unlike cars, there isn’t much protecting you when that performance gets away from you.

That’s why I find the current evolution of electric motorcycles so interesting.

For years, electric motorcycle companies largely chased gasoline motorcycles up the performance ladder. We got incredibly fast and powerful machines from companies like Energica and LiveWire.

Those bikes proved electric motorcycles could be fast.

But I’m increasingly interested in the opposite end of the spectrum.

Look at motorcycles such as LiveWire’s upcoming S4 Honcho.

It has been revealed that this isn’t an electric superbike designed around insane acceleration or a 150 mph (240 km/h) top speed. It’s a smaller motorcycle intended to offer approachable performance at a more accessible price.

It adds to a growing market already populated by highly acclaimed modest-sized electric motorcycles like those from Ryvid, Land, and Maeving.

And we’re seeing more machines begin to occupy this previously neglected territory between an e-bike and a full-size motorcycle.

That could make a huge difference when it comes to overall safety, as crotch rockets get replaced by sensible electric motorbikes.

Battery technology actually creates an interesting incentive here. Making an electric motorcycle ridiculously powerful is easy. Giving it enough battery to sustain high speeds for long distances without becoming extremely heavy and expensive is much, much harder.

So the economics and physics of batteries naturally make smaller urban and suburban motorcycles fairly compelling right now.

Instead of asking how to build another 150 mph (240 km/h) electric motorcycle, manufacturers can build a lighter machine that goes 60 or 70 mph (95-120 km/h), has enough range for everyday riding, and costs considerably less.

Ironically, one of the limitations most commonly leveled against electric motorcycles could turn out to have a safety upside.

This is where I think things get even more interesting.

For decades, the stereotypical progression into motorcycling might have involved learning on a dirt bike or small displacement motorcycle, then moving fairly quickly into larger machines. Often though, new riders simply took a licensing course and then bought their first 600cc sport bike to learn to ride.

But now we’re raising an entirely upcoming generation on electric two-wheelers.

Kids and teenagers are increasingly growing up riding e-bikes and small electric motos. Eventually, many of them are going to want something faster than a 20 or 28 mph e-bike.

A 50 mph (80 km/h) electric motorcycle is a pretty logical next step for the e-moto kids of today. Eventually, perhaps that rider graduates to something capable of 70 or 80 mph (120-130 km/h) and comfortable highway travel.

That’s a much more gradual performance curve than jumping from essentially no powered two-wheeler experience to a screaming 600cc supersport.

There’s another advantage too: electric motorcycles are mechanically easier to operate. There’s generally no clutch, no gearbox, and no concern about stalling. Twist the throttle and go.

That doesn’t necessarily make them safer – instant electric torque can certainly get an inexperienced rider into trouble – but it does remove several tasks from the mental workload of learning to ride.

Industry observers note that the rider can spend more attention on braking, cornering, traffic, positioning, and the thousand other things that actually keep you alive on a motorcycle. The reduction in cognitive load can mean more focus on control, if it’s used that way.

To be clear, I’m not arguing that electric motorcycles are inherently safe.

It has been revealed that they’re still motorcycles and they still lack cages. Well, most of them.

If an inattentive driver turns left in front of you, the chemistry powering your rear wheel isn’t going to make much difference.

And electric motorcycles can be outrageously powerful. In fact, the instantaneous torque of an electric motor can make poor throttle calibration especially unforgiving for inexperienced riders.

There also simply isn’t enough data yet to demonstrate that electric motorcycles have meaningfully lower fatality rates than comparable gasoline motorcycles.

But that’s not really my argument.

Industry observers note that my argument is that electrification may change what we consider a normal beginner motorcycle. And that could be much more key, helping to significantly reduce accidents and deaths.

According to recent reports, I’m never going to pretend motorcycles can become as safe as cars. The physics simply don’t work that way.

But the broad statistic of “motorcycles are dangerous” encompasses an enormous spectrum of machines and riders.

A sober, trained commuter wearing proper protective gear and riding a modestly powered motorcycle to work is doing something fundamentally different from an inexperienced 21-year-old seeing how fast his supersport can take an empty freeway ramp at 2 a.m.

Yet both contribute to the same broad motorcycle fatality statistics.

What excites me about this emerging generation of electric motorcycles isn’t that swapping gasoline for batteries magically fixes motorcycle safety. It obviously doesn’t.

I bought a motorcycle around age 60 after considering the risk factors I could control:.

In a recent development, I took a MSF basic riding course before buying the motorcycle. Best investment in the whole saga.

I never rode impaired. That was easy.

I always rode with full protection. That was doable but inconvenient and seriously uncomfortable in hot weather.

I never rode in rainy weather or at night. Again possible but limited my use of the motorcycle for commuting. Eventually my schedule changed to evening and stopped my motorcycle commuting altogether.

In a recent development, after a few close calls I started avoiding roads with more than one lane in each direction. That added quite a bit to my commute time.

In a recent development, I never rode when I was in a hurry. That meant more days I didn't use the motorcycle for commuting.

None of these precautions have anything to do with electric drive. After I sold my gas motorcycle I test rode an electric motorcycle and loved it. However I didn't buy it because it didn't reduce any of the risks and I wouldn't ride it more than the gas bike.

It’s that electrification could help create a new category of desirable, affordable motorcycles that don’t need 120 horsepower and a 160 mph top speed to be cool.

If younger riders grow up progressing from e-bikes to small e-motos and then to highway-capable electric motorcycles, perhaps we’ll wind up with a generation that sees a lightweight 60 or 70 mph motorcycle as a perfectly legitimate machine rather than merely a stepping stone to something ridiculously powerful.

Maybe electrification’s biggest contribution to motorcycle safety won’t be traction control, ABS, or sophisticated electronics.

Maybe it’ll simply make sensible motorcycles fun and cool again.

#121283. Does Adversity Hurt Less the Second Time?

Does Adversity Hurt Less the Second Time?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (991 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • My grandfather owned a black World War II winter coat, long and heavy, the kind exhibitionists in movies wear, and in high school and college, I wore it everywhere because it reminded me of this sweet man who would watch Woody Woodpecker cartoons on television with me such that his laugh shook the bed.
  • It has been revealed that nietzsche wrote that what doesn’t kill you makes you stronger, so by his logic, I should have shrugged off my next problem easily.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

My grandfather owned a black World War II winter coat, long and heavy, the kind exhibitionists in movies wear, and in high school and college, I wore it everywhere because it reminded me of this sweet man who would watch Woody Woodpecker cartoons on television with me such that his laugh shook the bed. One night, outside a Upcoming York City bar, I realized it was too warm for wool and threw the coat back in my car. When my friends and I came back a few hours later, the window was broken in, and the thief took one thing: my grandfather’s coat.

It has been revealed that nietzsche wrote that what doesn’t kill you makes you stronger, so by his logic, I should have shrugged off my next problem easily. Three psychiatric researchers in Australia borrowed this overplayed line in the title of their scientific article, "What Doesn't Kill You Doesn't Always Make You Stronger: The Impact of Repeated Exposure to Adverse Life Events on Mental Health." Their work addresses questions taken for granted in a sloppy literature on resilience.

Developmental psychologist Ann Masten coined the phrase that resilience is “ordinary magic” in 2001. It has since been dropped into commencement speeches and self-help books, usually shrunk down to the comforting idea that everyone has some. Masten’s own data say something far more precise. She spent years studying homeless families and described their reading and math grades:.

Our studies of homeless families have revealed striking variability within homeless populations, both in the degree of risk and also the level of competence or problems. For example, if one examines individual growth curves for children identified as homeless/highly mobile in the district, the variability becomes evident … Some children show consistent academic resilience, if one defines resilience as average or better reading or math achievement scores, whereas others show consistent problems, covering a range of 5 SD [five standard deviations] or more.

Variability means that some people experience amazing outcomes while others fall apart. Five standard deviations is a spread wide enough to stretch from the bottom 1 percent of the bell curve to the top 1 percent within a group of kids who all lack a stable bedroom. On average, homeless children scored below poor children who had housing, who in turn scored below children who were neither. Masten never said resilience is a universal human endowment.

The myth of universal human resilience has a price. If most people bounce back on their own, the logical policy is to leave them alone. They will be fine... eventually.

Asking whether people are resilient is about as useful as asking whether people are tall, because the answer depends on who, measured against what, and when. The better question is what happens when you experience the same difficulty twice and whether the second hurts more or less than the first.

The Australian psychiatrists studied 23,109 adults who, between 2002 and 2023, experienced adversity. They looked at people who:.

Every year, the same people answered the same question: How much of the time during the past four weeks:.

Scores ran from 0 to 100, which let the researchers compare how far a person sank after a first challenge with how far the same person sank after a second.

Some might say the first time your finances blow up, you can blame bad luck, such as a crooked landlord. The second time, the explanation arrows start pointing at you.

Industry observers note that in the study, a first major financial loss lowered scores by 6 to 7 points, the steepest drop of the seven events. A second loss lowered them by 7 to 8 points, and a third hurt about as much as the second—so the harm grew, and then it leveled off.

Industry observers note that the people hit repeatedly were poorer to begin with, earning less before their first event. That is, the study demonstrated people with tough lives experience terrible events more often. It’s not exactly the most awe-inspiring finding, but it should make us more compassionate. My hypothesis is that a second financial loss comes after the savings account is empty, and you have already asked friends for a loan. By then, you feel incompetent and risk fraying your social ties.

A first theft or break-in lowered scores by about 1 point out of 100—the smallest effect in the study. By those stats, my coat should have been a shrug, and it wasn’t. A question about property crime can’t distinguish a stolen car stereo from my grandfather’s WWII coat. The authors close their paper with the same mentality, arguing that how much an event hurts depends on what the lost thing means to the person and how much is in their psychological arsenal to absorb the pain.

In a recent development, divorce and serious personal illness or injury both did less harm the second time, so some might offer advice that your second divorce will sting less. As a divorced man, I’m in no hurry to find out, and you shouldn’t either.

A smaller mental health reaction can also mean a person stopped feeling much. For instance, people assaulted three or more times reacted less to each upcoming attack, and 64 percent of them were women, which unfortunately we know is often a sign of domestic violence.

I want to warn you and everyone you know that emotional numbing should not be misunderstood as resilience or growth.

So did losing my grandpa’s coat make me stronger? Not in the slightest. It was an isolated experience that pissed me off. You, too, have similar one-offs that do not fit tidy little psychological models. Do not assume resilience or breakdowns. Pay attention, ask questions, and listen to better understand the person beside you.

Young sea turtles make an unexpected home in the Gulf of Oman

  • “Our results show just how critical coastal wetlands can be to young green turtles,” Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that for one group of young sea turtles, a protected wetland in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) proved a perfect oasis. A team tracking nine juvenile green turtles (Chelonia mydas) found they were spending over 80 percent of their time in the Al Qurm Wa Lehhfaiiah Protected Area, a human-made lagoon on the UAE’s Gulf of Oman coast. Large numbers of turtles are also found in this basin built beyond the salt-tolerant trees and shrubs along the coast. A study published today in the journal Aquatic Conservation details the findings.

Sources indicate that in 2003, the basin was excavated as an extension of the Khor Kalba mangrove trees. The resulting Al Qurm Wa Lehhfaiiah Protected Area has been recognized as a wetland of international importance under the Ramsar Convention and as a Key Biodiversity Area since 2013.

“Our results show just how critical coastal wetlands can be to young green turtles,” Dr. Owen Exeter, a study co-author and marine conservation ecologist from the University of Exeter, remarked in a statement. “The fact these turtles are using the artificial basin appears to be a happy accident, and an example of how wildlife can find a way in a world increasingly shaped by humans. However, without the natural mangroves connecting to this system, it’s unlikely that this would have occurred.

According to the team, the floor of the basin is covered with algae, which likely means the turtles have enough food. A few sharks are making their way to this habitat.

The turtles are now also showing “strong reliance” in the man-made basin, with five times higher odds of being found there than in surrounding habitats.

Industry observers note that while this spot can be a refuge, the natural mangrove channels also play a critical role in connecting the juvenile turtles (those with a shell less than 23 inches across) to the sea. These channels allow them to move with the tides and show the importance of protecting the entire ecosystem, not just parts of it.

It has been revealed that “The government of Sharjah presently protects most of this area from building development, fishing and boating—preserving the last mangrove ecosystem on UAE’s east coast,” Exeter stated. “Coastal wetlands are tropical nature hotspots, providing essential nursery and foraging habitats for species including sea turtles. Wetlands are among the most threatened ecosystems globally, so we urgently need to understand how key species use both modified and protected wetlands.”.

It has been revealed that while these findings are positive for the turtles living in the protected area, their life cycle depends on nesting beaches. Many of these beaches have already been lost to coastal development, and fishing, vessel traffic, and pollution affect the other nearby areas.

One of the turtles swam over 430 miles south to central Oman, highlighting the need for conservation management of these mobile species once they are old enough to leave critical wetland sites.

“Overall, our findings show that coastal wetlands, including engineered ones, can provide valuable habitat for juvenile turtles, provided they are designed for ecological connectivity and subsequent human pressures and threats are minimised,” concluded study co-author Brendan Whittington-Jones from the Sharjah Environment and Protected Areas Authority (EPAA) who led the study.

The 10 Best Smartwatches for Men, Tested by Gear Editors

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AT MEN'S HEALTH, we love a good fitness tracker—but let’s be honest, they’re not exactly stylish.
  • Recent findings suggest that with the Galaxy Watch9, Samsung didn’t mess with a good thing.
  • Industry observers note that one of the most notable new additions is the Vitals tool, which learns your normal range for things like heart rate and blood oxygen, then flags you when something’s off.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AT MEN'S HEALTH, we love a good fitness tracker—but let’s be honest, they’re not exactly stylish. Most of them look great with running shorts and a workout tee—but less so when you’re in a crisp dress shirt and tailored trousers. That’s where the best smartwatches for men come in. They bridge the gap between performance tech and actual style—tracking your heart rate and steps without clashing with your fit. A great smartwatch can go from your 6 a.m. run to your 8 p.m. cocktail hour without missing a beat. Some, like the TAG Heuer Connected, look so sleek you could wear them for a black-tie event and look like you belong on the cover of a magazine. We’ve tested dozens to find the ones that deliver that perfect balance of design, durability, and data.

Recent findings suggest that with the Galaxy Watch9, Samsung didn’t mess with a good thing. The aluminum case, “squircle” shape, and bright 3,000-nit screen all carry over from the Watch8 that was our previous favorite—so at a glance you’d be hard-pressed to tell them apart. The key changes are under the hood: a bigger battery, a more power-efficient processor, and a smarter set of health tools that turn your sleep and workout data into advice you can act on.

Industry observers note that one of the most notable new additions is the Vitals tool, which learns your normal range for things like heart rate and blood oxygen, then flags you when something’s off. A jump in your resting heart rate or skin temperature, for instance, can signal a cold before you feel it—keep in mind these should be anecdotal. The other new features are for the data-driven crowd. A Heart Health Score rolls your sleep, activity, and blood-pressure trends into a single read on how your lifestyle is affecting your heart, with tips to improve it. My sleep schedule has been all over the place lately, making me feel lethargic at certain parts of the day, and the Watch9 has been recommending I go to bed earlier. Finally, a Fitness Index charts your body composition, cardio, endurance, flexibility, and strength on a spider graph so you can see where you’re strong and where you’re lagging.

There are carryovers from the Watch8 too, including the Running Coach that builds a blueprint off a 12-minute test run, with well-structured workouts, and the Antioxidant Index, which reads the carotenoid levels in your skin for a rough sense of your fruit and vegetable intake (to be taken with a grain of salt).

According to recent reports, in a brief head-to-head test against the Apple Watch Series 11, the Watch9’s heart rate held within a few beats on runs and walks. I’ve been following a Couch to 5K program for the past four weeks, and the heart-rate readings during each run are reliable enough to pace by. Daily Cardio Load has also been a significant help, nudging me to dial it back instead of pushing myself too hard, too soon.

Sources indicate that samsung dropped the older Exynos chip for Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Wear Elite, and everything feels snappier, from starting a workout to pulling up a stat mid-run to talking to Google’s Gemini. Now you just lift your wrist to say a command, rather than first saying a wake word.

The Watch9 keeps the excellent Dynamic Lug System, making it comfortable enough to sleep in, and its premium-yet-friendly design moves from a morning run to a business-casual meeting without looking out of place. It comes in 40mm and 44mm sizes with a wider band lineup, including Sport, Fabric, and a two-tone Misty. The battery is bigger on paper—390mAh on the 40mm, a 20 percent bump, and in my testing it still lands around a day of use. At $379.99, Samsung’s newest model costs a bit more than the Watch8 did at launch, but you’re getting the smartest, most feature-packed version yet.

Read More: Best Fitness Trackers for Men.

The Apple Watch SE used to be the Apple Watch you bought because you couldn’t justify spending more. Apple changed that with the SE 3 by adding an always-on display, the S10 chip, double-tap and wrist-flick gestures, 5G cellular on cellular models, and health features like Sleep Score and breathing irregularity detection through the Vitals app.

Over several weeks of testing, the SE 3 held up as a daily driver without feeling like a compromise. The always-on display made a real difference while exercising, and performance felt snappy across the board—from launching workouts to setting timers with on-device Siri. Fast charging is the other underrated upgrade. A 15-minute top-up while showering in the morning was enough to carry the watch through the rest of the day and overnight for sleep tracking.

According to recent reports, after a rough night (67 out of 100), I could see exactly how that Sleep Score was calculated and adjusted accordingly, scoring a 90 the next night. The Vitals app runs in the background and tracks wrist temperature and respiratory rate without any input. It hasn’t flagged anything yet, but that kind of passive monitoring adds value over time.

Sources indicate that the new Series 12 is also available at $399. For the extra $150, it adds an ECG app, a Blood Oxygen app, and hypertension notifications, none of which the SE 3 has. It also takes a background heart rate reading every five seconds, and its Readiness app turns recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep into a single score.

In a recent development, the Series 12’s display reaches 2,000 nits (the SE 3 gets to 1,000), the bezels are thinner, and the screen area is larger. Battery life is rated at 24 hours compared to the SE 3’s 18 hours, and five minutes on the charger gives up to 10 hours of sleep tracking, where the SE 3 gets up to eight hours from eight minutes. The Series 12 also adds a water temperature sensor and a depth gauge to six meters for snorkeling.

Sources indicate that we recommend the Series 12 if you use a watch to follow training load and recovery, if you swim or snorkel, or if you want more advanced health tracking features. But the SE 3 is the call if you want notifications and standard workout and sleep tracking on an Apple Watch that still has an always-on display, and you’re on more of a budget.

Read More: Apple Watch SE 3 Review.

If you want a GPS running watch that nails the fundamentals and is relatively affordable, the Coros Pace 4 should be at the top of your list. At $249, it competes on accuracy, battery life, and display quality with watches that cost significantly more, and at 40 grams with a silicone strap, it’s light enough to forget you’re wearing it.

The biggest upgrade from the Pace 3 is the AMOLED display, which is sharp and easy to read in bright sunlight. Battery life actually improved despite the brighter screen, jumping to 31 hours in max GPS mode with all satellite systems active, or 24 hours with always-on display enabled. A quick charge while you’re showering or eating a meal should top it off.

GPS tracking is where Coros built its reputation, and the Pace 4 delivers. Dual-frequency satellite support promises clean, accurate tracks that hold up even alongside buildings and under tree cover. The Pace 4 also features voice logging, so after finishing a run, the watch prompts you to record your thoughts, which get transcribed and saved in the Coros app. The watch also uses breadcrumb navigation rather than full maps, so if you rely on turn-by-turn directions while exploring upcoming routes, you’ll want to step up to the Coros Apex or a Garmin with offline maps.

Read More: The Gear I Used to Train for My Longest Race Yet.

According to recent reports, our contributing editor and watch expert Ted Stafford, who styles every Men’s Health cover, was seriously impressed by the TAG Heuer Connected Calibre E5. “I was impressed by how well the E5 straddles the line between traditional style and modern innovation,” he states. “It wears beautifully on the wrist, with a sleek, stylish design and a comfort-first build. Its intuitive interface also makes it refreshingly simple to navigate, even on the move or during high-intensity activities.”.

In fact, Stafford recently met with Tag Heuer’s team in Boston to test the Connected Calibre E5. During his 5K run, he appreciated how easy it was to glance at messages, check his heart rate, and accurately track his activity—all without slowing down. He also noted that the stainless bracelet stayed comfortable and secure the whole time. Another standout feature is the ability to customize the watch face. “Whether you’re in the mood for a sporty Carrera or a bold Formula 1 look, the E5 lets you effortlessly switch styles to match your day,” he notes. “This and all the other unique tech offerings make having a connected watch a win-win for me.”.

Recent findings suggest that what really makes the E5 shine, though, is how much it packs under the hood. You get dual-band GPS for pinpoint tracking, heart-rate and blood-oxygen sensors, and full sleep and stress tracking that rivals top fitness-focused wearables. The upcoming TAG Heuer OS runs smoother than ever, with cleaner visuals and tighter iPhone integration for those in the Apple ecosystem. Plus, it’s built like a tank with 50 meters of water resistance, a sapphire crystal display, and your choice of steel or titanium cases. Battery life clocks in at about two days of regular use, and fast charging gets you back to full in around 30 minutes.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 keeps the 49mm titanium case of the Ultra 3 and replaces the sensor on the back. The new Health Sensing System adds a circular optical sensing array, larger and more efficient LEDs for heart rate readings, and more surface area touching the skin for ECG readings. Earlier models took background heart rate readings every five minutes. The Ultra 4 takes one every five seconds and demonstrates it in a new heart rate complication, which is a data point you pin to the watch face. Faster readings also let the watch measure heart rate variability (the variation in time between heartbeats) as often as every five minutes while you’re at rest.

The Ultra 4 also adds Readiness, which combines Fitness, Vitals, and Sleep Score into a rating from 1 to 10 for how prepared your body is for the day. Readiness needs several consecutive nights of sleeping with the watch before it starts scoring. The S11 chip makes the watch feel quicker and powers a new step counter and better Siri, which our tester used to set timers more often than ever.

Recent findings suggest that apple rates the battery at up to 50 hours of normal use and up to 84 hours in Low Power Mode, with up to 18 hours of continuous workout tracking. In testing, the first charge lasted two nights of sleep. When the battery dropped to about 10 percent one night, our tester was almost three-quarters charged by the time he had brushed his teeth, gotten into bed, and set an alarm. Apple says 15 minutes on the charger gives up to 18 hours of use. Adventure watches from other brands can last weeks between charges, so the Ultra 4 still trails them.

The Ultra 4 costs $799 and the Series 12 costs $399. Both have the same sensors and health features, so the Ultra 4’s advantages are the bigger battery, the 49mm case, and adventure features like precision dual-frequency GPS, emergency SOS via satellite, and diving to 40 meters.

Read More: Apple Watch Ultra 4 Review.

According to recent reports, when it comes to premium running watches, the latest Suunto Race (the Race 2) packs a serious punch at $499—or $599 for the Titanium Trail version. The display is larger and brighter than the Race 1 while being thinner. That remarked, at 49mm, the Race 2 isn’t a small watch. Men’s Health Senior Gear and Reviews Editor Ryan Brower put it to the test, noting: “While I’ve enjoyed testing it, the Race 2 would be nice to have in a smaller size.”.

That bigger size, though, makes room for a faster processor and an impressive 55 hours of battery life in GPS mode (or up to 30 days with daily use and no training). “The battery claims really hold,” Brower claims. “I’ve only had to charge it a couple of times throughout months of testing. To be fair, I don’t wear it every day, but I did for a few stretches to get a sense of it.” Another big improvement is the redesigned charging clip, which Brower found far more effective and reliable than previous Suunto models that didn’t always connect easily.

Performance-wise, the Race 2 delivers more than 115 sport modes. Brower put many of those programs through their paces—treadmill running, running, trail running, strength training, hiking, climbing, rowing (technically paddling), and even surfing—and each one worked smoothly, serving up plenty of useful metrics. GPS tracking proved fairly accurate, and features like training load and recovery provided deeper insights when synced with the Suunto Coach or other training apps. Building a regimen and letting the watch help implement it, Brower notes, “can be a great tool for runners.”.

Sources indicate that the Race 2 leans into a rugged aesthetic with its large round case and durable polymer or titanium build. Its style clearly favors sport and outdoor fits, so the 49mm case can feel oversized or out of place in formal or office clothes. The standard strap is a breathable silicone, perfect for sweaty workouts or trail runs, and the Titanium Trail model adds a premium case finish for those who want a more elevated look in casual settings.

The Pixel Watch 5 looks almost identical to the Pixel Watch 4. It comes in the same 41mm and 45mm sizes, with a domed Actua 360 display under scratch-resistant Gorilla Glass that reaches 3,000 nits at its brightest. Most of the changes are inside and in the software. Google claims the new watch is 20 percent faster than the Pixel Watch 4, and it’s built around Gemini. Raise your wrist to talk to the assistant, and the watch face brings up things like flight info and your ETA when you need them.

The Pixel Watch 5 can detect a loss of pulse and prompt a call to emergency services. Satellite SOS lets you contact emergency services and revision family from remote areas without cell service, and Google includes it free for two years after activation. Fall Detection, Car Crash Detection, and Safety Check are back, too. Safety Check shares your location with emergency contacts if a timer runs out during a solo run or a late walk home and you don’t respond.

Latest this generation, the Pixel Watch 5 can show your blood pressure trends and track signs of insulin resistance over the course of a month. Google is clear that neither is a medical reading or a diagnosis, but both can flag patterns to bring up with your doctor. You also get the ECG app, irregular heart rhythm alerts, SpO2, HRV, skin temperature, and a nightly Sleep Score from what Google calls its most accurate sleep tracking yet. Each morning, Morning Brief combines your sleep recap, readiness, and the weather on one screen.

Google calls the watch’s dual-frequency GPS its best yet. It uses machine learning to keep runs through tall downtown buildings and hikes under thick tree cover on track. The watch tracks more than 50 activities. You can build strength sessions with exact reps, weights, and rest timers, and get audio and visual guidance as you go. A Google Health Premium subscription, which includes three free months, adds a Gemini-powered coach that adjusts your initiative around your schedule.

Industry observers note that google rates the battery at up to 30 hours for the 41mm model and up to 40 hours for the 45mm. That means charging most days, but the included Quick Charge Dock adds 15 hours in 15 minutes, so a short top-up in the morning gets you through a night of sleep tracking. The watch only works with Android phones, and at $399.99, it costs $50 more than the Pixel Watch 4 did at launch. If you’re an Android user who wants the strongest safety features on any smartwatch, it’s still the one to beat.

The Fēnix 9 is Garmin’s premium multisport GPS watch, built for people who take their training and outdoor adventures seriously. It comes in 43mm, 47mm, and 51mm cases, with the 43mm model being styled for smaller wrists. Every version has an AMOLED display with a titanium bezel and a scratch-resistant sapphire lens, and it offers a much brighter screen than the Fēnix 8’s. The watch is tested to U.S. military standards for heat, shock, and water resistance, and it’s rated for recreational dives to 40 meters.

Navigation has always been Garmin’s forte, and it’s where the latest model stands apart. Full-color topographic maps come preloaded, and the Fēnix 9 has twice the RAM of the Fēnix 8 and an updated map engine that pans 30 percent faster. Storage doubles to 64GB, which holds twice as many maps as before plus up to 7,000 songs from Spotify, Deezer, or Amazon Music. Tell the watch how far you want to go, and dynamic round-trip routing suggests a loop that brings you back. If you go off course, it maps a new route with the same mileage. NextFork demonstrates the distance to the next trail junction and the name of the trail, ClimbPro shows current and upcoming climbs on downloaded courses, and SatIQ adjusts GPS accuracy to save battery.

According to recent reports, garmin rates the 43mm model at up to 10 days in smartwatch mode. That's a different category from any Apple Watch or Samsung Galaxy Watch, and it means far less battery anxiety day to day. You don’t have to be quite as strategic when you charge as you would with other smartwatches.

It has been revealed that the training tools go deeper than ever before, too. New stamina features show how your endurance holds up over different distances and help you manage your effort during a race. Garmin Epic combines several days of activities into one summary in the Garmin Connect app, which is useful for a backpacking trip or a training camp. Rowers get VO2 max and power metrics, and rucking workouts let you enter your pack weight.

Recent findings suggest that returning features include Training Readiness, which scores your sleep, recovery, and training load each morning, along with HRV status, sleep coaching, PacePro race pacing, and an ECG app. A built-in speaker and microphone let you take calls from your wrist when the watch is paired with your iPhone or Android phone, and there's a built-in LED flashlight.

Sources indicate that the 43mm Fēnix 9 is pricey at $999.99, and more advanced connectivity features like inReach satellite messaging, SOS, and LTE calling require the more expensive Fēnix 9 Pro, so the standard model relies on your paired phone to send your live location if it detects an incident. But for athletes who log serious miles across multiple sports and want one watch that handles all of it, the Fēnix 9 is the way to go.

We got our hands on the G-Shock Move, and this thing is a beast—in the best way possible. Built with G-Shock’s signature toughness, it feels indestructible yet surprisingly comfortable on the wrist. I ran, lifted, and hiked with it, and it handled everything without a hiccup. Inside, you’ve got serious hardware: GPS, heart-rate monitoring, altimeter, compass, thermometer, and a gyroscope that tracks every stride, step, and elevation change with precision.

Recent findings suggest that what really impressed me was how capable it felt in different conditions. I tracked a few long runs with GPS fully active, and the data stayed consistent and accurate the whole time—no weird pace spikes or drop-offs. The battery life held up too; even when I pushed it hard, I still got several days before needing a recharge. And when it does run low, the solar-assisted charging converts sunlight into extra power, adding several hours—or even a day or two—of runtime if you’re outdoors. It’s rated for 200 meters of water resistance, so swimming, rain, and sweat are all fair game.

Living up to its name, the G-Shock Move supports more than a dozen sports, from trail running and cycling to gym training and open-water swimming, while also monitoring sleep, recovery, and blood-oxygen levels. The display’s bright and easy-to-read mid-workout, and the interface feels intuitive enough to switch modes on the fly. For guys who demand a watch that’s as tough and versatile as they are, this one’s the real deal.

In a recent development, the Fitbit Edge is a fitness tracker first, with just enough smartwatch features to cover the basics. You can read notifications, send quick replies, set alarms, control your music, get turn-by-turn directions from Google Maps, and find your phone. But there are no calls, no contactless payments, no voice assistant, and no app store.

That limited feature set is why the battery lasts up to seven days and charges back to full in 90 minutes. The rounded display is also 45 percent bigger and more than 40 percent brighter than on previous Fitbits, and it reveals your stats and coaching cues at a glance.

Built-in GPS and an altimeter let you map outdoor runs, rides, and hikes and track how much you climb without bringing your phone. The Edge also recognizes workouts automatically, so a walk or run still counts if you forget to start it. The tracker records heart rate, HRV, SpO2, breathing rate, skin temperature, and resting heart rate. Each night it also tracks your sleep stages and gives you a Sleep Score. High and low heart rate alerts and Irregular Rhythm Notifications flag potential heart issues.

A Google Health Premium membership, which comes with three free months and then costs $9.99 a month, unlocks a Gemini-powered coach that builds a training plan around your schedule. It also adds blood pressure and insulin resistance trends. Google says neither is a clinical reading nor a screening tool, but both can flag patterns to discuss with your doctor.

At $179.99, the Edge works with both iPhone and Android phones and comes with small and large bands in the box. It’s a good fit if a full smartwatch is more than you need but you still want to see texts and directions on your wrist. If you want calls, payments, and apps, look at the Pixel Watch 5 or Apple Watch SE 3 instead.
