The Lame Duck: A Leader's Exit Can Be Bad or Good

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (526 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • A leader’s time in the role is coming to an end.
  • According to recent reports, neglect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

It happens all the time. A leader’s time in the role is coming to an end. A leader who is completing the end of tenure in a top-level leadership position can either do an organization great harm or much good. What happens when a leader is a lame duck, with a known date for terminating their tenure? It all depends on the leader’s intent, their motivation, and how the leader’s team deals with it.

According to recent reports, neglect. What happens when a leader mentally disengages from their position and takes a “who cares” attitude? In one instance, a department director who was finishing his last few months simply stopped leading—communicating much less, canceling meetings that focused on moving the firm forward, and not providing much information or feedback to direct reports. The organization came to a virtual standstill that lasted for a while, and it took new, energetic leadership to recover.

Trashing the Place. Even worse, a leader can decide to cause real damage. This can occur when the leader has been fired or feels unfairly treated. The leader might end promising and/or profitable projects. Resources might be rerouted to the leader’s benefit. More subtly, the leader might pit team members against one another and create a toxic work culture.

Motivational Malaise. A leader’s lack of interest and activity as they come to the end of their tenure can be contagious, affecting the motivation of other employees (“If the leader doesn’t seem to care, why should I?” “The leader is taking a lot of personal time off, so I guess it’s OK.”). The leader’s negativity or simple disinterest can be infectious and affect the motivation of others.

Allow Others to Step Up to Leadership. A good leader develops leadership capacity in others. When a leader is exiting, it is notable to provide opportunities for direct reports to take on leadership roles and activities. A much-celebrated CEO who was retiring told me that he knew that the organization would be in good hands after his departure because he had worked to develop his successors’ leadership. Delegating responsibility and sharing the leadership is the key to developing followers into leaders.

Industry observers note that strengthen Existing Processes. When a leader’s departure is inevitable, it is a good time for the leader to do a comprehensive evaluation of the organization’s operations. Rather than winding things down, it’s a good time to focus on improvement. What could be working better? What new initiatives should be fast-tracked? Rather than taking it easy, the departing leader should ramp things up.

Leave a Legacy. An effective leader who is in the waning stages of tenure needs to realize that it is important to continue efforts to improve the organization and its operations. This is the legacy that a good leader leaves behind. The departure should be positive, formative, and free from regrets.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, one little bear cub in Southeastern Alaska’s Tongass National Forest is a true model of bravery. The park’s rangers have awarded the unnamed black bear (Ursus americanus) cub with the 2026 Courageous Cub award for persevering when he got himself in a little pickle this summer. The cub belongs to a forgetful mother bear named Dory, who had two cubs this season.

“This little cub of Dory’s went on a significant adventure. He got lost, ran down the trail a half mile and approached visitors as if to ask, ‘Are you my mommy?’ Then got scared and ran off in the wrong direction,” the Tongass rangers write. “Hours later he came running back up the trail sniffing out where mama was.”.

Black bears like this family have a very keen sense of smell. It is debated just how far away they can smell, but it is at least two miles and could be up to 20. Fortunately, the cub was able to use some of that sniffing power to find both Dory and his other sibling.

The rangers at Tongass National Forest are right now awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States. It covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau, and includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. This makes the creek a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

Recent findings suggest that according to Friends of Anan, at least 39 bears feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Similar to their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their behavior.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I DIDN’T START out as a “boot guy.” I always thought they were clunky, poorly stitched and didn’t provide enough insole support like my favorite Nike Air Force 1s. But 15 years ago, I bought my first pair of Timberland 6-Inch Premium Boots because a brutal winter hit the East Coast, and slipping around in sneakers wasn’t going to cut it. I needed something that could survive the rain, snow, and slush. It didn’t take long to realize that once fall hits, having a solid pair (or two) in rotation is a non-negotiable. That first leather lace-up carried me through snowball fights and more than a few questionable bar floors—and it sold me on what a good boot can do.

Since then, the Men’s Health style team and I have tested well over 50 pairs across every silhouette imaginable: cowboy boots, hiking boots, waterproof commuters, dressier Chelsea styles, heritage work boots—the whole lineup. I’ve worn them on shoots, to weddings, on rainy office days, and on long travel runs, and I can confirm: not every boot is bulky. The right pair can feel as clean and sleek as your favorite sneakers. So if you’re looking for something versatile enough to move from the office to the bar or carry you from one event to the next, we’ve got you covered. Our picks deliver comfort, durability, and style, whether you need a tough trail option, something practical for wet commutes, or a sleek pair for a night out.

Sources indicate that the iconic Blundstone #585 still reigns supreme for its comfort, durability, and style. Part Chelsea boot, part work boot, its leather feels soft with a pre-distressed texture, while inside is cushy and snug from the moment you put it on. We didn’t feel any tightness or have to wait a couple of wears for it to mold to our feet. Our editor Tim Kohut wears it at his standing desk for seven hours straight, and his feet never give in or develop blisters. He even took it on a weekend hike and felt comfortable the whole way, hills, dips, and all. The pull tabs also make it easy to slide your foot in and out.

I’ve worn warmer boots in my testing, but they were much bulkier. This pair has a lighter, slimmer build, yet works for general fall and winter gear. The boot’s leather upper dries in minutes, whether I get caught in light showers or trudge through three inches of snow. Yes, the material can scuff if you’re not careful, but a quick wipe with a damp cloth brings it right back. After months of near-daily wear, the elastic panels haven’t stretched out, the sole hasn’t flattened, and the leather has developed a natural patina versus looking beat up. Underfoot, the synthetic polyurethane midsole feels like a thick layer of cushioning, softening every step, especially on Fresh York’s uneven sidewalks.

In the toe area, my feet have wiggle room instead of feeling cramped. Whether for style or performance, this boot works in a variety of settings. I’ve worn mine with a sweater and dark denim for dinner as well as chinos for the office, and it pairs seamlessly with any casual staples like a flannel overshirt, tee, and jeans under a fall jacket. The price tag may give you pause, but most boots that I’ve spent over $100 on are worth it. You don’t have to baby this one. It looks good as latest after being worn everywhere, so it’s a reliable option for work, travel, and trail.

In a recent development, when our senior fitness and commerce editor Brett Williams slipped into the Beckett Simonon Bolton Chelsea, he immediately called out how sharp it looked. This Chelsea boot—a style originating in 19th-century Britain as a close-fitting riding boot with elastic side panels—elevates whatever you’re wearing. The super premium, full-grain calfskin leather has a natural sheen and structure, and the almond-shaped toe box gives it a sleek profile that reads dressy. Inside, the Vachetta leather lining helped keep his foot cool and surprisingly comfortable after hours at his standing desk.

In a recent development, brett wore it with suits, dress pants, and black denim on shoot days, and it held up across the board. And yes, Chelseas aren’t strictly “formal only” anymore, but the Bolton proves that a dress-leaning Chelsea can still be incredibly versatile. The stitched construction makes it lighter and more flexible than the typical Goodyear-welted options. It’s easily one of the best leather Chelsea boots on the market because it nails every detail: premium calfskin, a breathable lining, a sleek silhouette, and real comfort. Plenty of Chelseas look the part but feel clunky or overly stiff, so the $279 is justifiable.

The full-grain leather upper and sheepskin lining give it a polished look, but the real magic is underfoot: the heat-activated insole that molds to your feet after a few wears. Plus, the lightweight outsole feels closer to a cushy sneaker than a traditional boot.

In a recent development, sean wore it on rainy commutes, into the office, and around the city on weekend errands. He didn’t have any sore arches or slips on wet sidewalks. The leather ages nicely over time, and the overall vibe lands squarely in that “smart casual” sweet spot. It works with chinos and slim trousers, and can stretch to dark denim, but it’s not meant to stand in for a dress boot.

If you’ve dismissed cowboy boots as too costumey, Tecovas offers a sleek option that balances rugged style and pairs with a bunch of casual and dressy fits. The round-toe design features a tough, beautiful cowhide leather that wears well whether you’re dressing up or down. The cowhide leather gives the Cartwright a durable feel, while its classic round toe and signature stitching keep the design recognizable.

Industry observers note that surprisingly, I didn’t have to break this boot in. From the first wear, it felt comfortable without any pinching or stiffness. While it’s not as grippy on slippery surfaces as the Merrell and Timberland boots, it’s stable enough for most city sidewalks. Tecovas offers a few different colors, but we’re especially into the hazelnut, which looks great with dark jeans or dressier pants.

Industry observers note that what really makes this Tecovas pair stand out is how approachable it feels, especially if you’ve never owned a cowboy boot before. The 12-inch shaft—the part of the boot that rises from your ankle to your lower calf—isn’t overly tall or stiff, so it slips easily under straight or relaxed-fit jeans. Also, the 1½-inch heel is low and manageable, so you get a classic cowboy shape without feeling like you’re walking on a block. Fit-wise, it runs true to size and feels secure without squeezing the instep, which is often the biggest concern with Western-style boots. If you want the look without committing to something flashy or trend-driven, this is a smart, low-risk entry point that still feels elevated.

Timberland’s classic work boot has outlasted trendy styles for decades because it’s durable, has a timeless design, and goes with everything. Aptly named the “Butters”, it’s one of the most recognizable boots because of its signature cut and proportions: the high top, thick lug sole, and warm wheat-colored nubuck leather. It’s become a staple across music, streetwear and sports culture. I’ve had it in rotation since I was a teen and still weave it into my casual fits to this day. Yes, it takes one to three wears to break in, but after that you get a snug, customized fit that you can fine-tune with the laces.

Industry observers note that the Timberland boot’s cultural relevance hasn’t slowed down, either. A lot of fashion gents like Timothée Chalamet have been spotted wearing Timberland off-duty and even at red carpet events. It also taps into today’s men’s trends, especially the ongoing ’90s-Y2K revival, where baggier denim, boxy jackets, and easy, layered knits are back in rotation.

Sources indicate that this boot has full-grain and nubuck leather uppers that can handle scuffs and are fully waterproof, so rain and slush never ruin the look. It's sturdier and heavier than most fashion boots, because it was originally built for work, but it doesn't feel like you’re lugging around bricks all day. The bulk is part of the style, and why it pairs so well with relaxed denim, cargos, and winter fits. Whether I’m walking on wet sidewalks or cobblestone, the lug sole feels stable underfoot.

Industry observers note that if we’re judging purely on trail performance, the Merrell Thermo Chill 2 is the best pick for hiking. The mid-height design gives your ankles the extra support they need on uneven terrain, so you’re not wobbling around. Most hiking boot outsoles rely on standard rubber compounds that work well, but they usually sacrifice grip for durability or flexibility. With 200g insulation, this style makes for a perfect winter boot.

Industry observers note that it’s fully waterproof, so puddles, rain, or soggy grass aren’t going to slow you down. The main draw here is the exclusive footbed, which molds to your foot, over time, giving each step a cushioned, natural feel. Brower wore this boot on a weekend camping trip, splashing through soggy trails and wet grass, and by the end of it, his feet were dry and comfortable. The mesh on the tongue keeps things breathable, too, so when the sun comes out, your feet don’t feel like they’re baking. While it’s not as sleek as the Danner boot, it’s still a solid-looking boot that you can wear off the trail.

Most rugged boots are kind of ugly, but Danner delivers a trail-ready option that actually looks sharp. The rich tan color paired with red laces gives it a bold yet unique look for the trail. Outside of hikes, our Tech and Gear editor Ryan Brower likes to style it with a flannel shirt and jeans. He’s been wearing it consistently over the last couple fall seasons. It’s not the warmest option in freezing 30-degree temps, so it might be wise to wear with thicker socks. It’s made with full-grain leather uppers, which age beautifully and bead off rain. Plus, the waterproof liners keep water from getting inside.

Recent findings suggest that full-grain leather is also tougher and more durable than corrected grain or split leather (found in cheaper boots) that have been sanded or split down, losing their outer layers. The break-in period takes a little patience, but after a few wears, this boot feels comfortable and natural. The Vibram outsole grips especially well on uneven terrain, whether you’re climbing trails in the Oregon mountains or navigating slick city streets in Fresh York. Between the outsole and insole, there’s a fiberglass shank—a thin, supportive layer that reinforces the midfoot. It helps keep your feet stable, prevents the boot from twisting, and reduces fatigue on long walks.

Recent findings suggest that red Wing has been crafting durable, American-made workwear for more than a century, supplying tradesmen, factory workers and miners with boots built to last. The Classic Moc Boot continues that tradition with a roomy moc toe, weatherproof leather construction, and a comfortable wedge sole that makes long hours on your feet far more manageable. (A moc toe is a stitched toe design where the seam wraps around the front of the boot, giving extra room and durability.).

It has been revealed that men’s Health designer Jason Speakman broke it in on a hike in upstate Latest York. Since the leather is a bit hefty, it did take some getting used to. But after about two or three wears, he remarked it didn’t feel as cramped as other moc toe boots he's tested. There was no strain on his feet after going from rocks to packed trails, and they stayed comfortable even on uneven terrain. Aesthetically, it has the rugged, All-American vibe that works on a job site, weekend trail, or just rolling up to the beer hall in jeans. The full-grain oiled leather is super premium, so this option will last years and develop a cool, worn-in patina.

Industry observers note that after doing some work in the yard for hours on end, Speakman found the EVA midsole—which is a foam material that’s both lightweight and strong—makes this boot the most comfortable option for raking leaves and pushing a lawnmower. It also handles hard surfaces like concrete or brick, keeping your feet cushioned and protected from constant pounding.

If you’re looking for a hiking boot that won’t make your wallet flinch but still performs like something far more expensive, the Nortiv8’s offering is an easy win. On the trail it proved, while affordable, that it’s not cheaply made. Right out of the box, the waterproof synthetic leather and textile upper felt surprisingly substantial—not floppy or flimsy like some lower-cost boots. The material stood up to brush and rocks on a muddy forest loop, and after hours of hauling gear and setting up camp in wet grass, it still looked crisp with no signs of fraying.

The waterproof membrane lived up to its promise during shallow creek crossings and soggy morning hikes; my socks stayed dry every time, even when water pooled around my feet. Underfoot, the rubber lug outsole delivered dependable traction. I tested it while fishing and the grip felt stable and sturdy. The midsole’s cushioned EVA foam struck a nice balance too: supportive on long miles but soft enough that my feet didn’t feel trashed by day’s end. It’s not an ultralight trail runner, but for hiking, camping, fishing, and general outdoor wear, the way these materials work together is impressive for the price.

Not many boots can pull off a tailored suit, but Frye’s luxe ankle style is the rare exception. I’ve been wearing mine for the past couple months, and it instantly makes any semi-formal fit feel sharper. The design is simple but polished with a premium leather upper and is stitched around the edge for extra durability. I wore it in light rain and the material dried in seconds. I also found the inner-side zipper makes life so much easier when I’m slipping it on and off after a long day. It was refreshing that it didn’t require an annoying break-in period. When I first tried it on, I realized I had wiggle room in the toe area right away.

After five wears, the leather starts to crease naturally, but that adds personality to the boot without it looking worn. I’ve tested it on city streets and light rain, and the grip is solid enough to feel confident walking anywhere without slipping or scuffing the leather. The ankle height is flattering, the shape is not heavy-looking, and the richness of the leather colors pairs with different outfits. You can rock jeans and a sweater for a casual lunch, or dress it up with slacks and a blazer.

In a recent development, sure, this boot isn’t cheap, but the quality, durability, and timeless design make it worth the investment. You’re paying for a boot that will remain in good condition for years, look better as it ages, and feel comfortable from day one.

Sources indicate that leather is a reliable choice for everyday boots because it can be durable and develop character with wear. Full-grain and nubuck each have their own look and feel, but neither guarantees waterproof protection on its own. If you’re regularly walking through rain or slush, look for a waterproof membrane or specifically waterproof construction.

EVA foam midsoles are lightweight and cushioned, perfect for long days on your feet. Some boots use polyurethane midsoles, which are a bit heavier but offer more durability and stability, especially if you’re on rugged terrain.

Sources indicate that your traction and durability depend on this part. Vibram outsoles are often considered the gold standard for their grip and long-lasting wear. Rubber outsoles are common on everyday and outdoor boots because they can provide traction and abrasion resistance. Grip varies by rubber compound and tread pattern, so look for an outsole designed for the surfaces and conditions you’ll encounter.

According to recent reports, goodyear-welted boots can be a good investment because their construction often allows the outsole to be replaced when it wears down. The welt can also help limit water intrusion, although the construction alone doesn’t make a boot waterproof.

Our fashion team, led by longtime boots enthusiast and Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan, found the most comfortable and durable options out there. We put more than 50 pairs of boots through the wringer, wearing them across cobblestone New York streets, rainy city commutes, long-distance hikes, and casual weekends around town. In each test, we looked closely at grip, how the soles handled slick surfaces, insulation to keep feet warm in cold weather, and waterproofing to make sure soggy socks weren’t part of the deal. We also rewarded boots that could pull double duty: looking sharp with dress pants or a suit while still holding up for more rugged, off-duty wear.

  • In a recent development, ahead of the next phase in the United States’ recycled life, divers from the RV Explorer swam to document the vessel’s location and post-scuttling condition.
  • According to recent reports, “It was just epic,” diver Rustin Cassway told a local Philadelphia news outlet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it took a few hours longer than expected, but the SS United States now rests at the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico. The nearly 1,000-foot-long ocean liner sank off the coast of Pensacola, Florida, to a depth of about 190 feet on November 11, where it is now officially the world’s largest artificial reef. In the years ahead, biologists and conservationists will monitor the vessel’s remains as numerous marine species slowly convert the ship into their own home.

In a recent development, ahead of the next phase in the United States’ recycled life, divers from the RV Explorer swam to document the vessel’s location and post-scuttling condition. On November 13, the team released a brief video of their successful excursion. Interestingly, the footage reveals the ship is resting upright on the ocean floor despite initially sinking on its side.

According to recent reports, “It was just epic,” diver Rustin Cassway told a local Philadelphia news outlet. “It was very cleaned up. I mean, you could see people really took their time to clean it really nicely.”.

Recent findings suggest that the project marks the first time ecologists will be able to monitor a shipwreck’s transformation in real-time. Researchers now plan to conduct annual visits to the SS United States to chart not only the artificial reef’s progress, but how the ship’s materials may affect the surrounding ocean conditions.

In its heyday, the SS United States was the world’s fastest ocean liner. Larger than the RMS Titanic, she was the most powerful, advanced, and modern passenger liner when she first took to the ocean in 1952. In addition to the 1,700 passengers, 7,935 quarts of ice cream and 500 pounds of caviar were also on board. During that maiden voyage (July 3-7, 1952), she broke the transatlantic speed record held by the RMS Queen Mary by over 10 hours. The United States made the crossing from the United Kingdom to Newly introduced York in three days, 10 hours, and 40 minutes at an average speed of 40.96 mph.

Recent findings suggest that she was designed by naval architect William Francis Gibbs (August 24, 1886 – September 6, 1967), and was built to be converted into a troopship if the United States Navy needed during a time of war. But she never was called into military service. Instead, the United States transported immigrants and celebrities, including future President and First Lady John and Jacqueline Kennedy, actors Grace Kelly, Gary Cooper, and Marilyn Monroe, artist Salvador Dali, and musicians Duke Ellington and Irving Berlin. Walt Disney even filmed parts of the 1962 comedy Bon Voyage aboard the ship.

An engineering marvel, some of the key design features were in the rudder, radar mast, and propellers.

Recent findings suggest that the rudder was designed for good maneuverability at high speeds. The Titanic’s relatively small rudder was one factor behind the ship’s collision with an iceberg and tragic sinking in 1912.

Industry observers note that the SS United States had the latest radar equipment, which allowed the crew to see the locations of  other ships and objects in the ocean despite the weather. It was among the first ocean liners to use radar, which was located at one of the highest points on the ship, so in addition to her radar “eyes,” a lookout could be stationed there to warn the captain of any danger in the ship’s path.

Considered a top-secret design, the ship had four propellers—two with four blades and two with five. According to the SS United States Conservancy, this configuration was tested and selected for its superior hydrodynamic performance. The propeller design was overseen by a pioneering Gibbs & Cox engineer named Elaine Kaplan.

According to recent reports, ocean liners became a less attractive option once air travel became quicker and less expensive. The SS United States ceased operations in 1969, and stayed in drydock in several cities before becoming the world’s largest artificial reef.

#121256. Muscle Size vs. Strength: Which Matters More for Living Longer? Experts Explain

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1762 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Womenshealthmag ↗ Open Full Page

Muscle Size vs. Strength: Which Matters More for Living Longer? Experts Explain

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1762 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, when it comes to aging well, you've probably heard that building muscle is one of the best things you can do for your body.
  • It has been revealed that resistance training, which is often used as an umbrella term, can have different goals, including building muscle size and increasing maximal strength.
  • On the other hand, training for maximal strength focuses on improving how much force your muscles can produce.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when it comes to aging well, you've probably heard that building muscle is one of the best things you can do for your body. And it's true: Maintaining muscle mass is essential for staying healthy, mobile, and independent as you get older. But here's something you might not realize: Having more muscle doesn't necessarily mean you're stronger. And when it comes to living as long (and as well!) as possible, that distinction matters.

It has been revealed that resistance training, which is often used as an umbrella term, can have different goals, including building muscle size and increasing maximal strength. Training for muscle growth, known as hypertrophy training, focuses on increasing the size of your muscles, states Vonda Wright, MD, an orthopedic surgeon who researches longevity and muscle health.

On the other hand, training for maximal strength focuses on improving how much force your muscles can produce. It’s often measured by how much weight you can lift in a particular exercise, Dr. Wright explains. Although larger muscles have the potential to produce more force, muscle size alone doesn’t determine strength. “That’s why someone who is smaller can sometimes be stronger than someone with visibly larger muscles,” she adds.

According to recent reports, meet the experts: Vonda Wright, MD, is an orthopedic surgeon and author of Unbreakable. Mark Kovacs, PhD, CSCS, is an exercise physiologist, longevity and human performance specialist, and founder of the Kovacs Institute in Atlanta. Stuart Phillips, PhD, is a muscle researcher and professor of kinesiology at McMaster University. Ben Walker, CPT, is a personal trainer and founder of Anywhere Fitness in Dublin, Ireland.

Still, both adaptations play an important role in healthy aging—especially since muscle mass and strength naturally decline with age. Building muscle supports your joints and bones, helps regulate metabolic health, and gives you the strength and physical capacity to keep moving and stay active, states Mark Kovacs, PhD, CSCS, an exercise physiologist, longevity and human performance specialist, and founder of the Kovacs Institute. Strength, meanwhile, allows you to put that muscle to work, whether you’re carrying groceries, climbing stairs, or getting up from the floor, he explains.

Recent findings suggest that it’s imperative to build both strength and muscle for a long, healthy life. But if your goal is to stay active and independent well into your later years, one may be worth prioritizing over the other.

It has been revealed that resistance training can help you build muscle and become stronger, but these are distinct goals that emphasize different outcomes. Training for muscle growth focuses on increasing muscle size, while training for maximal strength focuses on improving how much force you can produce, says Kovacs. The two goals overlap, and people typically gain both muscle and strength through resistance training. But you can formulate your workouts to emphasize one outcome over the other, he adds.

Sources indicate that for instance, if your goal is maximal strength, the weight you lift matters more. So, training for strength means practicing movements with loads that feel heavy to you, claims Stuart Phillips, PhD, a muscle researcher and professor of kinesiology at McMaster University. Strength gains depend not only on muscle size, but also on how effectively your nervous system activates your muscles and how efficiently you perform the movement. “Lighter weights can still make you stronger, but taking them to failure doesn’t automatically make them equivalent to heavier training for maximizing strength,” Phillips explains. For this goal, he recommends 2 to 3 sets of roughly 4 to 8 reps with a challenging weight, stopping before your technique breaks down.

In terms of muscle growth, both lighter and heavier weights can build muscle—what matters is that your body is sufficiently challenged. Of course, lighter weights will require more repetitions to grow muscle, Phillips says. (In fact, his research highlights that performing roughly 20 to 25 repetitions with light weights produced similar muscle growth to sets of 8 to 12 repetitions with heavier weights when both were taken to failure.).

Sources indicate that as a rule of thumb, Phillips recommends choosing a weight that makes the last few reps feel challenging while leaving about two good reps in reserve. (If you finish 25 reps and feel like you could easily do five more, the weight is probably too light to provide enough of a stimulus to spark growth.) One way to gauge this is with the resistance-training rating of perceived exertion (RPE) scale, which measures how hard a set feels based on how many more reps you think you could complete with good form, he explains. The scale runs from 1 to 10: An RPE of eight means you could squeeze out about two more reps, a 9 means you have one left, and a 10 means you’ve reached failure and can’t complete another rep.

According to recent reports, the number of sets you perform matters for building muscle, too. Doing one challenging set per exercise consistently over time can grow muscle, Phillips says, but research suggests that performing multiple sets generally leads to greater muscle growth.

Strength, which is the maximum force you can produce in a particular task, directly influences how well you can move through everyday life. “Strong muscles support our skeleton, protect our joints, improve metabolic health, and allow us to continue doing the things we love at 50, 70, and 90,” says Dr. Wright. Strength helps us with getting up off the floor, carrying our own suitcase, climbing a mountain, playing with grandchildren, and living independently long-term.

It has been revealed that consider something as simple as getting out of a chair. When you’re younger and stronger, Kovacs notes that movement may require only a small percentage of your maximum strength. As you lose strength with age, though, that same movement requires more of what you have available. If you aren’t regularly training it, everyday activities can become increasingly difficult, he explains. But when you continue to build strength as you age, you have more to pull from, making those activities easier.

According to recent reports, additionally, research draws a direct connection between strength and a longer life: A 2026 study in JAMA Network Open looked at the association between muscular strength and mortality. Over 5,000 women ages 63 to 99 underwent testing for grip strength, chair stand performance, and a timed walk test. Participants also mailed health revision questionnaires annually between 2012 and 2014 until 2023. They found that higher muscle strength was associated with lower mortality.

According to recent reports, strength training is also associated with cardiometabolic benefits, endurance performance, and bone density—which are all important for living long and well. In fact, a small 2022 study in Sensors had 29 postmenopausal women with osteopenia or osteoporosis (when you have lower bone mineral density than normal) either do strength training exercises with heavy and moderately heavy weights, or no exercise at all, for six months. The group that strength trained had higher bone mineral density at the end of the trial period.

Recent findings suggest that muscle is one of your body’s best forms of insurance for getting older. Everyday activities depend on having enough muscle (as well as strength) to do them independently. “Muscle supports our joints and loads our bones, helping stimulate the bone-building process, but it’s also essential to mobility and functional strength," Dr. Wright explains. “If we want to continue getting ourselves off the ground, climbing stairs, carrying things, traveling, playing sports, and living independently, we need muscle to do it.”.

Recent findings suggest that research also concludes that less muscle mass is associated with a higher risk of mortality. A 2023 review in PLOS One observed 16 studies with over 81,000 participants and looked at the connection between their body composition and when they died. The review concluded that a low skeletal muscle mass index was significantly associated with an increased risk of all-cause mortality.

Additionally, having muscle mass can improve your metabolic health. A 2025 study in Nutrition & Metabolism had older participants with type 2 diabetes either build muscle through resistance training alone, resistance training and eating a whey protein supplement, or doing neither of the two, for 12 weeks. Those who completed the muscle-building interventions significantly improved their blood glucose control and insulin resistance.

Plus, lower muscle mass is linked to poor balance and a higher risk of falls. So, maintaining muscle helps protect your mobility and independence as you age, Dr. Wright adds. A 2020 study in Menopause Review had 122 women over 60 do physical performance tests (gait speed test, grip strength, and a timed up and go). Their body composition was measured, and they filled out a survey of how often they fell in the past year. Less muscle was associated with a higher risk of falls.

According to recent reports, A well-rounded workout plan should naturally progress both muscular size and strength. After all, they address different pieces of the same puzzle and one form of training can help you make progress in the other. As you build muscle, you generally increase the amount of tissue available to produce force, states Ben Walker, CPT, a certified personal trainer and founder of Anywhere Fitness in Dublin, Ireland. And as you train for strength, your brain and nervous system become better at coordinating and activating those muscles, he explains.

If you’re looking for a blueprint that’ll help you build both strength and muscle, check out our Women’s Health+ exclusive workout plans. Each one comes with four weeks of expert-programmed workouts, science-backed nutrition advice, and evidence-based recovery methods.

Remember, longevity isn’t about simply adding years to your life. It’s about extending your healthspan, or the number of years you remain healthy, mobile, and strong. “The goal is to bring our healthspan as close to our lifespan as possible, and for me, that means building a body that can carry you through the life you want to live,” notes Dr. Wright. That way, you’ll be ready to throw grandkids around at 60, deadlift hundreds of pounds at 70, and lift your own suitcase on vacation with your family in your 80s and beyond.

#121255. Why Your Brain Feels Tired When Your Body Isn't

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (766 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Why Your Brain Feels Tired When Your Body Isn't

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (766 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • You’re sitting down at your computer to answer one simple email.
  • Sources indicate that you read the first paragraph—and re-read it to make sure you got everything.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

You’re sitting down at your computer to answer one simple email.

Sources indicate that you read the first paragraph—and re-read it to make sure you got everything. But the second paragraph is harder to read because your attention keeps getting pulled away—to other messages, to your calendar for upcoming meetings, to a text message that just came in.

And even though you can go back to reading your work after that, you find that you can’t remember what you were trying to say in the first place.

It has been revealed that you are not physically tired. You haven’t done any physical activity, and you haven’t left your desk all day. So, why do you feel like your brain is done for the day?

Recent findings suggest that you might have been concentrating, making decisions, solving problems, or switching between tasks. Sometimes, switching between tasks can be the most tiring.

People who experience mental fatigue report thinking slowly, getting annoyed easily, and struggling to focus on a task in front of them.

This form of fatigue causes people to feel like they are at maximum capacity and don’t want to make any more decisions.

The mental fatigue you feel is not all in your head.

Recent findings suggest that in a recent study, 117 adults participated in a randomized crossover design. After 45 minutes of sustained mental effort, in addition to rating their mental fatigue, participants were given a rigorous set of cognitive tests to complete.

After a 45-minute control task of simple work, the same set of tests and ratings were administered.

Furthermore, in addition to the typical decline in performance associated with mental fatigue, the participants completed a set of physical tests of performance that were rated by the participants themselves for how much effort they required and how much exertion they produced.

Effortful mental activity affects perception of physical effort and performance, as shown by Work Time Varying studies (long periods of work with demanding tasks) of 30 to 90 minutes duration, using either computerized tasks and/or self-report.

Results found that within a work period of extended duration, there was an increase in reported fatigue and a decline in performance on reaction time and accuracy tasks.

Also reported was an increase in decline in attentional control with corresponding changes in EEG measures of attentional control.

So there’s actually something going on when you say that your brain is done.

There is one thing called "tired." That name covers a variety of situations, all of them to be dealt with differently.

Mental tiredness is not the same as feeling sleepy (physical tiredness), and physical tiredness (after, for example, having lifted heavy things or engaging in sport) is not the same as feeling mentally tired after a long and stressful day.

In a recent development, there is a major overlap between these states of fatigue: After a sleepless night, our cognitive functions are affected; and after a long, stressful day, we are tired physically as well as mentally. Yet, they are not the same and must be combated in different ways.

It has been revealed that mental fatigue from task-switching, i.e., alternating focus between different tasks, is a serious distraction from one’s work, and it can feel like a heavy burden. The term "multitasking" is often used to describe such work behavior. However, in reality, the brain isn't doing multiple things at once. Instead, it is constantly shifting attention between different tasks.

According to recent reports, these tasks do not have to feel "dreadful" in order to be detrimental to one’s health. Each task-switch seems to be minor in itself, yet in the end, it leads to a lot of starting and stopping throughout the day. Sitting for long periods of time is, of course, bad, but sitting at a desk all day is not necessarily worse than standing for long periods of time and being on the move all day.

While there is no one-size-fits-all solution to fighting fatigue at work, certain things can help.

It has been revealed that habay J, Arenales Arauz YL, Proost M, et al. Mental fatigue negatively impacts cognitive and physical performance outcomes: A large-scale randomized crossover trial. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2026;58(2):225-241. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000003852.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • “I could easily imagine these robots being used as toys before we see them on rescue missions,” Cecilie Ryberg, Aarhus University chemist and study co-author, remarked in a profile.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A silicone frog built by engineers at Denmark’s Aarhus University can’t swim nearly as fast as its amphibian inspiration, but it still manages to get the job done without any moving parts. The odd invention owes its slow-but-steady aquatic maneuvering to a set of six artificial muscles specially designed to contract when exposed to near-infrared light.

Sources indicate that the team’s novel system is detailed in a study recently published in the journal Advanced Materials Technologies. Although similar setups may one day boost the capabilities of soft robots tasked with search and rescue or environmental monitoring, its creators are a bit more realistic about this frog-bot’s near-term uses.

“I could easily imagine these robots being used as toys before we see them on rescue missions,” Cecilie Ryberg, Aarhus University chemist and study co-author, remarked in a profile. “I think people would have fun playing with a frog like this using a suitable light source.”.

Each of the robot’s muscles is built using crystal elastomers. These materials are specifically manufactured to contract while they are heating, and then revert back to their original shape once cooled. In this case, Ryberg and her collaborators also added a molecule that converts near-infrared light into heat. This allows the muscles to tighten after directly exposing them to a lamp. That said, the process isn’t as simple as sticking the elastomers onto their model frog and dropping it into water.

Industry observers note that “Getting the six muscles to work together was a major challenge,” explained Brigitte Städler, a study co-author and Aarhus University chemist. “If they don’t contract in a coordinated way, the frog won’t swim forwards. It may simply spin around.”.

Sources indicate that A lot of trial-and-error also went into concocting the elastomers themselves. In addition to contracting properly, the material needed the proper consistency to use in a 3D printer. To do this, Ryberg experimented with various molecular ingredients and molecule chain lengths to perfect the robot muscle recipe.

Sources indicate that “In a conventional 3D printer, you typically melt a solid plastic filament. Our material is more like very thick syrup or icing that you squeeze through a piping bag when decorating a cake,” noted Ryberg.

The final result is a light-powered soft robot that’s quite unique, but also not in any hurry. At its best pace, the frog swam a little over three inches in about two minutes. That may not get it to its destination swiftly, but the proof-of-concept successfully offers a new way to think about robotic design, and the ways engineers can power their creations. Until then, there is always the potential for robo-frog toys.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Industry observers note that BACK PAIN DOESN'T care about your massive aims to sail through life in comfort, making it hard to do everything from getting in a workout to sitting at your computer. Relief can come in many forms, including regularly stretching and strengthening the surrounding muscles, but sometimes, it can also involve using one of the best inversion tables to ease pressure on your back.

“An inversion table is a device that allows you to hang at an angle, or even upside down, with your feet secured,” explains Max Shlykov, MD, an orthopedic spine surgeon at the Maryland Spine Center. “This position stretches and decompresses the spine and surrounding muscles.”.

It has been revealed that it’s vital to get this out of the way now: An inversion table won’t magically cure your back pain or fix the underlying cause of it. But it can temporarily ease your pain and the tension that’s contributing to it. Inversion tables tend to be especially helpful for people with chronic back issues like herniated discs, sciatica, degenerative disc disease, muscle spasms, or general stiffness, according to Shayan Ghadamabadi, DPT, a physical therapist at Michigan State University Health Care Physical & Occupational Therapy.

Industry observers note that the best inversion tables are sturdy enough to support your height and weight, with adjustable hanging angles, Dr. Shlykov says. “Models that are more lightweight may be easier on your back to use and set up,” he adds.

Recent findings suggest that you’re not born knowing how to pick an inversion table, making it vital to choose wisely. Here’s what to consider when looking for one of these pain-relieving tools, plus sturdy options to try. Because you need to know how to actually use one of these tables, we included advice for beginners to help put you on the right path to greater comfort.

It has been revealed that teeter’s FitSpine X3 Inversion Table hits all our best marks thanks to its durability, extended ankle lock handles, and secure, comfortable fit. The device is made with heat-treated steel for unmatched strength and support, and the foam backrest prevents your body from slipping or sliding while inverted, according to Dr. Wallace.

The comfortable table is lined with acupressure nodes to target and release trigger points, and Dr. Wallace notes the FlexTech bed moves with your body to enhance decompression and improve range of motion. You can also rest assured about safety features, as the patented wrap-around ankle cups are secure and supportive. Dr. Mesiwala says this is crucial for proper relaxation and effectiveness. What’s more, the lumbar bridge can help release lower back tension and alleviate glute pain triggered by sciatica.

You’ll also get access to a free personal training app with a library of video and audio guides for on and off the inversion table, Dr. Verma states. The only qualm? It may be difficult or time-consuming to assemble.

Industry observers note that the Innova ITX9900 Heavy Duty Inversion Therapy Table is a budget-friendly option that doesn’t compromise on quality, according to Dr. Wallace. It offers a six-position adjustable pin system for safety locking and consistent inversion, a large, padded backrest, and soft-touch foam handlebars for easy access to getting in and out of position, he indicates. This table is great for anyone, but it’s particularly good for beginners thanks to its ease of use and adjustable headrest, height, and footrest.

This inversion table also features a True Balance System, which helps owners find their center of gravity for smooth, seamless inversion. Not only will this maximize tension release, but it can also improve spinal decompression. Another pro: The headrest is adjustable, too.

When it comes to getting a full, comfortable stretch, the EP-560 is a safe bet. It features patented wrap-around ankle supports, an ergonomic T-grip ankle lock, and an easy-dial foot platform for a more comfortable, secure fit. The backrest is also a game-changer. Most inversion tables use a simple foam material; the EP-560 ComforTrak backrest is designed to reduce friction and enhance spinal stretch and decompression. We also love that it’s pretty customizable. It comes with built-in tools for easy adjustability, including a Lumbar Bridge for deeper traction on the lower back and Acupressure Nodes that target muscle tension.

The device is made out of an ultra-durable, heat-treated steel, adding an extra layer of strength and support. If you’re a little closer to the 300-lb range, this is a solid option.

Recent findings suggest that it’s on the pricier side, but the Harison Electric Inversion Table is a top pick for both Dr. Mesiwala and Dr. Verma thanks to its adjustable footbed, memory-foam backrest, and heavy-duty build. The device is made with seamless welding and a steel frame to support up to 350 pounds, and the ergonomic ankle lock design is supportive without feeling too tight or restrictive. Security is also a top priority, and the table includes a high-quality safety belt that allows you to strap in while inverted (on top of the secure ankle holders).

Industry observers note that the table is heavier than other options on this list, but it’s foldable for easy storage. It also includes a 30-day trial and replacement of spare parts within one year for no extra cost.

Industry observers note that if you’re looking for an inversion table that doubles as a massager, here’s your pick. There are also multiple mode settings to suit your massage and heat preferences, and the included user manual provides all necessary instructions and details.

It has been revealed that this model has a upcoming, improved ankle-holding system to reduce pressure on the ankles when inverted, while still ensuring a secure, protective fit. There’s also a six-position pin system on the side of the machine that lets you adjust the angle without dismounting the device.

Industry observers note that each inversion table accommodates different heights, so it's important to read the fine print. The Teclor Inversion Table adjusts to fit people up to 6'8", making it a good option for taller users. It also can support up to 350 pounds, one of the largest weight capacities you’ll find.

Industry observers note that this is a relatively simple inversion table, and the low price supports that. But you’ll still get a comfortably padded back, cushioned handles, and an easy-to-reach handle for adjustability. The ankle-holding system is thickly padded, too. A double-locking system helps to ensure your device is firmly in place when it’s in use. When you’re done inverting, it folds up small enough to stash in a closet.

Consider the Teeter FitSpine LX9 the slightly more luxurious version of our top pick, the X3. This has all the elements users love about the X3, including that durable heat-treated steel frame and padded back, but in a slightly sleeker, user-friendly design. The LX9 has an eight-point floating suspension system for a large range of motion, along with reinforced padded handles for a comfortable grip.

Recent findings suggest that enjoy eight acupressure nodes to help relieve muscle tension while you hang. The included lumbar bridge is adjustable and works to tweak your hip alignment. The LX9 has a step-through design with a specialized boarding platform to make it easy to get on and off. There’s even a built-in storage caddy to hold your gear while you invert.

Industry observers note that using an inversion table isn’t as simple as diving into a upcoming set of dumbbells. These devices require you to move your body upside-down, making it important to know what you’re doing and how to ease into the process.

According to recent reports, it’s important to start with a “modest” angle vs. going into a full-out inversion when you’re starting out, according to Raymond Agostino, DPT, owner of Agostino Athletics in Fort Myers, Florida. “The goal is to introduce your body to the position and create a gentle traction effect without overwhelming your system,” he says.

Industry observers note that agostino suggests starting with a gentle recline, like 20 to 25 degrees for 30 to 45 seconds and see how you feel. “If you feel comfortable and don't experience dizziness, increased pain, or other symptoms, you can gradually increase the time or angle over future sessions,” he states. Agostino recommends only changing one variable at a time—angle and inversion time—to ease yourself in. “You don't need to go farther upside down and stay there longer all at once,” he says.

It has been revealed that when you’re inverted, you may feel a pressure sensation in your head or a mild “head rush,” Agostino says. “When your head is positioned below your heart, blood pressure and pressure within the eyes can increase, which is one reason inversion feels very different from simply lying flat,” he explains. You might also feel a feeling of fullness in your head or facial pressure. “Those sensations should remain mild and should resolve when you return upright,” according to Agostino.

Recent findings suggest that agostino points out that you don’t get a trophy for going completely upside down. “If a smaller angle provides the stretch or relief you're looking for, there may be no reason to progress to a full inversion,” he indicates.

Industry observers note that safety is paramount when shopping for an inversion table. "It’s ideal to find a product with comfortable ankle straps and safety locks to keep you secure and in place," states Kushagra Verma, MD, a board-certified orthopedic spine surgeon at DISC Sports and Spine Center. You also want to make sure the table can be controlled and manipulated by the user if you initiative to use the device alone. Inversion tables should be used with caution, especially if you’re a beginner, says Rahul Shah, MD, a board-certified orthopedic spine and neck surgeon at Premier Orthopaedic Associates. Additionally, older adults and those who have chronic dizziness, high blood pressure, glaucoma, inner ear problems, heart disease, and/or severe injuries should avoid inversion tables without talking to their doctor first, he says. Keep this in mind, too, per Agostino: “A little pressure may be expected. Feeling like something is wrong is not something you need to train yourself to tolerate.” If it feels like your back pain is worsening, or if you develop new numbness, tingling, weakness, or radiating pain, Agostino recommends that you stop using the inversion tale.

According to recent reports, sturdiness and durability are crucial for preventing accidents or instability while you’re upside down, Dr. Verma claims. He recommends always looking for a product made with high-quality materials, such as stainless steel, to provide better support and longevity. Be sure to read customer reviews and seek expert opinions on the machine's sturdiness when shopping. Of course, all the selections on our list have been vetted in this way.

According to recent reports, in addition to safety features, all experts agree that it’s crucial to consider how much weight an inversion table can safely hold. (The machine should clearly state this in the product description.) Because the machine puts you in a rather compromising position, maximum weight capacity is key for keeping you safe and at ease, Dr. Shah notes. Going over the weight capacity raises the odds that the table will break or flip while you’re on it, potentially injuring you in the process, Agostino says.

According to recent reports, it’s notable to consider the table's length to ensure it accommodates your size and height, notes Ali Mesiwala, MD, a neurosurgeon and complex spine expert at DISC Sports and Spine Center. Most inversion tables are adjustable for a customized fit, but it’s best to ensure the maximum height is within your range for effective use. The width of the table is another key factor, as a wider table can offer more stability during inversion, particularly if you’re on the taller or heavier side, says Brian Wallace, DC, a chiropractor at Pinewood Family Care. As a general rule of thumb, the width of the table should be wide enough for your core to conformably fit and not fall to either side, Dr. Shah adds.

Industry observers note that depending on your needs, different inversion tables include add-on features like lumbar spine support, heat, memory foam, or massage elements, Dr. Wallace states. These extra features are not a necessity, but they can be beneficial if you’re looking for added comfort and therapeutic benefits, he says. Just remember: extra add-ons should be considered second to the table's fundamental stability, comfort, and safety.

Recent findings suggest that an inversion table isn’t the cheapest tool you’ll use to reduce your back pain, but there is a range to consider. Most tables will run you anywhere from $150 to $450, with higher-priced models having additional features like heat, memory foam, and massage.

Recent findings suggest that to track down the best inversion tables, Men’s Health editors, including contributor Korin Miller, consulted three orthopedic surgeons, a neurosurgeon, a chiropractor, and two physical therapists to learn more about the notable features to look for in an inversion table. From there, we looked at the most popular inversion tables on the market and narrowed the field based on our experts’ requirements. Each inversion table was ranked based on factors such as size, weight capacity, and safety features. This story was first published in August, and was updated in November to reflect the most recent products on the market, along with advice on how to use these machines.

Extended inversion can cause excessive blood flow to the head and lead to nausea, vomiting, and dizziness, so Dr. Mesiwala recommends using an inversion table for a maximum of five minutes at a time, up to twice a day. If you’re a beginner, he suggests only inverting for 30 seconds once a day as you get your bearings.

It has been revealed that the best time to use an inversion table is typically when your muscles are relaxed, such as after a workout at the end of the day, states Dr. Wallace. Remember: You should not be inverted for long periods, and it’s best to start slowly and work your way up to time and frequency.

This is ultimately up to you. Some people feel comfortable with their arms by their sides or crossed over their chest, while others prefer to stretch them overhead. You can also put your arms on the support bars. Essentially, you should do whatever feels comfortable to you.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

I REMEMBER being about 10 years old and spending hours in my grandmother’s product-strewn bathroom. In the middle of her pink-tiled bathroom was a small alcove with a skirted makeup table. Perched on top were probably a dozen, maybe more, intricately detailed glass perfume bottles and coordinating scented powders. The fragranced dusting powders were applied with oversized, almost-feathery puffs to absorb oil from the skin and leave it smelling fresh and clean, while the perfume itself acted like a topper, locking in the coordinating scent.

I was transfixed by the ritual of it. Scent has always had an emotional lure of sorts. Whether it transports you back in time or conjures a mood, the connections that fragrances evoke are personal and emotional. All that unfolds once a fragrance makes contact with the skin. As the notes dance and bloom, the scent really takes hold. But what if the skin-scent connection went one step further? Could a fragrance improve the tone, texture, quality, and health of our skin?

It’s no longer a theoretical—it’s reality.

Dual-purpose beauty products used to be a one-off. Nowadays, it’s expected that a product will tackle two concerns at once. “We’ve already seen growing interest in functional fragrances, scents formulated with sensitive skin in mind, and alternative fragrance formats like hair mists and body oils, so it’s not surprising to see brands exploring ways to incorporate skincare ingredients into traditional fragrance formats,” claims Darryl Do, a senior perfumer and fragrance expert at Delbia Do Fragrance & Flavors. The idea of perfume that offers skincare benefits is fitting, and, quite honestly, maybe even a little late to the game. “It feels relevant as consumers become more conscious of the ingredients in their beauty products and what they intend to deliver,” Do continues.

Sources indicate that meet the experts: Darryl Do is a senior perfumer and fragrance expert at Delbia Do Fragrance & Flavors. Jenna Queller, MD, is a dermatologist and founder of DermWorks in Boca Raton. Charlene Valledor is a cosmetic chemist and the co-founder and president of SOS Beauty. Farah K. Ahmed is president and CEO of the fragrance creators association (FCA).

It has been revealed that as skincare and scent merges into a brand-new category, some are wondering what took so long. “Scent has long been part of wellness rituals,” notes Farah K. Ahmed, President & CEO Fragrance Creators Association (FCA). “What’s different today is that we have science showing that functional fragrances actually work.” We spoke with scent experts and a cosmetic chemist for the backstory on the trend and how to make the most of fragrances infused with skincare so you can reap the benefits.

Skin and scent have a long-standing connection. “In the fragrance industry, the term “skin scent” describes fragrances that are close to the natural scent of skin in order to complement it rather than overpower it,” says Do. But how a scent wears on the skin varies.

Industry observers note that it’s all comes down to body chemistry, which includes pH, how much natural oil is produced by your skin, moisture and perspiration levels, and natural odor, explains Charlene Valledor, a cosmetic chemist and the co-founder and president of SOS Beauty. That’s why the very same perfume can smell wildly different from one person to the next. Someone with a skin pH of 5.75, more sebum, or who eats a spicy diet, for example, will provide a different environment than someone with a skin pH of 4.75, drier skin, and eats virtually no spicy foods.

Industry observers note that but it doesn’t stop there: What you apply to your skin before perfume also influences how a fragrance takes hold. By the time most people finish their morning routine, they’ve already created a fragrance profile and applying perfume introduces another layer on top of that existing baseline, Do says.

Unfortunately, your skin doesn’t always play nicely with certain scents. The ingredients in the bottle themselves, which includes everything from the concentration of alcohol to the presence of essential oils can cause itching, redness, and general irritation. “Fragrance can directly disrupt skin’s protective barrier or trigger an outright allergic reaction,” explains board-certified dermatologist Jenna Queller, MD, founder of DermWorks in Boca Raton, FL. “Irritation can happen to anyone, particularly when the skin is already dry or compromised. An allergy is different: the immune system has become sensitized to a specific ingredient.”.

According to recent reports, dr. Queller claims that while certain compounds like cinnamal, eugenol, isoeugenol, and geraniol are well-known contact allergens and can damage or irritate the outer layer of skin and weaken the protective barrier, others, such as limonene and linalool, which are commonly found in citrus, floral, and herbal fragrances, can become more allergenic after exposure to air. “A higher concentrations can increase the risk of irritation,” she says. “However, no single concentration guarantees a product is safe for everyone. If you develop a true allergy, even a small amount can trigger a reaction.”.

Recent findings suggest that deciphering how much allergen is in a perfume—even in a natural or organic scent or essential oil, which isn’t necessarily a safe option for sensitive skin—is difficult. “You can’t judge a fragrance by how strong it smells,” Dr. Queller suggests. “Subtle scents can contain allergens, which is why the ingredient list matters more than the intensity.” If your skin is sensitive or dry, or you are rosacea- or eczema-prone, a fragrance intolerance or allergy, which often manifests as redness, itching, dryness, burning, and even swelling, hives, or blisters, is likely to form more easily, especially since she indicates the skin barrier may already be impaired.

So, what’s the best way to wear a fragrance while also safeguarding your skin’s health, especially if one of the trendier skincare-infused fragrances may not be a good fit? Dr. Queller suggests applying the scent to clothing rather than directly to the skin, although she states it’s not a guarantee because fragrance can transfer to the skin. Of course, each scents’ chemical composition can vary so naturally, a bit of trial and error may be involved to determine which irritate you specifically.

Recent findings suggest that the latest fragrance technology is innovative because it not only helps you avoid irritant reactions, it promises to care for a nurture skin directly. In fact, it seems we’re moving toward a world in which dual-purpose fragrances can leave you smelling good and feeling soft. It makes sense when you learn that keratinocytes—the primary cells in your epidermis—contain olfactory receptors that respond to certain fragrances, notes Dr. Queller. “Skin has its own sensory biology,” she says, “and research suggests scent may influence important cellular functions, including skin regeneration and wound healing.” In fact, one study indicated that Sandalore, a sandalwood note, activates a receptor that speeds up cell growth and migration to help close cuts and sores. Another research paper found that the same pathway prolonged the growth phase of cultured human hair follicles.

It’s a welcome development. We all live extremely busy, over-scheduled lives and most of us want beauty products that do more than one thing. The new Nakery Beauty Skin + Hair Exosome Perfume captures this ethos brilliantly. It combines plant-derived exosomes, thought to boost collagen, reduce inflammation, and support healthier-looking skin, with one of two scents: a warm blend of vanilla, amber, and almond or an oceanic mix of sheer musk, sea air notes, and driftwood. Similarly, Bella Hadid’s alcohol-free, essential oil-powered Orebella collection promises to hydrate skin with a bi-phase formula that simultaneously moisturizes while delivering a long-lasting scent. Another offering worth noting is Salt + Stone’s Body Mist. In six intoxicating scents, each light-as-air-mist is infused with glycerin and red algae for smooth, touchable skin. The idea of all of these is that rather than leaving your outer layer dehydrated and more susceptible to aging—a common complaint with scents formulated with alcohol—these products support dry skin and enhance its moisture levels.

Future Society’s unscented Base Scent follows a similar path in a different way. It works with the skin’s natural microbiome to help the body smell better. It relies on aspergillus ferment, zinc, and arginine, and you can wear it on its own or layer it over perfume to create a more neutral body scent over time. The microbiome also factors significantly into Argentum’s Les Perfumes Infinis collection. Water-based and free of potentially drying alcohol, each of the twelve scents is formulated in such a way as to not disrupt the delicate balance of bacteria naturally found on your outer layer.

Nakery Beauty Skin + Hair Exosome Perfume.

This fragrance, proven to last up to twelve hours, harnesses the power of plant-derived exosomes and an advanced hydration complex to hydrate skin and strengthen its barrier.

All of Orebella’s scents, including this brand-upcoming blend of creamy milk, woody amber, and fresh bergamot features a base of hydrating snow mushroom and the brand’s signature five-oil blend.

Salt & Stone Bergamot & Hinoki Body and Hair Fragrance Mist.

According to recent reports, salt + Stone’s body products have rightfully gained a cult following and their hair & body mists are no different. What does make them different is that they contain humectant glycerin to help skin hang onto moisture and red algae to promote smoothness. This bergamot and hinoki blend is one of their latest.

Sources indicate that A scent with no scent? Yup. This one is formulated with prebiotics that work with your skin’s natural microbiome to keep your natural scent more consistent and balanced.

ARgENTUM Les Parfums Infinis LOVER Eau de Parfum.

It has been revealed that each of these alcohol- and solvent-free fragrances is gentle on skin and blended based upon one of the main elements (Earth, Air, Water). Lover, for example, is a mix of geranium, rose, and berries meant to evoke a garden after a rainfall.

Industry observers note that so, can a few spritzes of a skin-boosting fragrance achieve the same goals as a watery serum or thicker moisturizer? Potentially, but as Dr. Queller shares, it really comes down to the formulation. “A fragrance that incorporates ingredients like hyaluronic acid, glycerin, ceramides, or nourishing emollients can help improve skin hydration and support the skin barrier.” Her advice? Look beyond the label and marketing claims. “A beautifully formulated fragrance can offer skincare benefits, but that doesn’t automatically make it suitable for sensitive skin.”.

Sources indicate that what is undoubtedly true is that the skin-scent connection remains strong, perhaps stronger than ever, and this new fragrance category may provide more options for those who may not have been able to wear scent before. These next-generation fragrances go one step further than functional fragrances, which can boost your mood, productivity, and wellness, to focus on skin health in a way that was never tackled before. So go ahead and douse yourself in one of these new skin health-boosting fragrances and wait for everyone to ask, “What perfume are you wearing?”.
