📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, finding an electric bike for a teenager can be surprisingly tricky. Parents generally want something safe, manageable, and from a reputable company. Teenagers, meanwhile, generally want something that doesn’t look like it was picked out by their parents.

The newly rolled out Juiced Scrambler Mini looks like it could do a pretty good job of threading that needle.

The fresh youth-sized e-bike takes the mini-motorcycle styling of Juiced’s larger Scrambler models and shrinks it down around 16-inch fat tires, creating a bike designed for riders between 4’0″ and 5’3″ (122 to 160 cm). But perhaps more importantly for parents, Juiced also built in a PIN-protected speed limiter known as Speed Lock that lets adults decide just how fast the bike can go.

Sources indicate that the Scrambler Mini ships set to a 10 mph (16 km/h) Beginner Mode, but its maximum speed can be adjusted anywhere from 1-20 mph (32 km/h) and then locked behind a four-digit PIN. Juiced notes that riders aged 8-12 should not exceed 10 mph, while riders 13 and older can use the bike at speeds up to 20 mph, subject of course to local laws and regulations. In almost every state and jurisdiction though, the bike will fit Class 2 designation for street-legal riding and bike lane operation.

According to recent reports, that setup seems like a pretty smart way to approach youth e-bikes. Instead of buying a slow bike that a teenager may quickly outgrow – or handing them a much faster machine before a parent thinks they’re ready – the same bike can essentially grow with the rider (with speed titrated by a parent or guardian).

And from the kid’s perspective, it certainly doesn’t look like a safety-first children’s bike.

The Scrambler Mini gets the same sort of moto-inspired styling that has defined Juiced’s Scrambler lineup, including a long bench seat, dual-crown-style fork, chunky 16 x 4-inch tires, and several appropriately loud color options including Blackberry, Fruit Punch, Blueberry, and Pink Lemonade.

Industry observers note that there’s some decent hardware underneath that styling, too. The rear hub motor is rated at 500W nominal and 1,092W peak with 80 Nm of torque. A removable 48V 10Ah battery using LG cells provides 480Wh of capacity, with Juiced claiming up to 40 miles (64 km) of range. Four levels of cadence-based pedal assist are included, as is a right-side thumb throttle.

According to recent reports, the bike also features Talon hydraulic disc brakes with large 180mm rotors front and rear, 50mm of front suspension travel, an integrated backlit LCD, a headlight, and a rear taillight with brake-light functionality. The single-speed bike weighs 59 lb (26.8 kg), has a 27.15-inch seat height, and is rated for up to 275 lb (125 kg) of payload.

Those parts are far above what we normally see on e-bikes targeted towards teens, with most teen-focused e-bikes sporting cheaper components like mechanical brakes and rigid forks.

Industry observers note that the Scrambler Mini is listed at $1,099, though Juiced is currently offering a Black Friday sale that drops the price by another $150 to just $949. The company says preorders are expected to begin shipping the week of December 7.

That price also comes with something increasingly important in the crowded youth e-bike market: an actual company standing behind the bike. Juiced was founded in 2009, rapidly becoming a leader in the market for powerful and stylish e-bikes. But after the brand’s financial troubles a few years ago, Lectric eBikes stepped in to take Juiced under its wing in 2025. The relaunched Juiced now offers a three-year manufacturer warranty and US-based support, plus the peace of mind that comes with backing from North America’s largest e-bike company, Lectric eBikes.

That last part may be just as appealing to parents as the speed limiter, though the 3-year warranty is definitely a deal sweetener, too.

There’s always going to be some controversy around the idea of e-bikes marketed towards teens, but I’m for it when done responsibly. Let’s face it: e-bikes are incredibly popular and teens are already going to be riding them, even if it means borrowing a friend’s e-bike because they don’t have their own. So if they’re going to be riding, the least we can do is put them on a safer, higher-quality bike so they learn the right skills in the right environment. And hey, it sure beats teens sitting alone in their rooms texting each other all afternoon.

Industry observers note that when it comes to choosing an e-bike, there are already plenty of cheap mini e-bikes and electric dirt bike-style machines floating around online, and many are undoubtedly going to look tempting to teenagers. The Scrambler Mini seems to take a different approach, giving young riders the styling, fat tires, throttle, and mini-moto attitude they actually want, while giving parents control over how much of that performance they can access.

It’s still an e-bike capable of 20 mph, and that means parents need to make decisions about where, when, and how their kids ride it. And there’s even an argument to be made for removing the throttle and turning it into a Class 1 e-bike in the beginning, requiring a teen to pedal it to engage the motor. But I’d much rather see that conversation happening around a bike with hydraulic brakes, lights, a programmable speed limit, and a real tech giant standing behind it than around some anonymous electric mini-bike bought from the depths of the internet.

And if the teenager thinks it looks cool enough to actually ride, that’s probably the point.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A nuclear submarine recently returned to Scotland after setting a Royal Navy record of 217 days underwater.
  • “The fleet was designed around three-month tours, and that was considered to be a long time to be stuck underwater in a metal box with no contact with the outside world,” nuclear submarine expert David Cullen told The Guardian on November 15.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A nuclear submarine recently returned to Scotland after setting a Royal Navy record of 217 days underwater. The HMS Vengeance’s seven-month deployment overtook the 205-day milestone set by the HMS Vanguard in April. But with the Vengeance crew finally back home, critics now argue the two submarines’ lengthy back-to-back voyages are causes for concern, not celebration.

“The fleet was designed around three-month tours, and that was considered to be a long time to be stuck underwater in a metal box with no contact with the outside world,” nuclear submarine expert David Cullen told The Guardian on November 15.

Industry observers note that the 17,526-ton, nearly 500-foot-long HMS Vengeance is one of Britain’s four Vanguard-class submarines constructed to carry monstrous Trident nuclear missiles. First launched in 1998, the vessel features 16 missile tubes, each loaded with one Trident containing up to a dozen, 100-kiloton multiple independently targetable reentry vehicles (MIRVs). The MIRV is specifically engineered to simultaneously deploy a payload of individual nuclear weapons aimed at a list of targets. The Royal Navy continuously keeps at least one Vanguard submarine at sea, which hypothetically allows the United Kingdom to still conduct nuclear strikes in the event its land-based systems are compromised during a nuclear war.

Industry observers note that vanguard submarines were originally built to host around 140 crewmembers during three-to-four month deployments. Although a 100-day excursion was once considered rare, underwater stints are now often double the length of time, forcing sailors to stack extra provisions along already cramped corridors and inside any additional nooks. The U.K. government attributes the extended missions to budgetary cuts that have dramatically slowed down the pace of multimillion-dollar vessel maintenance projects.

Deployment aboard a submarine like the Vengeance is considered one of the navy’s most psychologically difficult assignments. The nuclear sub remains underwater in total radio silence for the entire length of a patrol to keep its position secret. The vessel can travel to a depth of around 984 feet, but it may occasionally ascend to shallower waters to communicate via a transmission buoy or floating wire antenna. Crewmembers may receive a weekly, 120-word “Familygram” message, but each dispatch is previewed by naval officials. These readers retain the right to censor any bad news or information they feel may compromise sailors’ effectiveness. Regardless of what a sailor ultimately reads, they are strictly prohibited from responding.

The toll on crew is steep, but it’s particularly difficult for the women comprising roughly 10-percent of the navy. In 2022, whistleblower Sophie Brook generated international headlines after reporting a “constant campaign of sexual bullying” while serving as one of the Royal Navy’s first female submariners. In 2024, First Sea Lord Adm. Sir Ben Key called the crew misogyny “intolerable” and apologized to the growing number of women who subsequently came forward with their own stories. The Royal Navy’s investigations ultimately resulted in the firing, demotion, and disciplining of dozens of servicemen—including Key’s own termination.

According to recent reports, key’s successor, Gen. Sir Gwyn Jenkins, remarked he had “nothing but tremendous respect” for Trident crews earlier this month, while admitting the need to “improve our submarine maintenance.”.

The Vanguard fleet was designed for about 25 years of service, but will likely accumulate roughly four decades of sailing by the time its first replacement is ready. That submarine, the HMS Dreadnought, isn’t expected to sail until around 2032.

Latest Update: Driving the Scion Kei Truck: Fun, But Not a Real Solution for Most Americans

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What started as a government-subsidized program to provide cheap, industrious transportation for a Japanese economy that had been ravaged by World War II has become a genuine American fixation.
  • As with all vehicles not originally built to U.S.
  • Officially known as the Scion by Toyota Kei-01, the rebadged Daihatsu Hijet is powered by a 660-cc three-cylinder gasoline engine making around 53 hp, which is fed through a continuously variable automatic transmission.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What started as a government-subsidized program to provide cheap, industrious transportation for a Japanese economy that had been ravaged by World War II has become a genuine American fixation. In mountainous resort towns in Colorado, Faulkner farmland in the Delta, and Northeast metropolises, the pint-size Kei truck has become a popular target for importers bringing examples from Japan. Now Toyota is set to dump fuel on that fire, as a brand-latest kei truck from the resurrected Scion brand will be offered in the U.S. market in 2027.

As with all vehicles not originally built to U.S. standards, federal Department of Transportation rules have limited American kei enthusiasts to importing 25-year-old examples of the miniature trucks. To be frank, most of these tired examples drive as one would expect of a work truck with a quarter century under its belt. Toyota’s incoming example is the exact opposite, as I got the chance to find out during a half-dozen laps of a half-mile cone course at Eagles Canyon Raceway outside Dallas.

Officially known as the Scion by Toyota Kei-01, the rebadged Daihatsu Hijet is powered by a 660-cc three-cylinder gasoline engine making around 53 hp, which is fed through a continuously variable automatic transmission. The Kei-01 is limited to 25 mph, far short of the 70 mph or so a Japanese-market Hijet can accomplish. That threshold was deliberately chosen to comply with federal safety requirements for low-speed vehicles, which mandate that the vehicle go faster than 20 mph but not faster than 25.

Sources indicate that yet that modest limit didn’t mean acceleration was lacking. When I moved the hilariously toylike shifter into drive and matted the gas, the Kei-01 jumped off the line like a puppy smelling sausages, growling and uncoordinated. The lack of gear ratios kept the tiny engine at high rpm, although the missing tach meant I couldn’t verify how fast it was spinning. Regardless, maximum speed was easily reached, according to the speedometer displaying kilometers per hour.

It has been revealed that the ergonomics of a kei truck meant I sat on top of the front wheels and had the Toyota-badged steering wheel tilted into my lap. Also, this being a product designed for the Japanese market, the steering wheel was positioned on the right; Toyota has no plans to reverse the layout for us. With 14-inch wheels and what are barely soccer-ball-diameter tires, the Kei-01 was agile to a fault; I suspect you could pretty much turn it inside a single Costco parking space. Directional changes happened rapidly, although the steering is high geared, and even slow-speed maneuvers elicited a special charm. That remarked, I wouldn’t want to haul it around a tight corner at any rate of speed. And the ride quality could be described generously as rudimentary. I bounced up and down in my adjustable seat over Toyota’s provided gravel course, the interior loudly rattling the whole time. However, as a dedicated work truck, this was hardly disqualifying.

Recent findings suggest that A button in the center console promised locking four-wheel-drive, though I didn’t get to use it. Slowing the Kei-01, with its curb weight of just over 2000 pounds, was as easy as letting off the accelerator. But front disc and rear drum brakes seemed powerful enough. Considering the modest limiter, you could just yank the analog, wire-operated parking brake.

Toyota hasn’t skimped on features. A central touchscreen tucked into the dashboard will supposedly have Apple CarPlay functionality when the Kei-01 arrives in the U.S. next year. Push-button start and slider-style climate controls will also be fitted as standard. For those who have bemoaned the rise of haptic-touch features, the Kei-01 will be the freshest breath of interior design air you’ve had in some time. Icons on the Kei-01’s dashboard even promised ADAS features like lane-departure control and collision warnings. Some of the touch surfaces were hard, and the doors felt featherlight, but who really cares?

The Kei-01’s payload capacity, scaled to its diminutive dimensions, is just 600 pounds. But the three sides of the load bed can be folded down separately, boosting utility, meaning that trips to Home Depot are more likely to be limited by speed than cargo weight. A storage deck behind the seats is well suited for backpacks and toolboxes, and there are flat storage spaces on the dashboard and built into the roofline.

Before you check your credit score, there is a brutal catch to the possibility of buying the Kei-01. Toyota has stated it won’t sell the vehicle to individuals initially, with access limited to fleet operators.

The blueprint is to target luxury resorts, university administrations, and other institutions with the need for such compact utility. This makes sense given both the likely lack of profit in individual trucks and the logic of putting the trucks into the hands of what are likely to be safe, responsible customers with their own private road networks. Toyota hasn’t revealed pricing yet, but the Kei-01 will almost certainly carry a sizable upcharge over the equivalent Hijet, which costs about $9000 in Japan, with U.S. versions being built in Indiana.

According to recent reports, the brutal truth is that a maximum speed of 25 mph means the Scion Kei-01 simply isn’t suited to road use in much of the U.S. Even in the center of cities like Fresh York, where speed limits are largely set at that number, traffic normally flows considerably faster when free to do so. The prospect of trying to drive a Kei-01 on a faster-flowing highway surrounded by inattentive traffic is slightly terrifying. Toyota’s decision to keep the bulk of Kei-01s away from public roads is prudent, if a little disappointing. I’ve never had more fun going 25 mph.

#121204. How to Deal With People Who Always Excuse Their Bad Behavior

How to Deal With People Who Always Excuse Their Bad Behavior

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (883 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • You’ve met them; I’ve met them: folks who seem always critical or controlling, forgetful or unreliable, and often good at apologizing later.
  • Recent findings suggest that you want to be sympathetic and understanding, but over time, it all gets old.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

You’ve met them; I’ve met them: folks who seem always critical or controlling, forgetful or unreliable, and often good at apologizing later. But the apology often ends with a comment like, “I guess it’s just the way I am; I’ve been this way my whole life.” Or, “Because I’ve been doing _____ for so long, I guess my brain is wired to think in terms of ___.” Or, “Because I struggle with—ADHD, depression, anxiety, etc.—I can’t always do _____—e.g., not be late or follow through.”.

Recent findings suggest that you want to be sympathetic and understanding, but over time, it all gets old. In your heart of hearts, it starts to feel like a default excuse—their way of dismissing your feelings, of not considering or caring about you, and of leaving you not only frustrated but, at times, even emotionally manipulated.

In a recent development, what’s going on? Why do some people lean on personality weaknesses or mental health diagnoses to explain or excuse what is often simply bad behavior? Here are five common sources:.

Your father-in-law always seems critical of you, but in his mind, he is just expressing his opinion, making conversation, or even being helpful by offering suggestions. Pointing out that you feel criticized doesn’t help—he either thinks you’re being too sensitive or rationalizes it by blaming his ingrained habits: Because I’ve been supervising people my whole life, I guess I’m just wired to see the negative.

Industry observers note that for some, it’s understandable to be exhausted from trying to manage their depression, anxiety, ADHD, trauma reactions, etc. They've been through dozens of treatments, dozens of drugs that make minimal change at best, but no real relief. They are left feeling that this is what they have to deal with and, often, that they're sorry it affects you as well.

It has been revealed that this takes resignation to a higher level, where their struggles have solidified into their overall self-concept: I’m not just a person who struggles with high anxiety, but I am an anxious person, or You don’t understand—I have ______. Sometimes these folks can, understandably, seem overly assertive and rigid, or, once they've informed you, expect you to be automatically accepting and accommodating. If you are not, they can rapidly get upset.

Recent findings suggest that sorry I can’t come into work today, show up for the party, finish my work assignment, or so on because I’m having a flare, I forgot to take my meds, or my _________ is really bad. This goes from explanation to manipulation because they are lying, and their motive is clear: to use their real condition to get what they want. This is often a characterological problem where they lack empathy and use people as tools for their own ends.

Sources indicate that so how should you respond in these situations? At a basic level, it’s about shaping a two-sided relationship where you can only control your side. Here are some suggestions.

If your father-in-law keeps brushing off your comments about his criticism, even though you’ve gently explained how it affects you, it’s time to drill down: Ben, I know your comments come from good intentions, and you probably think I’m being overly sensitive, but I don’t understand how, if you care about me—and I believe you do—you don’t make an effort to stop doing what feels hurtful to me.

One obvious path is to have a conversation about that—the giving up—not as a therapist or as someone trying to fix them, but simply as someone who cares about them and wants to understand why they are so discouraged. Your deeper understanding can help you feel less frustrated and more accepting, and the conversation may help them be more sensitive to you.

Sources indicate that time to set boundaries. If you have the clout, call them out on their behavior—require a doctor’s note when they are out sick, or hold them to deadlines at work. If the relationship is more peer-to-peer, do what you need to stop feeling repeatedly taken advantage of: Speak up and tell them how you feel, but more importantly, stop making excuses for them, stop doing the heavy lifting in the relationship, and maybe end it.

Industry observers note that whether it's your dismissive father-in-law, your overly assertive or discouraged friend, or your manipulative employee, they may react negatively to your response, whatever it may be. This is about repairing communication. Here, you work on your side of the relationship by acknowledging their feelings and clarifying what you were trying to convey, without responding in kind or feeling the need to back down. Be sensitive and calm, yet assertive.

Relationships are no longer healthy when they feel out of balance—when you’re not getting enough back for what you give, when you feel used, abused, or simply dismissed. Step back, assess the relationship climate, and advocate for yourself to get what you need.

Is it time to stop making excuses for them and accepting what you get?

Sources indicate that taibbi, R. (2019). Boot camp therapy: Action-oriented approaches to anxiety, anger & depression. New York: Norton.

In a recent development, MANY OF US are spending time at a home office for at least a few hours per week these days. Whether it's working your 9-5, surfing the web, or maybe a little gaming, it's become somewhat normal for hours to slip by without moving much more than your fingers on the keyboard. Unless you're making a concerted effort to get your daily steps in, there's a good chance you could use a little help.

But there is hope for breaking up your most sedentary days: a treadmill desk. While it can't substitute for a rigorous workout (say, one on a traditional treadmill), an under-desk treadmill, like the best under-desk exercise bikes, can help you burn calories and get some steps while sending emails, watching TV, or frankly, any otherwise sedentary activity. Plus, most of them fit nicely beneath your favorite standing desk. And no, you don't need to hit 10,000 steps a day to reap the benefits.

In a recent development, A 2021 study found that using a treadmill desk can increase energy expenditure and metabolic rate, and may help prevent the health risks associated with sedentary work environments. So yeah, that means an under-desk treadmill just may help you stay in shape. And no, it's not a substitute for a cardio workout. But hey, getting a little more activity into your day is never a bad thing—and it doesn't hurt to wear walking shoes while doing it, too.

Industry observers note that sitting for extended periods has been linked to various health problems, including obesity, poor posture, musculoskeletal problems, cardiovascular disease, and even diabetes. And upping your daily step count with a treadmill desk is an approachable way to reduce sedentary behavior and its associated health risks.

In a recent development, increasing your daily movements by even 10 minutes can still make a positive impact on your long-term health. So if you're looking to add an under-desk treadmill to your work-from-home setup, we've got you covered. For the past two years, Men's Health's fitness team has researched and tested over a dozen under-desk treadmills from top home gym and cardio machine brands to find the best treadmill desks to buy in 2026.

Our editors and writers have researched various treadmills and walking pads by conducting market research, scouring forums, and drawing on our in-house team’s knowledge and expertise. From there, we sought to test some models in our office and home offices and to gather the experiences of fellow editors who frequently use walking pads. During our testing, we evaluated each under-desk treadmill on its cost, noise level, size, assembly process, stability, and ease of use. From our findings, we whittled it down to the following guide of the six best under-desk treadmills.

This makes it easy to customize your workout without stopping or bending down. Buyers have noted the remote battery is not included, so be aware.

It has been revealed that the treadmill is also Bluetooth-enabled, so you can pair it with a fitness app while you exercise. But with a weight capacity of just 220 pounds and a compact walking surface, it's not the most suitable choice for bigger or taller guys.

Most of the ultra-budget-friendly models we tested are bare-bones treadmill desks with modest features. The Unsit Under Desk Treadmill is in a class all its own. At nearly $2,600, it's the most expensive model we found. But that premium price tag also sets this one well above every other model in our roundup, too.The wide frame and belt provide 55% more usable walking space. That equates to easier, more comfortable walking with more naturally paced strides to help prevent soreness and injuries. It's also safer, because you're not trying to "fit" your natural gait into an unnaturally small footprint. This model is arguably the quietest on this list—"library quiet," according to Unsit and many reviewers. It's also built with heavy-duty, commercial-grade materials (supports up to 400 pounds) so it's designed to last for years.

It's also the only model we've found with a dedicated smartphone app. It connects the under-desk treadmill to your phone to track steps, distance, calories, and other stats all with a one-touch control setup.

On the downside, that beefy construction makes this the heaviest desk treadmill on this list at more than 160 pounds. We were surprised to find that the maximum speed is only 2 miles per hour. This is definitely more of an under-desk treadmill designed specifically to use while you work, rather than a portable treadmill that happens to fit in your office. Because, really, who is literally running during their hourly Zoom meetings?

In a recent development, this probably goes without saying, but you’ll want to double-check that the treadmill desks you’re shopping for will physically fit your home office. Pay close attention to the overall dimensions, so you can be sure it will fit under your desk. It also helps to have a few feet in every direction around the treadmill to allow enough freedom of movement.

Like all home gym equipment, stability equals safety. You want a treadmill that’s sturdy enough to support you properly. Look for metal frames, which often mean a heavier, more stable construction. If spending a little more money will "upgrade" your purchase from a cheaper, less stable frame to a stronger one, opt for the more expensive option. That increased peace of mind is always money well spent.

It has been revealed that if the treadmill desk setup you’re considering includes an attached or complementary desk, be sure it adjusts to a height that’s comfortable for you. Most feature variable table heights, so be sure it can be adjusted to a position that’s ideal for your workflow. Also, treadmills often offer an adjustable speed range, typically in 0.1-mile-per-hour increments. This guarantees the versatility to adapt to your growing fitness needs.

Belt-driven treadmill desks and under-desk treadmill models make noise just like standard treadmills. Not every manufacturer lists the average noise level of its treadmill. But, if a quieter workspace is key to you, be sure to ask or research reviews from other treadmill desk buyers to see what they have to say.

Recent findings suggest that many treadmill desks require at least light assembly. If you’re not DIY-inclined or just prefer your at-home gym equipment arrive preassembled, check the manufacturer’s website to see just how much assembly is required. In some cases, your retailer may offer assembly, either free or for an additional fee.

In a recent development, these days, many Americans are becoming sedentary. And we know how hard it is to pull yourself away from work, between meetings and deadlines, to go for a quick walk, but treadmill desks offer a solution to that dilemma.

Sources indicate that compared with traditional sitting desks, treadmill desks allow you to increase your physical activity levels while working. This can help improve your cardiovascular health, increase calorie burn, and reduce the risk of chronic diseases associated with a sedentary lifestyle. And who doesn't love a tool that helps you multitask these days?

Recent findings suggest that while research isn't conclusive, some studies have shown that using a treadmill desk can even improve productivity and cognitive function. Walking increases blood flow and oxygenation to the brain, which can enhance mental clarity and focus.

But it is notable to note that a treadmill desk may not be suitable for everyone. If you have an existing health condition, it's important to consult a healthcare provider before making any significant changes to your activity levels.

The Woodland version is bigger and more powerful than the standard Toyota bZ, and it may be a better deal right now.

Toyota now sells three electric SUVs in the US (see which one is the best fit for you): the bZ (previously called the bZ4Z), C-HR, and bZ Woodland.

The C-HR is a smaller, sportier crossover SUV, while the bZ Woodland adds a larger, more rugged option.

Toyota is right now offering a deal on the 2026 bZ Woodland for Black Friday that might be worth a look.

Industry observers note that the deal includes 0% APR financing for 72 months, plus an extra $1,000 Holiday Bonus Cash. Toyota stated that if you finance a newly introduced 2026 bZ Woodland for 72 payments, it will cost $13.89 for every $1,000 financed.

In comparison, the standard 2026 bZ is available with 1.99% interest for 72 months at $14.75 for every $1,000 financed.

It has been revealed that for leasing, the standard 2026 Toyota bZ is cheaper, starting at $369 per month. The deal is for a 36-month lease with $4,369 due at signing for an effective cost of $490 per month.

However, that’s for the single-motor FWD version. Upgrading to AWD will cost around $606 a month for the same 36-month lease with $4,369 due at signing.

It has been revealed that toyota is promoting 2026 bZ Woodland leases as low as $449 a month. That’s also for a 36-month lease with $4,448 due at signing.

The Toyota bZ Woodland comes standard with a dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain, delivering a combined 375 horsepower, which is 37 hp more than the standard bZ SUV with AWD.

Toyota’s standard bZ is offered with FWD and AWD powertrains. FWD models deliver either 165 hp (XLE FWD) or 221 hp (XLE FWD Plus and Limited FWD), while AWD models produce a combined 338 hp.

The Woodland model is also 6″ longer than the standard bZ, opening up an additional 30 cubic feet of cargo space on the inside.

Toyota’s bigger SUV also adds a rugged look and off-road capabilities with 8.3″ of ground clearance and up to 3,500 lbs of towing capacity.

Other rugged upgrades are standard, including All-Terrain tires, black side molding, roof rails, and black wheel arch cladding.

Inside, both come with a 7″ digital cluster and a large 14″ touchscreen running the latest Toyota Audio Multimedia system with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

In a recent development, although it uses the same 74.7-kWh battery as the standard bZ, the Woodland version offers slightly less driving range because of the added power and off-road equipment. The 2027 bZ Woodland has an estimated range of up to 281 miles with all-season tires, or 260 miles with the optional all-terrain tires.

According to recent reports, in comparison, the bZ is available with two battery packs: 57.7 kWh and 74.7 kWh. The base XLE FWD uses the 57.7 kWh battery, while the XLE AWD and FWD Plus, Limited AWD, and FWD models use the 74.7 kWh battery.

The standard 57.7 kWh battery provides an EPA range of up to 236 miles, while the 74.7 kWh battery provides up to 314 miles for FWD and 288 miles for AWD.

Both the bZ and bZ Woodland have a native NACS port, so drivers can use Tesla Superchargers without a separate adapter. It takes around 30 minutes to charge the battery from 10% to 80%.

The 2027 Toyota bZ Woodland is available in Base and Premium trims, starting at $45,380, or over $10,000 more than the standard bZ.

Which one would you choose? The standard Toyota bZ or the bZ Woodland? Let us know in the comments.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Finding the right fitness tracker is less about buying the most advanced wearable out there and more about choosing the one that will actually work for how you’ll use it to help you meet your fitness goals.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Finding the right fitness tracker is less about buying the most advanced wearable out there and more about choosing the one that will actually work for how you’ll use it to help you meet your fitness goals. You may want a smartwatch that can handle calls and texts along with fitness data tracking, or maybe you’re looking for a distraction-free screenless band that quietly tracks your metrics in the background. If running is your thing, you may want a smartwatch with GPS accuracy and real-time training metrics that are easy to read during a run, and if you’re focused on improving sleep, you may prefer a smart ring that won’t feel bulky overnight.

For this guide, we considered a range of fitness trackers for different training styles and tracking needs, from simple bands for everyday activity tracking to running watches, smartwatches, screenless wearables, and smart rings, all designed to monitor sleep, recovery, fitness, and health trends over time.

Whoop earned the top spot for the best overall fitness tracker because it provides deeper understanding of your data while also giving context of what all that data means. I’ve been using a Whoop for the past several years, and of all the fitness tracker options I’ve tested, it remains my hands-down favorite. It delivers some of the most useful recovery, sleep, and strain insights in a distraction-free design that’s so comfortable I often completely forget that I’m wearing it. The battery life is impressive, and I only have to charge mine twice a month.

It has been revealed that whoop 5.0 is built on the foundation of an app that offers analysis of your metrics paired with context, so you actually learn what all the numbers mean for your health and training. The screen-free design means that instead of buzzing constantly or encouraging you to check another display, it quietly tracks your metrics in the background and turns that data into recovery, strain, sleep data to give you an overall picture of your fitness within an app.

The sensor platform uses multi-wavelength optical heart rate sensors, skin-temperature sensing, blood oxygen monitoring, and accelerometer and gyroscope motion sensors to collect data continuously, tracking your resting heart rate, heart rate variability, respiratory rate, blood oxygen, skin temperature, sleep stages, strain, and recovery.

In a recent development, the app then interprets those numbers, in a way that feels more actionable than raw data alone, to generate a daily readiness score that indicates how much physical exertion your body is up for on any given day (00033though it’s always important to listen to your body regardless of what a wearable states). If you wake up with a low recovery score, for example, Whoop may recommend reducing workout intensity. If your sleep debt is climbing, it will show how much rest you need to get back on track.

It also offers other behavior change suggestions that could improve how you feel based on the data it collects about you and your habits over time. In fact, the in-depth habit tracking feature offers some of the most valuable insights into how day-to-day behaviors affect us physiologically. As a trainer, this has been one of the features I've seen make the most long-term impact with clients, as it really helps them connect the dots and understand how everything is interrelated.

Whoop 5.0 does require a membership and there are three different tiers, the main difference being the level of insights and analysis. Whoop One covers the core Whoop experience, including sleep, strain, recovery, steps, activity monitoring, heart-rate tracking, and women’s hormonal insights, which helps us see how menstrual cycle phases may relate to sleep, recovery, and performance. Whoop Peak adds a broader health and wellness layer, including health monitor, stress monitor, healthspan, and more advanced coaching-style insights for people who want to connect daily habits with longer-term performance and recovery trends (this is the tier I personally go with). Whoop Life is the most advanced tier, adding heart-health features such as ECG, irregular heart rhythm notifications, and blood pressure insights where available. Ultimately, the difference between the tiers is less about the tracker experience itself and more about how much interpretation, health context, and advanced monitoring you want.

The tradeoff is cost. Since Whoop uses a membership model, it will end up being more expensive over time than a tracker that doesn’t require a subscription. It also is not the best choice if you want live pace, distance, or workout stats on your wrist during a run. For that, a Garmin, Apple Watch, Samsung Galaxy Watch, or COROS watch will be more practical.

According to recent reports, the Google Fitbit Inspire earned its spot as the best budget pick because it gives you the core fitness-tracking features most people want in a slim and approachable design. It’s not trying to be a full smartwatch or a performance running watch. Instead, it focuses on the basics: steps, heart rate, workouts, sleep, active minutes, and general wellness trends.

That simplicity makes the Fitbit Inspire a good entry point for someone who wants to become more aware of their fitness data without getting buried in advanced metrics. It can track walks, gym workouts, casual runs, and sleep, while the Fitbit app makes the data easy to understand. You can quickly see how much movement you got throughout the day, how long you slept, and how your habits are trending over time. Additionally, you’ll get a stress management score, guided breathing sessions, and reminders to move.

It has been revealed that it is also one of the easiest trackers to wear all day. The band is slim enough to feel less bulky than a smartwatch, and the display is small but still easy to use for checking basic stats. If your main goals are walking more, staying accountable, improving sleep habits, or getting started with activity tracking, the Inspire offers strong value.

The main limitation is that it’s not necessarily built for serious training. Depending on the model, the GPS may rely on your phone rather than being fully built into the device, and runners who want advanced pace analysis, training load, recovery guidance, or race tools will likely outgrow it. But for the price, it’s one of the most practical fitness trackers for everyday use.

The Apple Watch Series 12 blends health tracking, workout features, smartwatch convenience, and safety tools better than almost any other wearable. If you already use an iPhone, this is the most seamless option in our guide.

Recent findings suggest that the Series 12 features more advanced sensor capabilities, including an upgraded optical heart sensor that measures heart rate every five seconds, and tracks HRV more frequently. WH associate fitness editor Addison Aloin wrote in her review that the Series 12 has “a great baseline of health and fitness features.”.

The Series 12 tracks a wide range of workouts, including running, walking, cycling, strength training, HIIT, yoga, Pilates, swimming, hiking, and many more. During activity, the display is bright and you can easily view data like pace, distance, heart rate, time, and workout zones during runs and workouts. It also integrates smoothly with Apple Fitness+, the Health app, and third-party training apps.

In a recent development, one of the most meaningful updates the Series 12 got is a fresh readiness score, which uses recent activity, training load, your sleep score, and overnight metrics like heart rate, respiratory rate, skin temperature, and recovery HRV to estimate how prepared your body is for exertion. The score runs from 0 to 10 and gives you a recommendation for your day, such as Recover, Pace Yourself, Ready, or Go For It. “My only complaint is that it’s kind of hard to find the readiness score on the watch and in the Health app,” Aloin claims.

Sources indicate that since it’s so much more than just a tracker you wear during workout, the Apple Watch also offers a lot of versatility. It can handle notifications, calls, music, maps, timers, contactless payments, fall detection, and emergency features, making it a strong option for anyone who wants one device that can move between workouts and everyday life.

It is also a good pick for people who like motivational nudges. Apple’s activity rings are simple, visual, and surprisingly effective if you respond well to daily goals. If you want coaching-style feedback without digging through complex training dashboards, the Series 12’s newer software can translate health and fitness data into easily digestible prompts.

It has been revealed that the Series 12 offers up to 24 hours of everyday battery life, and Apple says 15 minutes of charging can add up to 12 hours of battery. That makes it more manageable for overnight sleep tracking, but it still requires more planning than fitness trackers that last several days or longer on a single charge. “I’ve found the battery life is awesome for everyday use, but usually does need a charge every other day or so,” Aloin says.

Sources indicate that read More: Apple Watch Series 12 vs. Ultra 4.

The Google Fitbit Air gives you the quiet, distraction-free experience of a screenless wearable at a more approachable price point than premium recovery bands. The Fitbit Air tracks core metrics like activity, heart rate, sleep, and wellness trends over time, then sends that information to your phone.

Since there’s no screen, you’re not checking your wrist throughout the day. That makes it a strong option for anyone who wants to be more mindful about movement and sleep but doesn’t want a smartwatch. It’s also a good fit for people who are curious about screenless tracking but are not ready to commit to a more expensive platform. It offers a simpler, lower-pressure way to see whether passive health tracking actually helps your routine.

The Fitbit app is another advantage. Fitbit’s platform is approachable, especially for beginners, and tends to present health data in a way that feels less intimidating than more athlete-focused apps. That makes the Air a strong choice for casual customers who want guidance without performance overload.

In a recent development, the main limitation is that a screenless budget tracker will not replace a running watch or smartwatch. You will not get the same real-time workout stats, app support, phone features, or advanced training analysis. But if you want affordable, low-distraction tracking, Fitbit Air is a compelling pick.

It has been revealed that the Coros Pace 4 is our best lightweight pick because it delivers serious training features in a watch that feels easy to wear. After testing the watch for two months, MH deputy features editor Carina Hsieh noted that it feels so lightweight that you forget it’s there. It’s especially appealing for runners and fitness-minded owners who want more data than a basic tracker can provide but don’t want a bulky smartwatch.

Coros has built a strong reputation among runners because its watches tend to offer excellent battery life, practical training tools, and reliable GPS. The Pace 4 continues that tradition. “I was pleasantly surprised by how responsive and quick the GPS signal was on runs,” Hsieh said. She also noted that the watch had an exceptionally long battery life during her testing, and that she only had to charge it twice in two months.

Sources indicate that for runners, the Pace 4 can track pace, distance, heart rate, route data, workouts, recovery, and training trends. Features like race predictions, virtual pacing, breadcrumb navigation, and personalized training tools make it feel like a strong contender for anyone who is a serious runner. It is also useful for people who cross-train, since it can handle gym workouts, cycling, walking, and other activities.

A major reason to choose the Pace 4 over other smartwatches is that it feels purpose-built for fitness. You’re not paying for a huge app ecosystem or phone-like features. Instead, you’re getting a lightweight training watch that can help you understand your fitness, recovery, and progress.

Industry observers note that the Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 is the best fitness tracker for Android consumers, especially anyone with a Samsung Galaxy phone. It offers a polished smartwatch experience with robust health and fitness tools, making it a bit like an Android equivalent to the Apple Watch. WH beauty editor Nicole Saunders, who has tested multiple wearables over the years, notes she usually struggles to wear trackers consistently because the bands were uncomfortable overnight. But the Galaxy Watch 9 changed that. “The band is surprisingly comfortable to wear and, dare I say, actually looks good,” she said.

It has been revealed that this smartwatch tracks everyday activity, steps, heart rate, workouts, stress, sleep, and recovery-style metrics. It also includes Samsung’s Vitals feature, which monitors overnight patterns including heart rate, respiratory rate, blood oxygen, skin temperature, and other sleep-related signals, then compares them against your personal baseline. Saunders indicates it took about a full week for her baseline to set up, and anything outside of her normal range appeared in orange in the app, making it easy to compare metrics and spot subtle changes over time.

It also tracks a wide range of exercise modes, and its running features are useful for people who want coaching-style tools. Samsung’s body composition measurement feature can also be helpful for observing trends over time, though the numbers should be treated as estimates rather than medical-grade measurements. Saunders also liked the sleep features, including sleep quality tracking and snore detection, which she found both funny and potentially useful for better understanding nighttime habits.

The watch pairs easily with Galaxy phones, and the Samsung Health app organizes fitness and wellness data in an approachable way. If you want a tracker that can monitor workouts in the morning, handle notifications during the day, and track sleep at night, the Galaxy Watch 9 is a strong choice. In her testing, Saunders found it to be stylish and effective, adding that it would make a great gift for someone starting a health journey or looking for more detailed insights.

It has been revealed that the Oura Ring 5 offers robust health and sleep tracking in the most discreet package of all the fitness trackers in this guide. If you don’t like wearing a watch around the clock or simply prefer jewelry over a wristband, Oura is the easiest fitness tracker to live with. In her review, WH associate editor Olivia Luppino said it’s the only fitness tracker she’s ever used that she hasn’t wanted to take off.

In a recent development, the Oura Ring’s biggest strength is passive health tracking. It’s designed to unobtrusively monitor your body in the background, and then translate that information into readiness, sleep, activity, stress, temperature, and recovery insights in an easy to use app. It can be especially helpful for people who want to understand how sleep, illness, stress, menstrual cycle changes, and daily habits affect energy.

According to recent reports, for sleep tracking, the Ring 5 is one of the more comfortable options since a ring is less bulky than a watch, and many people find it easier to wear overnight. The app also makes sleep data easy to understand, showing not just how long you slept but how restorative that sleep may have been.

The tradeoff is workout tracking. Oura can track activity and has improved its fitness features, but it’s still not the best choice for people who want real-time stats during runs, strength workouts, or cycling sessions. It can also interfere with grip during weightlifting and kettlebell training. If you want to glance at pace, heart rate, or intervals mid-workout, choose a watch. If you want discreet, all-day and all-night health tracking, choose a smart ring.

For runners, the Garmin Forerunner 570 sits in a sweet spot between advanced training watches and an everyday wearable. Garmin makes several excellent Forerunner models, but the 570 offers a mix of running metrics, GPS tools, recovery insights, smartwatch features, and comfortable wearability for runners who want more than the basics without jumping straight to flagship option.

The Forerunner 570 is designed to be useful for structured training with its capability to track runs, intervals, long runs, tempo sessions, races, recovery runs, and cross-training workouts. It also gives runners access to Garmin’s broader training ecosystem, including performance metrics, suggested workouts, recovery guidance, HRV status, sleep data, training readiness-style insights, and race-related tools. For someone training for a 5K, half marathon, marathon, or simply trying to become a more consistent runner, those features can be super useful.

Industry observers note that it has a bright AMOLED display, touchscreen support as well as physical buttons, a feature that’s especially notable for runners since touchscreens can sometimes be frustrating with sweat, rain, or gloves. Battery life varies from 8 hours to up to 10 days depending on how many features you’re using.

The biggest drawback is price. Though it’s not the priciest Forerunner offering out there, the Forerunner 570 is not inexpensive, and newer runners who only want pace, distance, and heart rate may be perfectly happy with a more affordable Forerunner model. But runners who want a capable watch they won’t outgrow, the 570 is a great option.

The Garmin Cirqa is the best screenless tracker for lovers of the Garmin fitness ecosystem, since it integrates seamlessly with Garmin’s other tech. It delivers health and activity tracking without adding another display to your life, and is especially well suited for anyone who wants to use Garmin Connect but doesn't want to wear a full Garmin watch all day long.

That makes Cirqa especially useful for athletes who already own a Garmin running, cycling, or outdoor watch. You may want to wear your Forerunner for workouts and during runs, but prefer something smaller and screen-free for sleep, recovery, or everyday tracking. The Cirqa fills that gap.

Sources indicate that it also has a cost advantage over some screenless competitors because it doesn’t require a subscription. That makes it appealing for Garmin loyalists who want ongoing tracking without committing to a monthly membership.

The Cirqa isn’t the best choice if you want live workout stats, on-wrist coaching, or a display for pace and distance, and a Garmin watch would be better for that. But as a low-distraction daily tracker that complements Garmin’s training platform, Cirqa is a welcome addition to the category.

Industry observers note that the Google Fitbit Edge bridges the gap between a simple Fitbit band and a full smartwatch, making it a strong choice if you want a display but don’t want a bulkier smartwatch. It gives you a screen for checking stats, starting workouts, reviewing progress, and seeing basic information at a glance.

Sources indicate that compared with the Fitbit Air, the Edge is more interactive, compared with the Inspire, it’s a more advanced option, and compared with a Pixel Watch, it’s simpler to use and more fitness focused. It offers enough features to be useful throughout the day, tracking activity, workouts, sleep, heart-rate trends, and daily wellness data, while still keeping the overall experience lighter than a smartwatch. If you want a compact Google Fitbit tracker with a screen and stronger features than the entry-level models, the Edge is the best fit.

Sources indicate that A good heart rate monitor is one of the most important features to look for in a fitness tracker, whether you’re training seriously or just getting started. Heart rate data can help you better understand exercise intensity, track effort during workouts, and monitor resting heart rate over time, which can be a useful marker of cardiovascular fitness. While wrist-based trackers typically aren’t as precise as chest straps, they can still offer a helpful read on exertion levels during moderate to intense activity, according to a 2019 study in Cardiovascular Diagnosis & Therapy.

It has been revealed that sleep tracking can be a useful feature because sleep plays a major role in recovery, energy, mood, and overall performance. By tracking patterns like sleep duration, consistency, and overnight restlessness, a fitness tracker can help you spot habits that may be affecting how you feel the next day. Many models also break down sleep stages, show trends over time, and offer recovery or readiness insights based on your nightly data. While the numbers aren’t always perfect, they can provide a helpful starting point for understanding your routine and making small changes, like adjusting bedtime, limiting late caffeine, or improving sleep consistency.

Weight may not seem that vital at first, but it matters when you’re wearing a fitness tracker all day and night. A larger, heavier model can feel more noticeable over time, especially during sleep or long workouts. There’s no single ideal size, and the best option will depend on how you proposal to use it.

If you run, hike, or spend a lot of time outdoors, it may be worth choosing a more durable model, even if it’s slightly bulkier. For everyday wear, walking, strength training, or mostly indoor workouts, a lighter, lower-profile tracker may be more comfortable. Ultimately, the right fit comes down to your activity level, wrist size, and what you’ll actually want to keep wearing.

Recent findings suggest that many of the best fitness trackers can run for days or even weeks on a single charge, such as the Whoop 5.0. But battery doesn't always equate to quality, given that an option like the Apple Watch Series 12 needs to be charged every day and it’s still one of our absolute favorites. Ultimately it comes down to how a trackers charging needs will fit into your routine.

As with all tech, you want a fitness tracker that’s easy to use. If your upcoming tracker isn’t intuitive for you to set up or use daily, you’re far less likely to use it consistently. Ultimately, the only way to know for sure is to try it out yourself to see if it works for you. That's why it’s smart to buy a fitness tracker with a generous return policy.

I’ve been a certified personal trainer for more than a decade, and together with other Women’s Health editors, I’m constantly testing the latest fitness trackers across key factors like durability, comfort, features, and accuracy. We tested them during our workouts, on our runs, in Pilates class, and more. And of course, we tested them during sleep. Whether you’re training regularly or just want something for everyday activity tracking, the models we tested for the latest revision range from basic fitness trackers to powerful smartwatches and everything in between.

Losing Weight in Your 50s May Protect Your Heart Health Later in Life

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Losing weight in your 50s, even a modest amount, may help protect your heart health later in life, according to fresh research.Adults who lost weight in their early 50s saw their blood pressure, “good” cholesterol and inflammation change at about the same rate as adults who stayed at a healthy weight, according to a study from researchers at University College London and the University of Glasgow.Adults who gained weight in their early 50s saw those same measures worsen faster by their early 60s, the researchers reported.
  • Charis Bridger-Staatz, PhD, a senior research fellow at UCL, led the study.
  • The findings can apply to Americans because British and U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Losing weight in your 50s, even a modest amount, may help protect your heart health later in life, according to fresh research.Adults who lost weight in their early 50s saw their blood pressure, “good” cholesterol and inflammation change at about the same rate as adults who stayed at a healthy weight, according to a study from researchers at University College London and the University of Glasgow.Adults who gained weight in their early 50s saw those same measures worsen faster by their early 60s, the researchers reported. The authors posted the study on a research-sharing website on September 4. Other scientists have not yet peer-reviewed the work.

Charis Bridger-Staatz, PhD, a senior research fellow at UCL, led the study. She told Healthline the main takeaway for adults over 50 was that “it’s not too late to try and do things that are going to improve your health.”Nearly half of U.S. adults ages 40 to 59 had obesity from 2021 to 2023, the highest rate of any adult age group, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Among all U.S. adults, around 31.7% were overweight, according to the CDC.

The findings can apply to Americans because British and U.S. adults share similar weight patterns, noted Solveig Cunningham, PhD, a professor of global health at Emory University’s Rollins School of Public Health. Cunningham, who was not involved in the research, told Healthline that Americans tend to gain weight across adulthood.

“By the time you get into your 50s, close to the majority of Americans already have obesity. Many others have overweight,” she noted.The World Health Organization (WHO) calls obesity a chronic disease. Healthcare professionals diagnose overweight and obesity using a person’s weight and height, or body mass index (BMI).

Bridger-Staatz said the team set out to learn who lost weight and kept it off before GLP-1 weight loss medications became available, and whether that weight loss improved health over time.

She stated researchers had long assumed that “once people had become overweight or developed obesity, people didn’t really lose weight and certainly not sustained it.”The team also asked, she said, “can we try and say something positive about health that isn’t just this kind of like doom and gloom?”The researchers used the British 1958 National Child Development Study, which has followed about 17,500 people born during one week in 1958. Of those, 6,309 took part in a health check in their early 60s, according to the report.The team compared each person’s highest weight between ages 23 and 42 with their weight between ages 50 and 55. Researchers sorted people by whether they gained or lost more than 5% of their body weight and kept the change. For a 200-pound person, 5% equals 10 pounds.To track heart health, the team compared blood tests and blood pressure readings at ages 44 and 62 with those of people who maintained a healthy weight.“We know everyone’s heart health is kind of going to get a little bit worse over that time because you are aging and that’s expected,” Bridger-Staatz said. The question, she said, was, “Does it slow the rate at which people’s heart health is getting worse?”.

Weight loss slowed the decline in heart health for people who were overweight and for people with obesity, according to the report.People who were overweight and lost weight had the strongest positive results. By age 62, their body fat-to-lean tissue ratio matched that of the healthy-weight group. The authors wrote that differences in body fat may partly explain why weight changes affected heart health.People with obesity who lost weight had less body fat at 62 than people in the other obesity groups, according to the report.Sudhakara Chennareddy, MD, prevention cardiologist in the Center for Cardiovascular Prevention, Metabolism and Lipids at Georgia Heart Institute, told Healthline those results are what he’d expect. He was not involved in the research.“Even losing 5% has beneficial effects on the cardiovascular side effects,” he remarked. Long-term blood sugar was the exception. For people with obesity who lost weight, it rose more than in the healthy-weight group, though the authors reported that the result was not statistically significant.

A 2025 study of more than 15,000 U.S. adults, published in Endocrinology, Diabetes & Metabolism, found that adults who had previously had obesity tended to have higher blood sugar than those who had never had it, even after their BMI dropped.

Sources indicate that “It’s not the patient’s fault… We need to treat this one like any other chronic disease, like we treat hypertension or we treat diabetes,” Chennareddy noted.Compared with the healthy-weight group, people who gained weight in their early 50s had faster increases in blood pressure, blood fats, and inflammation, and declines in “good” cholesterol. Obesity is a chronic metabolic disease that leads to inflammation in the body, which can raise the risk of heart attack and stroke and worsen cholesterol levels, Chennareddy said. “The more weight they gain, they develop prediabetes and diabetes and fatty liver disease as well,” he said.These changes were largest for people who developed obesity or already had obesity and gained more weight, the researchers reported. This group also saw faster increases in long-term blood sugar levels.About 37% of participants gained more than 5% of their body weight in their early 50s. Only about 6% lost weight and kept it off, according to the study.“To me, that’s sort of the stronger message,” Cunningham said of the findings. Her advice for adults in their 50s is to avoid gaining weight.

People with obesity who lost and then gained the weight back saw faster drops in “good” cholesterol and faster rises in inflammation and long-term blood sugar.

By age 62, they weighed slightly less, on average, than people whose obesity remained steady, according to the report’s data. They also carried more body fat and had more inflammation.Weight cycling can do more harm than steady weight, Chennareddy noted. He gave the example of someone who gains 20 pounds, loses 30 and then gains 20 again. “That is even more detrimental,” he said.When people lose weight, the body slows its resting metabolism, he said. When the weight comes back, “most of the weight they gain is fat, not muscle,” he said. Even someone who loses and regains 5% to 7% of their body weight may end up with slightly less muscle and more fat, he said.Some research has shown that weight fluctuation is associated with a higher risk of high blood pressure and cardiovascular disease-related death.

The study’s weight changes took place between about 2008 and 2013, according to the study’s timeline.

Wegovy, a GLP-1 medication for weight management, launched in the United Kingdom in September 2023, according to the UK Department of Health and Social Care.Cunningham said the weight-cycling findings raised questions for people who take GLP-1 medications. She said drugmakers’ own data show that “once you get off of those, your weight is going to go right back to where it was before, possibly even worse.”That could create the same up-and-down pattern, Cunningham said. She added that researchers don’t yet know “what happens in the really long term” for people who take these medications.

Industry observers note that the study highlighted links between weight changes and heart health and cannot prove that weight changes caused the results, according to the authors. They wrote that the small number of people who lost weight made those results less precise.Bridger-Staatz also stated the team did not look at why or how people lost weight.

According to recent reports, cunningham remarked adults lose muscle and bone mass with age, and that the loss is especially pronounced for women in their 50s and older. “Maintaining muscles and maintaining bones is so, so important,” she said.Staying active helps people keep muscle, even without weight loss, Cunningham said. “Even a little bit of activity…just keep moving,” she said.GLP-1 medications work best as part of a “comprehensive proposal,” Chennareddy said. With his patients, he said he recommends continuous improvement rather than setting a goal to lose a specific amount of weight within a set period.Patients who treat weight loss as “a gradual process” do better long term, he said.“The most important thing is not to do fad diets,” Chennareddy said.For people losing weight, Chennareddy recommended:.

Anyone considering changes to their weight can talk with a healthcare professional about their weight history and goals.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that being stranded at the airport is no fun. You can only eat so many Auntie Anne's pretzels and play Candy Crush for so long; eventually, you need to get to your destination. But what if that destination is 1600 miles away, every flight in the country is grounded, and there are no rental cars or trains available?

Well, you could take an Uber to a local Ford dealership and drop $48,000 on a new Ford Bronco. And according to a report from NBC News, that is exactly what Tara Harding did.

According to NBC, Harding and two of her employees were in Charlotte, North Carolina for training, and were set to fly back home to Bismarck, North Dakota last Friday. That is, until the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) grounded all flights across the country. Thousands of flights were cancelled or delayed as a result.

In a recent development, the three women began to look at alternate transportation options, but none of them had any luck. There were no rental cars, buses, trains, or ride shares that could get them home. They were stuck in Charlotte. Harding called her husband to let him know, which is when her mother-in-law made a suggestion: “Why don’t you guys go buy a car?”.

It has been revealed that harding decided to investigate that possibility. Being what she described to NBC as a self-proclaimed “Ford girl,” Harding texted a local Ford dealer. The salesman said he would wait until the women arrived, which they did around 7:45 pm. Two hours and $48,000 later, Harding was the proud owner of a latest Ford Bronco. The road trip was on.

Harding is a nurse practitioner, and she owns her own clinic; she had patients scheduled for Monday, and she remarked she wanted to get her employees back home to their family. So, they covered the 1600 miles by driving 27 hours straight. The women took turns behind the wheel, sleeping while the others drove, while gas stations and drive-thrus provided the necessary fuel for both the Bronco and its occupants.

Originally, Harding noted she planned to sell the Bronco once she got home. However, she added that while she was catching up on sleep, her husband took it for three drives and decided he wanted to keep it. So, the nationwide flight may have cost Harding $48,000—but at least she now has a cool new Bronco, and one heck of a story to tell.

Latest Update: Peeping woodcocks are evolutionary oddballs

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (518 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As far as birds go, the eight known species of woodcock (genus Scolopax) look like they specifically evolved to go viral on the internet.
  • Woodcocks are part of the larger sandpiper family, but unlike their migratory relatives, most only travel extremely short seasonal distances.
  • In a recent development, “The distribution of woodcocks and snipes around the world is really unusual,” John Bates, the curator of birds at the Field Museum’s Negaunee Integrative Research Center in Chicago, stated in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As far as birds go, the eight known species of woodcock (genus Scolopax) look like they specifically evolved to go viral on the internet. You’ve probably seen at least a few videos of the birds on social media darting across beaches and being incredibly vocal. As if their small, squat bodies and comically long beaks weren’t enough, they also vocalize with distinctively cartoonish peeping tweets during their mating displays.

Woodcocks are part of the larger sandpiper family, but unlike their migratory relatives, most only travel extremely short seasonal distances. Six of the eight species are only found on specific islands, and some of them don’t even migrate at all. So how did these evolutionary oddballs even get their start—and stop migrating? To piece together their unique avian story, biologists analyzed the DNA of all eight woodcock species and 22 species of snipe.

In a recent development, “The distribution of woodcocks and snipes around the world is really unusual,” John Bates, the curator of birds at the Field Museum’s Negaunee Integrative Research Center in Chicago, stated in a statement. “They’re not terribly aerodynamic, and yet they’ve clearly gotten around.”.

According to recent reports, bates and his colleagues published the results of their work today in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS). The years-long endeavor involved not only examining preserved woodcock specimens housed in the Field Museum, but a fossilized sandpiper previously excavated from a cave site in Haiti. The remains found on the island of Hispaniola are around 1,000 years old, but that is still extremely young in the grand history of shorebirds.

It has been revealed that the earliest members of the sandpiper family began in the northern hemisphere before slowly migrating to islands along lower latitudes. Those birds subsequently migrated much shorter distances after settling in the warmer climates. However, they didn’t remain sedentary. Based on the DNA analysis detailed in their study, Bates and his team theorize that snipes from Africa eventually traveled across the Atlantic Ocean, then evolved into upcoming species in South America. From there, more of the birds made their way over the Pacific Ocean to New Zealand.

Their examinations also cleared up a bit of confusion. Biologists initially believed the fossilized sandpiper from Haiti was a woodcock, but the most recent data now shows that it’s a snipe.

Recent findings suggest that “Snipes and woodcocks have been around for 20 to 25 million years,” Bates explained. “Over that time, as fresh species have evolved and moved around the world, their migratory patterns have changed, too.”.

These changes are likely to continue amid today’s dramatic climate shifts, but that may pose a problem for the beloved woodcocks.

According to recent reports, “These are definitely birds that would be affected by changing habitats and changing climates,” said Bates. “Some of these woodcocks are found only in the mountain forests on islands between Asia and Australia, and if those forests get cut down, the birds are going to be gone too.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Volkswagen’s revived Scout brand finally has vehicles coming off the line in South Carolina, but they’re validation units, not customer cars. Scout confirms the first deliveries of the Traveler SUV and Terra pickup won’t happen until 2028.

That’s two years later than the 2026 production start the company was talking about before it even broke ground on its $2 billion factory.

According to recent reports, according to Scout’s announcement dated November 12, construction at the Production Center north of Columbia is in its final phase and most of the manufacturing equipment is installed. The Body Shop, Paint Shop, and Assembly Shop are all being used for the first validation builds.

The Body Shop is the most automated part of the plant. Scout says more than 750 robots join roughly 160 parts into each body, laying down about 5,000 weld points per vehicle, with AI-supported weld monitoring and a metrology system checking the results. At full capacity, the shop is designed to handle about 40 vehicles per hour.

Bodies then go through an electrified paint shop before landing in final assembly, where they’re married to the chassis and get their wiring, glass, seats, and wheels.

CEO Scott Keogh is clearly happy to have something physical to point to, saying that “what we are building in Blythewood is no longer a promise on paper.”.

Scout also shared photos of a Terra pickup and a Traveler parked inside the plant. Its own fine print notes that they show “concept and validation vehicles” with optional features, so don’t read too much into what’s on display:.

Fair enough. But Scout is also careful about what this stage is. Teams are confirming the equipment is installed and works, and checking engineering, buildability, and parts maturity. Process validation and scaling up to production speed come later. Validation builds will continue “into 2027,” followed by pre-production builds, and then customer deliveries in 2028.

The company notes the plant will create more than 4,000 jobs, and it’s spending another $300 million on an onsite supplier park expected to support about 1,000 supplier jobs.

When Keogh laid out the strategy in late 2023, Scout noted it would start production in 2026 with deliveries shortly after. That was still the target when Scout broke ground in Blythewood in February 2024.

By the Traveler and Terra unveiling in October 2024, production had moved to 2027. Keogh then said in March that he expects the first customer to get a vehicle “sometime in 2028,” and that’s now the official line in Scout’s own press materials.

It might not even be the end of it. Industry forecaster AutoForecast Solutions has the Traveler starting production in September 2028 and the Terra in March 2030. Scout hasn’t confirmed those dates, but it hasn’t given more precise ones either.

The product itself has also changed under the hood. Scout debuted as a pure EV brand, then added the “Harvester” range-extender option at the reveal. According to Keogh, Scout has more than 160,000 reservations, and 87% of them are for the gas-generator version. Those are $100 refundable reservations, not orders.

Der Spiegel reported earlier this year that integrating the range extender, which wasn’t part of the original plan, was among the technical problems pushing the timeline back.

In a recent development, for comparison, Tesla unveiled the Cybertruck in November 2019 and delivered the first ones four years later, a delay that was widely mocked. Scout is now on a similar four-year path from reveal to customer, and that’s for the SUV it’s launching first.

According to recent reports, A working body shop with 750 robots isn’t vaporware. Scout has a real factory, a real workforce, and two vehicles that people clearly want. 160,000 reservations is a big number for a brand that hasn’t sold a single vehicle in 46 years.

In a recent development, but validation builds are an early step, not a finish line. Scout still has to go through pre-production, prove its processes, and ramp to rate, and every one of those stages is where newly introduced automakers usually lose time. Rivian and Lucid both learned that the hard way.

It has been revealed that september 28? So we're 23 months away? I'm surprised the validation build yadda yadda stuff is supposed to take so long. It's not like VW doesn't know how to do this stuff, and that's a lot of money and equipment to sit mostly idle while 180,000 reservations holders are waiting for their cars. Maybe they're waiting for the market to change or are considering a whole other brand or product line?

Sources indicate that and the market Scout was designed for in 2022 no longer exists. The EV tax credit is gone, and most of Scout’s own reservation holders picked the gas generator. In the US, the range-extender market is still early, unlike in China, where they are already popular.

But by 2028, Ford, Ram, and Jeep all strategy to have range-extended trucks and SUVs on sale. Scout’s main advantage was being early with a cool, rugged, American-built electric truck. That advantage shrinks every quarter.

We’re still rooting for these vehicles. The Traveler and Terra are among the best-looking designs in the segment. But a $100 reservation is easy to walk away from, and the question is how many of those 160,000 people are still waiting in 2028.

#121195. Life in Isolation: Are We Living in a Human Zoo?
