For a solar farm or data center operator, that means a single manufacturer can take equipment out of service, resell parts with remaining useful life, and recycle the rest. Customers can track where the materials go and bring them back into their own supply chains.

Korea Zinc will hold a majority stake. Solarcycle’s Suvi Sharma will lead Jupiter as CEO, and PedalPoint’s Kevin Hahm will be CFO. Microsoft and Prologis Ventures are among Solarcycle’s existing investors.

As Electrek reported in January, Solarcycle’s Cedartown, Georgia, plant was processing thousands of old solar panels a week when it opened. Solarcycle said the plant could handle up to 5 gigawatts’ worth of panels annually at full capacity, recovering materials such as glass, aluminum, copper, and silver.

Industry observers note that the Tennessee plant adds a US refining step. Korea Zinc is developing the facility, called Project Crucible, with US government backing. It expects to start production in phases in 2029. The plant is designed to process about 1.1 million tons of raw materials per year and produce roughly 540,000 tons of finished products.

#121163. The Gift of Gratitude

The Gift of Gratitude

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1450 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 22, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.
  • Certain times of the year or milestone moments can increase the frequency with which we turn to appreciating the good, though this practice actually has value every single day of the year.
  • Sources indicate that the positive psychology movement has helped individuals focus more on what is strong rather than only on what is wrong.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 22, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.

Certain times of the year or milestone moments can increase the frequency with which we turn to appreciating the good, though this practice actually has value every single day of the year.

Sources indicate that the positive psychology movement has helped individuals focus more on what is strong rather than only on what is wrong. As a therapist who works with individuals at various life stages and in situations of distress, I know and embrace the fact that we can’t ignore the overwhelming symptoms, heartache, trauma, and pain; however, I also believe that every individual has strengths and reserves of resilience that deserve to be incorporated and highlighted.

Some people find this practice of being thankful and looking for gratitude moments to be relatively easy, but others find this much more difficult and unnatural.

Several tips are offered here for consideration to build the gratitude muscle.

It has been revealed that like the recent movement to incorporate more bloom-scrolling rather than just doom-scrolling on our phones, the notion of being on the lookout for more positivity can turn out to be a welcome shift for many. We know the gloom and doom exist, and we have plenty of opportunities to focus on it, but also actively seeking out more of the positive, the good, and the upbeat can be incredibly beneficial. Rather than dismissing the negative news or ignoring the overwhelming, we are making room for balance in our bodies and brains.

We can be in charge of our media meal plan and how we choose to budget our time and attention.

The idea of being on the lookout for gratitude moments is sometimes mistaken for waiting for those “big-ticket” items in life, like a windfall of money, a long-awaited vacation, or a promotion at work. While momentous moments are terrific, they tend to be rarer. However, the small moments of appreciating a delicious meal, a story about an everyday hero, a more scenic route home, the feel of a favorite blanket, or a beautiful bird on a branch are available to us on a much more regular basis.

Recent findings suggest that there is a Japanese concept of Ma, which translates to the gap, interval, or space between things. This is often referenced in Japanese architecture, art, or conversation, but the notion of embracing space or pause can also be utilized in this pursuit of the positive. The gap or interval is not empty or useless; instead, it represents a meaningful void full of potential. So even in those moments between hearing difficult news, awaiting dreaded test results, or anticipating the next migraine headache, we can attempt to orient to something small, quiet, amusing, or pleasant for which we can feel grateful.

We can absolutely embrace the big, but we might as well also be on the lookout for the small because they are much more plentiful, readily available, and repeatable.

Being aware of possible triggers in our environment can have value and usefulness, but orienting toward noticing the glimmers internally and externally is often underutilized.

Glimmers are those small moments of calm or joy that can cue safety and relaxation for the nervous system. The notion of looking for glimmers was introduced by Deb Dana and based on work by Stephen Porges1, and this practice cues the body toward a state of safety and grounding rather than the fight-flight-freeze mode of response that is activated under threat.

Even on really bad days (or maybe even especially on really bad days), we can choose to notice some good or gratifying things.

Glimmers are the opposite of triggers; both exist in our world, and we deserve to be able to know how to be alert to both.

When we are actively looking for more positive, joyful, beautiful, interesting, or unique in our daily world, we begin to see more of it. Sometimes that elegant, sturdy tree, beautifully colored house, smell of our favorite beverage, or sparkling ray of sunlight coming through the window at a certain time of day has gone unnoticed until we take the time to notice. And once we notice, we tend to orient to seeing it again and again—along with that more satisfying sense of appreciation on repeat.

It has been revealed that orienting to some good news, a funny joke, the stuffy nose that finally cleared up, an enthusiastic pet greeting, or a beloved song on the playlist can all be wonderful in the moment, but what really allows the biggest benefit is to allow the positivity to fully soak in. Like attending to a spill on the counter, dipping a sponge into the corner of the spill for just a moment won’t be as effective as slowly, carefully moving the sponge around the spill to fully absorb the liquid.

When we pause to fully notice the benefits, orient the multi-sensorial delights, and stay with it for several moments, we are more wholeheartedly allowing the affirmative and encouraging to register in our systems. And if we choose to later repeat this positive moment in a journal or in a recounting to someone else, the benefits multiply and the positivity is reinforced.

In a recent development, intentionally, mindfully staying aware of the positive is a happiness hack. And savoring the moment can be a superpower.

Various research studies support the notion that optimistic, grateful people are happier, calmer, more empathetic, less stressed, have better physical health, and even live longer2. Neuroimaging results (MRI and fMRI) also show that practicing gratitude engages key brain regions involved in reward processing and emotional regulation3. These findings support the incredible connection between mind and body.

Industry observers note that studied gratitude interventions include gratitude journals, gratitude letters or texts, and other methods of counting more blessings than burdens. Although there are various self-administered psychological interventions that can improve overall well-being (such as spending time in nature, mindfulness, or acts of kindness), psychological science does consistently show that gratitude practices improve overall mental and physical health.

In a recent development, even if this skill of looking for gratitude, positivity, and thankfulness doesn’t come easily or naturally to you, strive to refrain from self-blame about this. People have a wide variety of circumstances that can influence their ability to orient toward the good, and some of this is influenced by such things as external life circumstances and even genetics. The negativity bias in human brains is also well established and did have an evolutionary benefit4, but times are different now. A broader, more balanced perspective can help. And because brains are neuroplastic, practice in these skills makes for more permanence with these skills.

Be on the lookout for the lovely, and you, too, can optimize your inner optimist.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A FEW MONTHS ago, my friend Jack Espy stopped by Men’s Health HQ, and as we were talking shop and swapping stories with MH senior editor Ryan Brower about our favorite fitness-workout-wellness gear, I asked them both to name their single favorite product.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

A FEW MONTHS ago, my friend Jack Espy stopped by Men’s Health HQ, and as we were talking shop and swapping stories with MH senior editor Ryan Brower about our favorite fitness-workout-wellness gear, I asked them both to name their single favorite product.

Jack chose his Garmin watch and raved about its amazing battery life. Ryan named his Adidas Adizero Evo SL running shoes. As for me? It was hard: the one thing, among allll the things, that actually moves the needle? After thinking for a full 20 seconds, it finally hit me:.

Weird and kind of random, right?

I thought so, too. I’ve never cared that much about how much I weigh, mostly because I didn’t have to and I didn’t want to. I’ve always been on the leaner side, so for most of my adult life, the extent of what I knew about my weight came down to whether my pants fit.

It has been revealed that then, about a decade ago, I started getting more serious about putting on muscle, and my trainer at the time, the massive-armed and bigger-brained David Otey, introduced me to a kind of body-composition testing, a.k.a. “bioelectrical impedance analysis,” or BIA. The tech has been used to estimate body composition for decades, and you’ve probably seen one of the more sophisticated machines at your gym or doctor’s office. Step onto a platform, grab a pair of handles, wait 30 seconds, and the machine spits out a breakdown of how much of you is body fat, skeletal muscle mass, and more.

Recent findings suggest that david walked me through how BIA works: The machine sends a teeny-tiny electrical current through your body. Electricity moves more easily through lean tissue than through fat, so by measuring how that current travels through you, the machine can estimate how much fat and muscle you’re carrying.

In 2019, I bought an InBody Dial H20N for my bathroom. By then, BIA was well established in the consumer “smart scale” market, and InBody’s scale was among the more advanced at-home options, using sensors at both your hands and feet to take a more complete reading of your body than the foot-only models that were common at the time. The app tracks every measurement, so I can see not just what my body looks like on any given day but how it has changed over time.

To understand why I love the damn thing, it’s notable to know that I weigh roughly the same today as when I first brought the scale home seven years ago.

A conventional (dumb) scale would look at seven years of strength training, workouts I wanted to skip, workouts I probably should have skipped, and a totally unreasonable amount of thought about what I put into my body and deliver its verdict: Congrats, you weigh the same!

According to recent reports, but the InBody tells a different story. When I look back at my results from 2019, it estimated that I carried about 84 pounds of skeletal muscle mass and 33 pounds of body fat. Today, it demonstrates I’ve got around 95 pounds of skeletal muscle and 24 pounds of body fat. Yep: According to the scale, I’ve added 11 pounds of muscle while losing about 9 pounds of fat—all while my total body weight has barely moved. (I won’t mention that I did all this during a stage of life when building muscle, and simply holding on to it, gets harder than it was when I was 25. But I will mention Men’s Health has done an amazing guide to body recomposition that is worth checking out.).

According to recent reports, now, a necessary reality check: Those body-comp numbers aren’t exact measurements in the same way that the number staring back at me from a dumb scale is a measurement. They’re estimates. My hydration levels can throw them off. What I just ate can throw them off. A hard workout can really throw them off.

Recent findings suggest that still, in studies comparing the InBody to much fancier ways of measuring body composition, the scale holds up surprisingly well for something that lives in your bathroom. There’s even a newly introduced model, the H40, that Inbody claims is even more precise. (I keep meaning to buy it, but then something breaks in my house and a new scale gets knocked down the priority list.).

Industry observers note that none of this means that I obsess over whether I have 94.7 pounds of muscle on Tuesday and 93.9 on Thursday. What makes this useful to me aren’t the exact numbers; it’s the direction they’re headed in. I still don’t really care how much I weigh—I wear the same pants size as when I was 25 and 35, and all my blood work is fine. But I’m trying to carry more muscle, less fat, and a stronger, more capable body into the second half of my life. I just want to know that some of my ass-busting efforts are paying off.

Industry observers note that A dumb scale can’t tell me that. But a smart scale—this smart scale—is giving me all the direction I need.

Richard Dorment is the editorial director of Men’s Health and Women’s Health.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that around the world, the number of uncontacted Indigenous tribes continues to dwindle. Indigenous rights advocates estimate that half of the nearly 200 communities still existing in comparative isolation could disappear within a decade, without proper safeguards against climate change, land loss, fame-seeking opportunists, and illegal industrial encroachments. Unfortunately, the situation has apparently grown so dire that some Indigenous groups are reaching out for help—and exposing themselves to potentially deadly foreign diseases in the process.

In a recent development, on November 17, the nonprofit advocacy group Survival International reported a recent incident in which 20 members of the Awá people intentionally contacted local government officials in the Brazilian Amazon. Although proficient hunter-gatherers, the group requested yams before taking them back into the rainforest.

“This is a troubling indication of how the continued invasion of uncontacted peoples’ forests puts otherwise self-sufficient Indigenous people in real danger,” Survival International director Caroline Pearce stated in a statement.

The Awá are one of the world’s last uncontacted Indigenous tribes, whose ties to the Brazilian rainforest stretch back centuries. They faced their first attacks from European settlers during the 1800s, which eventually forced them to adopt a nomadic lifestyle to avoid future encounters. Brazil finally supplied the Awá with settlement areas during the mid-1980s, but it still took years before the government properly invested in demarcated land. In the meantime, numerous deadly interactions with loggers, farmers, and other illegal intruders had reduced the Awá community to barely 300 people. Of those, advocates estimate only about one-third of the hunter-gatherers remain completely isolated from the outside world.

“The Brazilian government must commit the resources necessary to protect [the region of] Arariboia from the loggers and ranchers who are razing it, in flagrant defiance of the law,” Pearce added.

According to recent reports, in addition to the advocacy work by Survival International, the Awá are supported by a team of Indigenous members of the Guajajara community known as the Forest Guardians. These volunteers have spent years pushing back against illegal cattle ranchers and loggers attempting to claim land in Arariboia, often dying as a result of their efforts.

“The Forest Guardians have always worked to protect the Awá against encroachment, even at the cost of losing warriors in battle,” the organization remarked. “We demand immediate action from the relevant authorities…to ensure what the Awá believe is best for them, safeguarding their lives, health, safety and dignity. FOR THE AWÁ, FOR THE TENETEHAR [language], AND FOR THE FOREST!”.

Healthier Salt Substitute May Prevent Millions of Deaths From Heart Disease

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (871 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A simple swap for salt could spare millions of cardiovascular disease-related deaths, new research suggests.
  • In a study published in Nature Health on November 4, researchers at The George Institute for Global Health modeled the potential impact of 193 countries switching from regular table salt to potassium-enriched salt.
  • They found the switch could prevent nearly 3 million deaths and more than 10 million latest cases of heart and kidney disease worldwide each year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A simple swap for salt could spare millions of cardiovascular disease-related deaths, new research suggests.

In a study published in Nature Health on November 4, researchers at The George Institute for Global Health modeled the potential impact of 193 countries switching from regular table salt to potassium-enriched salt.

They found the switch could prevent nearly 3 million deaths and more than 10 million latest cases of heart and kidney disease worldwide each year.

In the United States, this simple salt swap could prevent nearly 105,000 deaths and about 492,000 new cases a year, the researchers estimated.

About 130.6 million U.S. adults have cardiovascular disease, according to the American Heart Association (AHA).

Liping Huang, PhD, a senior data analyst in the Food Policy Division at The George Institute for Global Health and co-lead author of the study, told Healthline the team started with current blood pressure levels by sex, age, and country.

Sources indicate that the researchers then estimated how replacing all salt with a salt substitute would change people’s sodium and potassium intake, blood pressure, and disease risk, she remarked.The team modeled a blend of 75% sodium chloride and 25% potassium chloride. The study estimated these yearly results worldwide:.

The authors wrote that the model relied on data from a few years ago and on many assumptions, and that any large-scale switch would take years.

Potassium-enriched salt replaces some of the sodium chloride in regular table salt with potassium chloride, according to The George Institute.Asked where other salts like kosher salt and sea salt fit in, Huang remarked those salts may contain some trace elements “which has those health halos around them, but essentially they’re still primarily sodium chloride.”Huang noted that potassium-enriched salt tastes “about the same as a regular table salt.” She said it’s possible a small number of people with a sensitive palate could taste a difference.

According to recent reports, huang stated that “it’s really hard for people to cut back their salt intake.”“But the easier way is just to replace part of the sodium chloride in our normal salt with potassium chloride, because increasing potassium intake also helps to reduce blood pressure,” she said.The two minerals play opposite roles in the body, according to Cheng-Han Chen, MD, a board certified interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA. Chen wasn’t involved in the study.

“While sodium causes water retention and increased blood pressure, potassium will help the kidneys remove sodium from the body and lower blood pressure,” Chen told Healthline.Huang said she worked on an earlier trial of about 21,000 people in 600 rural villages in northern China in 2021.

People who used potassium-enriched salt had a 14% lower risk of stroke, a 13% lower risk of cardiovascular events, and a 12% lower risk of early death than those who used regular salt, according to a 2021 study in The Latest England Journal of Medicine that summarized the trial’s results.

The World Health Organization (WHO) endorsed potassium-enriched salt in a 2025 guideline, saying it can reduce blood pressure and the risk of cardiovascular disease.

Recent findings suggest that the AHA noted potassium-based salt substitutes can help lower blood pressure in some adults. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued labeling guidance in 2020 allowing an alternate name for potassium chloride on ingredient labels to include the word “salt.”“We think that blood pressure begins to improve as soon as 1 week after cutting back on sodium intake. The full benefit typically takes up to 4 weeks,” Chen said.

“We generally recommend a daily sodium limit of 2,300 milligrams (mg), ideally under 1,500 mg a day. Most people consume over 3,000 mg of sodium a day, well above the recommended limit,” Chen said.The WHO recommends less than 2,000 mg of sodium per day and suggests at least 3,510 mg of potassium a day.In the United States, more than 70% of salt intake comes from processed and restaurant foods, according to the AHA.

Huang said that some people with advanced chronic kidney disease should avoid potassium-enriched salt.When the kidneys don’t work well, the body may not clear extra potassium efficiently, she said. That can lead to hyperkalemia, or high potassium levels in the blood, which can raise the risk of cardiac arrest, Huang said.Among people with stage 3 to stage 5 kidney disease, switching to salt substitutes could prevent about 750,000 deaths a year by lowering blood pressure and cause about 100,000 deaths a year from hyperkalemia, the researchers estimated.The AHA said that people with kidney disease or who take medications that affect potassium should check with a healthcare professional before using these products.

Sources indicate that an estimated 37 million U.S. adults have chronic kidney disease, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Potassium-enriched salt is available at supermarkets in the U.S. Many major U.S. grocery chains, including Kroger, Walmart, and Publix, carry two types of products, according to their websites:.

Potassium-enriched salt typically costs about twice as much as regular salt, according to the study.Huang said she hoped people would see the results and start thinking of the switch as “a simple thing I can do for their own health.”.

Greenworks’ OPTIMUS is built around the tech giant’s 400V high-voltage electrical platform and mates a pair of compact electric motors that combine for 110 equivalent (?) hp. Those motors draw power from a 19 kWh lithium-ion battery pack with enough efficiency to hit a 40 MPH top speed and cover up to 68 miles of range under typical operating conditions.

Industry observers note that when it’s time to haul, OPTIMUS offers buyers a 2,500 lb. towing capacity and 1,300 lb. payload capacity along with 11 full inches of ground clearance and a beefy, 6,000 lb. electric winch. Independent suspension, oversized all-terrain tires, torque vectoring differentials, and multiple terrain modes round out the spec sheet and a picture of a machine that’s designed to handle some seriously demanding off-road applications.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when the mid-engine C111 sports-car concept made its debut at the Frankfurt auto show in 1969, would-be buyers sent blank checks to Mercedes-Benz headquarters. Despite the fervent interest, however, the C111 never went into production, although a handful of prototypes were built over the years. Now Mercedes-Benz has announced that it will auction off one of those cars, making it (at long last) the first C111 to reach private hands. And would-be buyers who wish to take home the C111 will need to muster that same blank-check energy.

See all results for used Mercedes-Benz for sale near 34786.

The C111 was conceived as the modern-day successor to the W198 300SL Gullwing of the 1950s. The two-seat supercar featured a mid-mounted rotary engine, a fiberglass body, and gullwing doors. The following year, an evolved C111-II was unveiled at the 1970 Geneva auto show with a 345-hp 2.4-liter four-rotor engine. The 1973 global oil embargo and the costs to meet rising emissions standards caused the company to shelve the proposal for series production, although several more C111 prototypes were made, including a C111-II-D with a diesel engine in 1976 and a diesel-powered C111-III in 1978. A total of 17 cars were made; 13 still exist. Mercedes has kept them all, until now.

The car being sold is a C111-II built in August 1970. It’s fitted with a 2.4-liter rotary engine making 345 horsepower at 7700 rpm, a five-speed manual transmission, anti-lock brakes, twin fuel tanks, and a Becker Europa radio. Weighing 2734 pounds, the C111-II had a claimed top speed of 186 mph and a 0-to-60-mph time of 4.8 seconds. It was used as a test car, including at the Hockenheimring.

It has been revealed that like most of the C111s, this car is painted Weissherbst orange; the seats are upholstered in houndstooth fabric. The car sits on modern 8-x-15-inch alloy wheels; the original magnesium wheels from 1970 are included, but with the caveat that they “are now suitable only for display purposes.” The anti-lock brake system is not functional.

The car has been on display at the Mercedes-Benz Museum since 2006. It was sympathetically restored in 2024 in preparation for an appearance at Pebble Beach. The odometer shows 24,766 km (15,389 miles).

It has been revealed that the car is being auctioned by RM Sotheby’s this coming February in Paris. The proceeds of the sale will help fund the museum, including an initiative to digitize its contents, part of the “Mercedes-Benz Museum 2.0” project.

See all results for used Mercedes-Benz for sale near 34786.

Sources indicate that to reassure the future buyer that the value of their C111 won’t be diluted by additional examples coming onto the market, Mercedes-Benz has committed to a 25-year moratorium on any future sales of the remaining cars. Mercedes-Benz collectors, call your bankers.

  • Industry observers note that the migration begins with the first rainfall of the wet season, typically in October or November, but can be as late as December or January.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The crabs are coming. Millions upon millions of them. Christmas Island red crabs (Gecarcoidea natalis) have officially begun their annual migration on the tiny Australian territory in the Indian Ocean.

Industry observers note that the migration begins with the first rainfall of the wet season, typically in October or November, but can be as late as December or January. Red crabs from all over Christmas Island will leave their homes in the forest at the same time and start their march towards the ocean. Once they reach the ocean, they will mate and spawn. The male crabs lead the migration, while the females join in along the way.

It has been revealed that according to Christmas Island National Park, the speed and timing of the migration is determined by the moon’s phases. “Red crabs always spawn before dawn on a receding high-tide during the last quarter of the moon,” the park rangers write. “Incredibly, they know exactly when to leave their burrows to make this lunar date.”.

However, the crabs will wait until the first rainfall to begin their journey, so they sometimes have to hurry. If the rains arrive close to their optimal spawning date, the crabs will move to the ocean very swiftly. If the rain comes early, the crustaceans may take their time, “stopping to eat and drink on their way to the coast.” If rain begins too late to make the spawning date, some of the crabs will remain in their burrows and begin their migration the following month.

The result is spectacular. Tens of millions of bright red crustaceans the size of a soda can spread out over the 12-mile-wide island on their way to the ocean. They begin their march inland and will reach their destination in about nine days. In 2008, naturalist and documentarian Sir David Attenborough described the annual event as one of his best television moments.

Over the next few days Parks Australia will run livestreams of the migration for about 60 minutes. The exact timing and number of livestreams can’t be scheduled in advance since it is completely dependent on the crabs.

“We will aim to livestream in the morning, but the crabs will have the final say on when and how many days they will venture across the bridge,” the rangers write.

Filming occurs at the red crab bridge, a 16-foot-tall structure built to help the crabs cross the busy road. The crabs will migrate past this bridge for about three to four days.

Why Being Home for the Holidays Makes You Feel 15 Again

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 22, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

In a recent development, every year, my clients tell me some version of the same story. I've been making so much progress, but after five minutes at my parents' house, it all goes out the window.

This topic frequently comes up in my sessions during the holiday season. They've spent months learning to better manage their emotions, or set healthier boundaries, and they’re enjoying the benefits of that work in their day-to-day lives.

Then, when they go home for the holidays, they automatically fall back into old habits. They're arguing with their siblings like teenagers, getting defensive when their parents offer unsolicited advice, and agreeing to things they don't want to do just to keep the peace.

Recent findings suggest that does slipping back into familiar family dynamics mean you haven't actually changed? That underneath all that growth, you're still the same person you were at 17?

Industry observers note that long story short, the answer is “no.” Sliding into old roles is a completely normal, well-documented phenomenon in personality science. Let’s talk about why this happens—and what to do about it.

Recent findings suggest that personality traits are a descriptive summary of how you typically think and behave. Do you generally experience big emotions or are you less reactive? Do you usually blueprint ahead or fly by the seat of your pants? Are you typically the person driving the conversation, or do you often find yourself hanging back to observe during social situations?

Sources indicate that importantly, personality is not black and white. Even though we often think about personality traits as categories (e.g., introvert vs. extrovert), traits actually exist on a continuum. People can fall anywhere along that spectrum (e.g., always introverted, often introverted, 50/50 depending on the situation, often extraverted, always extraverted).

Where you fall on a particular personality trait reflects how you tend to think, feel, and behave on average, across different situations. For example, you might be more extraverted when you're out with friends and much quieter in a work meeting.

Recent findings suggest that you can shift that average, making it more likely that you'll think, feel, and behave in ways that align with your values. But even as your personality shifts, some situations will still bring out more or less of a particular trait. In other words, if you've become generally more confident and even-keeled in your everyday life, a few days of feeling insecure or emotionally reactive around your family doesn't mean you've lost the progress you've made.

According to recent reports, and those personality averages do shift across our lives. Research highlights that, on average, people become more emotionally stable, more conscientious, and better able to get along with others as they age.

Much of this personality change takes place between ages 20 and 40, a period when many people leave their family homes and gain greater freedom to choose who they spend time with and how they spend their days.

Sources indicate that these new environments can encourage different patterns of behavior. Maybe growing up, you learned that raising your voice was the only way to get your point across. But in your adult friendships and romantic relationships, communicating calmly may be much more effective. As these healthier ways of interacting are reinforced over time, you may gradually become a more agreeable person.

It has been revealed that even if you've changed considerably over the years, your family may expect you to behave like your old self, and those expectations may pull you to fall back into old habits. For example, if you grew up trying to keep the peace by sacrificing your needs, you might find yourself agreeing to sleep in a separate room from your partner to appease your parents, even if you’ve been actively making progress toward being more assertive.

And the stress of the holidays doesn't help. When we're tired or otherwise stretched thin, we're more likely to fall back on well-practiced responses. The behaviors your family pulls from you were learned early and reinforced repeatedly, so under stress, your brain dusts them off because they require less energy than the newer patterns you might be working on.

The good news is that being around your family gives you an opportunity to practice the fresh ways of thinking and behaving you’ve been working on. Think of it like playing a video game on hard mode: The skills are the same, but the challenges are tougher. You can't necessarily change how your family treats you, but you can make small changes in how you respond to them. And over time, those small changes can help create a different dynamic. If you want to start showing up differently, The Personality Action Proposal helps you identify one specific action that could make the biggest difference in changing an old pattern and create a plan to put it into practice.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that residents of Newly introduced Smyrna Beach, Florida, can finally breathe a sigh of relief. A dangerous menace to society has been taken off the streets after police apprehended a 75-year-old man accused of leading deputies on a high-stakes electric bike chase at speeds reaching a blistering 16 mph (26 km/h).

According to the Volusia Sheriff’s Office, 75-year-old Robert Joseph Mitchell was riding his electric bicycle along the beach on November 13 when a sheriff’s deputy clocked him traveling 16 mph in a 10 mph zone (26 km/h in a 16 km/h zone).

The deputy attempted to stop Mitchell, who allegedly responded with a middle finger and some choice words before continuing on his way.

What followed was apparently the world’s slowest police chase.

Industry observers note that mitchell reportedly continued riding along the beach, eventually exiting onto city streets, where he allegedly rode against traffic before making it back to his home. Deputies followed him, and when Mitchell attempted to retreat into his garage, he reportedly resisted arrest by grabbing onto a golf cart and refusing to let go.

According to recent reports, the ordeal ended with Mitchell in custody, facing four charges, including felony fleeing or attempting to elude law enforcement, resisting an officer without violence, speeding on the beach, and riding outside the designated beach driving area. His bond was set at $4,000.

Recent findings suggest that and just like that, another dangerous electric bicycle criminal was brought to justice. This was clearly a success story like no other, and American streets are now safer.

Now, before anyone gets too worked up, let’s be clear: I’m not suggesting that e-bike riders should be allowed to ignore traffic laws, endanger pedestrians, or flee from police. Reports indicate that Mitchell was riding recklessly around beachgoers, including children, and that’s certainly something worth addressing. And once he allegedly decided to flee from deputies, he turned what could have been a minor infraction into a much more serious situation.

But can we also acknowledge how absurd this whole thing is?

We’ve reached a point where a 75-year-old man riding a bicycle at 16 mph can end up the subject of a police pursuit and felony charges, while we’ve largely accepted that multi-ton vehicles routinely kill and seriously injure people on our roads as an unavoidable cost of modern transportation.

According to recent reports, every day, drivers speed through neighborhoods, roll through stop signs, stare at their phones, and operate vehicles capable of killing pedestrians with a moment’s inattention. Or perhaps I shouldn’t say ‘capable’, but rather that they do. 40,000 people every year die in the US from car violence. Yet somehow, electric bicycles have become one of the great transportation menaces of our time, despite contributing much, much less to major bodily harm or death.

It has been revealed that and yes, there are absolutely legitimate concerns about dangerous riding. I’ve repeatedly argued that we need better enforcement, especially when it comes to teenagers riding high-powered electric dirt bikes and e-motos at 40 mph (64 km/h) down sidewalks and bike paths. Those aren’t electric bicycles, and treating them as such has created a real problem for everyone.

But if we’re going to devote police resources to cracking down on dangerous two-wheeled behavior, perhaps we could start there instead of turning a 1 mph beach ride into the crime of the century.

Industry observers note that what is absurd is that he didn't simply stop and follow the officer's directions to slow down. If he is going to try to flee from the police by riding dangerously including going against traffic then he should face charges. As presumably a first time offender, he'll be given probation if he agrees not to do it again.

To be fair, Mitchell’s alleged behavior after being stopped certainly didn’t help his case. But the larger point remains: our priorities around road safety have become wildly distorted.

We’ve normalized the dangers of cars so thoroughly that we barely blink at the daily carnage they cause, yet we’re increasingly treating comparatively low-speed electric bicycles as an existential threat to public safety.

Recent findings suggest that I’m all for enforcing sensible e-bike rules. I’m all for throwing the book at major infractions and scofflaws who pose a public menace. But I’m also for applying a little perspective.

Recent findings suggest that because if a 75-year-old man riding an electric bicycle at 16 mph is among our most pressing transportation safety concerns, then I have some very good news about the state of our roads. But unfortunately, there is no good news to share today.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fresh research suggests that caffeinated energy drinks and stimulant supplements are associated with significantly higher risks of serious heart problems, including cardiac arrest and heart attack in young adults.
  • The findings, to be presented at the American Heart Association (AHA) Scientific Sessions 2026 November 6–9 in Chicago, are preliminary and can’t prove that energy drinks cause heart problems.
  • Still, the results highlight concerning cardiovascular effects of these popular products, particularly among adults under 35 who consume them regularly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fresh research suggests that caffeinated energy drinks and stimulant supplements are associated with significantly higher risks of serious heart problems, including cardiac arrest and heart attack in young adults.

The findings, to be presented at the American Heart Association (AHA) Scientific Sessions 2026 November 6–9 in Chicago, are preliminary and can’t prove that energy drinks cause heart problems.

Still, the results highlight concerning cardiovascular effects of these popular products, particularly among adults under 35 who consume them regularly.

“These products are marketed as everyday pick-me-ups and sold next to soda and bottled water, so most people assume they carry no real risk,” study author Sai Samayamanthula, a fourth-year medical student at the University of Virginia School of Medicine in Charlottesville, VA, remarked in a news release.

“For many healthy people, if these products are consumed occasionally, the risk is probably small. However, individuals who consume energy drinks or other stimulant-containing supplements regularly can quickly exceed the recommended daily limit for caffeine, so it’s important for people to know that there may be a risk of cardiovascular harm with these products,” Samayamanthula continued.

Researchers from the University of Virginia School of Medicine analyzed 28,345 reports submitted to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) between 2017 and 2025.

Of these, 854 involved caffeinated energy drinks or stimulant supplements, while the remaining reports involved non-stimulant products.

In a recent development, compared with non-stimulant products, cardiac arrest was reported approximately 11 times more often with energy drinks and stimulant supplements. Heart attacks were reported 4.5 times more often, while ventricular arrhythmias and palpitations were reported about four times more frequently.

Nearly 45% of heart-related reports involved adults ages 18 to 34.

Industry observers note that “Our findings support the case for more systematic safety monitoring of caffeine- and stimulant-containing products. In addition, healthcare professionals should remember to ask their younger patients who have palpitations, chest pain or fainting spells if they recently or regularly consume these products,” Samayamanthula mentioned.

Gregory M. Marcus, MD, professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine, and chair of the 2026 AHA scientific statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease, wasn’t involved in the study, but remarked the research “raises concerns that products with very high amounts of caffeine may be harmful to the cardiovascular system.”.

“Although there are biological reasons why that connection could be possible, the study does not prove that caffeine products cause these events, because other factors may have influenced the results found in this analysis,” Marcus remarked in a news release.

“More research is needed to understand whether these stimulant products are truly responsible for the reported heart-related events.”.

Cheng-Han Chen, MD, board certified interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA, said the findings, although concerning, are not surprising. Chen wasn’t involved in the study.

“We know that energy drinks can have significant effects on the cardiovascular system, primarily because of their stimulant properties,” he told Healthline.

Recent findings suggest that “Caffeine can increase blood pressure and heart rate, while other ingredients, such as guarana and taurine, may further contribute to cardiovascular stimulation and increased stress hormone levels. What is particularly concerning is the potential for these products to trigger serious complications, including abnormal heart rhythms, especially in people with underlying cardiovascular conditions.”.

Chen agreed that occasional energy drink consumption is unlikely to have long-term consequences for heart health in most healthy individuals. However, he said that “frequent or excessive consumption can potentially increase the risk of hypertension and cardiac arrhythmias.”.

An AHA scientific statement published in July 2026 notes that up to 400 milligrams of caffeine daily is generally considered safe for most healthy adults. That’s roughly equivalent to four or five 8-ounce cups of brewed coffee, depending on how it’s prepared.

However, some energy drinks contain up to three times as much caffeine per fluid ounce as brewed coffee.

Certain energy drinks may also contain stimulants, such as guarana, yerba mate, theobromine, synephrine, and yohimbine.

These ingredients may compound caffeine’s effects on the cardiovascular system.

According to recent reports, “Caffeine stimulates the cardiovascular system, primarily by increasing sympathetic nervous system activity. This can cause the heart to beat faster, raise blood pressure, and increase the workload on the heart,” Chen said.

“Energy drinks may contain additional stimulants, such as guarana and taurine, which can further increase blood pressure and stress hormone levels. With excessive consumption, these effects can become more pronounced and potentially interfere with the heart’s normal electrical activity, increasing the risk of abnormal heart rhythms. People with underlying cardiovascular conditions, particularly hypertension or a predisposition to arrhythmias, may be especially vulnerable to these effects.”.

Industry observers note that other research has echoed these concerns. A 2025 review suggests that high-volume energy drink consumption can prolong the heart’s QTc interval, increase blood pressure, and raise heart rate beyond the effects of caffeine alone.

“There is growing concern about the cardiovascular effects of energy drinks and stimulant-containing supplements, particularly among younger adults,” Chen noted.

“One challenge is that younger individuals may not recognize that these products can have significant effects on their heart and blood pressure, especially when consumed frequently or in combination with other caffeinated products.”.

Young adults accounted for a substantial portion of the FDA reports included in the study, highlighting potential cardiovascular concerns for this age group.

People with existing heart conditions, a history of irregular heart rhythms, or heightened caffeine sensitivity may face additional risks. Those with undiagnosed genetic heart conditions may also be vulnerable.

A 2024 study identified cases of sudden cardiac arrest occurring shortly after energy drink consumption, particularly among people with underlying inherited heart conditions.

“As a cardiologist, I am particularly concerned about people who may have underlying cardiovascular conditions that have not yet been diagnosed,” Chen said.

It has been revealed that “Excessive stimulant intake can potentially trigger symptoms such as palpitations, chest discomfort, and lightheadedness. In susceptible individuals, it may also increase the risk of more serious complications, including abnormal heart rhythms.”.

Additionally, combining energy drinks with strenuous exercise or alcohol may introduce additional cardiovascular risks.

The findings suggest an association between energy drinks, stimulant supplements, and reported cardiovascular events, but they are preliminary and do not establish cause and effect.

The FDA database also relied on voluntary adverse-event reports, meaning some events may never be reported, while others may receive disproportionate attention.

Researchers also do not yet know how many people consumed these products without experiencing any problems. Without this variable, the reports cannot establish actual risk.

It has been revealed that other factors, including underlying health conditions, medications, and lifestyle habits, may also influence the results. More systematic research and controlled clinical trials are needed.

For most healthy adults, consuming up to 400 milligrams of caffeine per day is generally considered safe.

However, Chen noted that individual tolerance for caffeine may vary, and people with underlying cardiovascular conditions, particularly high blood pressure or abnormal heart rhythms, may need to limit or avoid caffeine altogether.

“Energy drinks can vary considerably in their caffeine content and serving sizes,” Chen noted.

In a recent development, “Depending on the product, a single can may contain anywhere from 80 to 300 milligrams of caffeine. This means that consuming even one or two energy drinks can put someone close to or above the recommended daily limit, particularly when combined with coffee, tea, or other caffeinated supplements.”.

Seek emergency medical attention if you experience chest pain, particularly if it’s accompanied by shortness of breath, fainting, or other symptoms of a possible heart attack.

If you live with a heart condition, ask your doctor about your daily caffeine intake to determine whether you need to cut back.

According to Chen, warning signs of excessive stimulant intake may include:.

“Depending on the severity of these symptoms, medical attention may be necessary,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that still, most people may not need to give up caffeine entirely. Monitoring your habits could help protect your heart health. This may include:.

“I encourage people to read product labels carefully and be aware of their total daily caffeine consumption,” Chen noted. “I particularly recommend that people with underlying cardiovascular conditions avoid energy drinks.”.

Industry observers note that A tiny, four-limbed soft robot resembling the cross between an octopus and an earthworm does more than inch across difficult terrain. With a process known as mechanoluminescence, the device glows as it moves and stretches without the need for external batteries or electronics. It’s not flimsy, either. Writing in a study recently published in the journal Small Structures, the soft robot’s inventors explained their design maintains its illuminating abilities after more than 1,000 stretching cycles.

Sources indicate that at South Korea’s Daegu Gyeongbuk Institute of Science and Technology (DGIST), engineer and study co-author Soon Moon Jeong believes the underlying dynamics at play are a promising newly introduced way to analyze and pinpoint deformations in a soft robot. It’s also potentially even more effective than existing softer options, since it doesn’t require additional components that might otherwise restrict the device’s movement.

Sources indicate that jeong’s team first designed a thin but resilient “tubular mechanoluminescent fiber” made from glowing particles of zinc sulfide and flexible polymers. They then filled elastic silicone tubes with the mixture, and wove them together into a mesh-like case for their pneumatic soft robot model. As the robot’s limbs stretch and contract, the zinc sulfide-infused polymer filling glows bright green specifically in the areas undergoing stress. Laboratory testing indicated their novel fibers withstood being pulled over twice their original length, and kept glowing after over 1,000 exercises.

It has been revealed that jeong stated his team is now focusing on improving the robot’s light emissions and resiliency. If successful, their mechanoluminescent fibers may be used in wearable medical devices or even artificial skins.

“The woven fiber-network configuration provides qualitative visual indication of deformation over the robotic body, offering a simple strategy for realizing self-visualizing soft robotic systems,” wrote the study’s authors, adding that their invention showcases the potential foundations for “next-generation self-visualizing intelligent soft systems.”.

Mercedes-Benz Will Sell a C111 Rotary Supercar Prototype for the First Time in History

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (742 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that there’s no shortage of rare, collectable, crazy-desirable classic Mercedes-Benz vehicles out there for the discerning car collector.
  • Sources indicate that but no matter how rich, how connected, how much of a master of the universe you are, you’ve never been able to buy one of Mercedes-Benz’s most ground-breaking machines: the rotary-powered C111.
  • In a recent development, fans of the brand certainly need no introduction to this wedge-shaped beauty, but for those of you who might not be as current on your Mercedes history, the C111 was revealed at the 1969 International Motor Show (IAA) in Frankfurt, less than two months after Neil Armstrong plopped his boots on the moon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that there’s no shortage of rare, collectable, crazy-desirable classic Mercedes-Benz vehicles out there for the discerning car collector. Some of the Three-Pointed Star’s cars have gone down in history among the most expensive automobiles ever sold; there’s the $11.8 million 1936 Mercedes-Benz 540 K Special Roadster by Sindelfingen, the $10.2 million 2002 Mercedes-Benz CLK GTR Roadster, and of course, the 1955 300 SLR Uhlenhaut Coupé that sold for over $140 million back in 2022, making it the world’s most valuable car.

Sources indicate that but no matter how rich, how connected, how much of a master of the universe you are, you’ve never been able to buy one of Mercedes-Benz’s most ground-breaking machines: the rotary-powered C111. Or at least, that was the case. Come next year, for the very first time, one lucky person will be able to take the Apollo-era wundercar home.

In a recent development, fans of the brand certainly need no introduction to this wedge-shaped beauty, but for those of you who might not be as current on your Mercedes history, the C111 was revealed at the 1969 International Motor Show (IAA) in Frankfurt, less than two months after Neil Armstrong plopped his boots on the moon. The idea was to create a gullwinged successor to the iconic W198-gen 300SL that dominated racing in the 1950s, packed with then-impressive technology: Wankel rotary engines, fiberglass bodywork, and multi-link rear suspension, all wrapped in a gorgeous period design.

Industry observers note that yet while 17 prototypes were ultimately made, the car never entered production. Rumor has it that interested parties practically channeled Philip J. Fry shouting “Shut up and take my money” by mailing blank checks to the company’s home office, but Mercedes said no dice, citing the Wankel motor’s inability to play nicely with the 1973 oil crisis. (That also kept the motor from winding up in the S-Class, as Mercedes-Benz Classic head of collection Dennis Heck said.) Instead, the copies served as company test beds for years, performing tasks like high-speed testing at Nardo with a variety of different powertrains and aerodynamic kits.

The car in question that will be up for grabs is the third one ever made, a C111-II variant known internally as “Car 33” that comes equipped with its original 2.4-liter 4-rotor engine making 345 horsepower and 289 lb-ft connected to a 5-speed manual gearbox. It was used as part of the Mercedes test fleet, trialing features like anti-lock brakes and a component to empty its twin fuel tanks at even rates—a handy feature in a car capable of 186 miles per hour.

The car was restored to working order two years ago at the Mercedes-Benz Classic Center, although the patina of the Weißherbst-colored exterior and gray-and-white houndstooth patterned interior was kept delightfully intact. As of last month’s photo shoot, its odometer revealed 24,766 kilometers—15,355 miles.

The C111 in question will hit the auction block on February 3, 2027, at the Palais du Louvre as part of RM Sotheby’s Retromobile Paris auctions, with the funds raised by the sale used to help the automaker further develop the Mercedes-Benz museum in Stuttgart, including the creation of a digital twin of the museum that will let people access it virtually.

Given its provenance, I would not expect it to go cheap. Neither does the tech giant. “We do believe it will come to a significant double-digit euro [price at auction],” CEO of Mercedes-Benz Heritage GmbH Marcus Breitschwerdt told Road & Track.

According to recent reports, “It’s gonna be in excess of twenty-five [million] euros,” RM Sotheby’s president Gord Duff added. “There will be strong activity. It’s one of those things you could never get until now.”.

Sources indicate that and if you’re thinking, Ehh, they’ve broken the seal on sales, I’ll wait until they auction off another one—well, you’d better be prepared to hold off until 2051 or so, because Mercedes says this sale includes a contractual commitment that it will not sell any more C111s for the next 25 years. Should you be interested in bidding, you can find out more here.

Will Sabel Courtney is a contributing editor at Road & Track. A 12-year veteran of journalism, he formerly worked at Gear Patrol, The Drive, and RIDES Magazine, and contributed to the New York Daily News and Jalopnik, among other outlets. You can often find him test-driving new cars in New York City, cursing the slow-moving traffic surrounding him.

#121148. Why the Most Politically Savvy Colleague Gets Things Done

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1104 w)

Why the Most Politically Savvy Colleague Gets Things Done

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1104 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 22, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • A project lead needs budget for a project.
  • Recent findings suggest that so in the week before the meeting, she has three separate conversations with people who will make or break the decision.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 22, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

A project lead needs budget for a project. She knows the formal process: Write the proposal, present it at the monthly meeting, and then wait for feedback. She also knows how decisions are actually made in her organization.

Recent findings suggest that so in the week before the meeting, she has three separate conversations with people who will make or break the decision. First, she talks with the finance director, who worries about cost overruns at the end of every quarter. Then, she talks with the operations head, whose team always gets dragged into projects that sometimes go nowhere. Next, she talks to the program lead who will "volunteer" to manage the project.

Industry observers note that by the time she presents, the decision has effectively been made. People raise issues briefly as a formality because they already feel assured, and some even answer their own questions because they like the solution they were shown in advance.

According to recent reports, there are a couple of ways to look at this approach. It's definitely an effective approach. Some people would call it clever, but not everyone would mean that as a compliment.

Industry observers note that the resourceful style is one of the "dark side" personality styles: everyday patterns that can help or hinder us at work, depending on how strongly they show up and in what form. Its most extreme form resembles what psychologists call Machiavellianism, a cynical, self-serving approach to other people.

It has been revealed that people who do this as a regular course of action share this way of viewing the world, navigating work through relationships—many of them transactional. They understand how power structures and networks truly exist in reality, separate from the official org chart or chain of command. They rapidly pick up on who makes decisions, or who suggests the ideas that get picked up more often than not.

They tend to be strategic, focused on outcomes, and can be very adaptable when the route to a goal changes or fresh obstacles emerge.

Researchers have studied the useful side of this for decades under the name "political skill." Ferris and colleagues (2005) developed a measure of it with four parts: social astuteness (reading people and situations), interpersonal influence, networking ability, and apparent sincerity (coming across as genuine).

Recent findings suggest that A meta-analysis by Munyon and colleagues (2015) found that political skill was linked to higher productivity, career success, a better reputation, and greater job satisfaction. It predicted task performance even after accounting for broad personality traits and general intelligence.

According to recent reports, when the researchers looked at the four aspects separately, networking, influence, and apparent sincerity predicted performance. Social astuteness on its own did not. Reading the room is a useful start, but the rarer skill is reading a room and influencing your place in it.

Sources indicate that at their best, resourceful people do exactly that. They get around obstacles that stall everyone else, and find the person who can make a decision or make the obstacles go away. They can get other people to support them to make unpopular decisions, and if they get the desired results, some people will respect and admire them for it.

Recent findings suggest that this can be done proactively and prosocially, or in ways that are counterproductive and manipulative. Organizations and even small teams are political whether or not anyone likes it, and someone who can find ways of making things work is necessary for any high-functioning team.

Industry observers note that the dark side emerges when people become collateral damage. Consider a colleague who builds trust with a peer during a brutal restructuring, learns that the peer is burned out and looking for another job, and later uses that confidence to edge them out of a key role when budgets tighten.

As I discussed in a post on destructive behavior in the remote office, a manipulative person can work this way with surgical precision, especially when much of the work happens across different and poorly organized communication channels.

It has been revealed that however, it is possible to operate in some gray areas while still maintaining respectful and mutually beneficial relationships. Arguably, it's a more successful strategy in the longer term.

The research on Machiavellianism shows the cost of being too ruthless. A meta-analysis by O'Boyle and colleagues (2012) found it was linked to more counterproductive work behavior, meaning behavior that harms colleagues or the organization. Its link to lower job performance was small and inconsistent, which fits the idea that this style can deliver short-term results while eroding the reliability and trust that long-term work requires.

It helps to compare this style with more combative, rule-breaking tendencies that are compulsive instead of calculated. Combative people tend to push boundaries, take visible risks, and ask forgiveness rather than permission. Resourceful people usually leave the rules intact and work the system instead. They do not need to skip the approval process when they have already lined up the approvers.

Industry observers note that that can make the resourceful style harder to spot, and its destructive form harder to challenge. Nothing improper has technically happened. The damage is a loss of trust amongst teams.

As I argued in "The Surprising Upside of Your Dark Side," the question to ask of personality styles is: How do you use them?

People who read power well will always have an advantage in certain types of work. Whether others experience them as a valuable ally or a threat depends less on how well they play the game than on what they are trying to accomplish.

Industry observers note that ferris, G. R., Treadway, D. C., Kolodinsky, R. W., Hochwarter, W. A., Kacmar, C. J., Douglas, C., & Frink, D. D. (2005). Development and validation of the Political Skill Inventory. Journal of Management, 31(1), 126–152. https://doi.org/10.1177/0149206304271386.

It has been revealed that macRae, I. (2022). Dark social: Understanding the darker side of work, personality and social media. Bloomsbury.

Sources indicate that munyon, T. P., Summers, J. K., Thompson, K. M., & Ferris, G. R. (2015). Political skill and work outcomes: A theoretical extension, meta-analytic investigation, and agenda for the future. Personnel Psychology, 68(1), 143–184. https://doi.org/10.1111/peps.12066.

In a recent development, O'Boyle, E. H., Jr., Forsyth, D. R., Banks, G. C., & McDaniel, M. A. (2012). A meta-analysis of the Dark Triad and work behavior: A social exchange perspective. Journal of Applied Psychology, 97(3), 557–579. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0025679.
